titleStmt.title: Speculum naturale, version SM trifaria, books 16-22

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin du corpus zoomathia sous zoo68/1l (Vincentius Belvacensis, Speculum naturale, version dite "SM trifaria"). Le fichier source zoo68/1l ne contient que l'extrait zoologiquement pertinent de cette vaste encyclopedie, soit les livres 16 a 22 : 16 "De avibus" (oiseaux, 703 citations), 17 "De piscibus" (poissons, 500), 18 "De animalibus domesticis" (betail, 457), 19 "De bestiis silvestribus" (betes sauvages, 640), 20 "De reptilibus" (reptiles, 778), 21 (physiologie animale generale, 163) et 22 (regime et comportement animal, 154), soit 3395 citations et 867 chapitres au total. SEUL LE LIVRE 16 "De avibus" (oiseaux, 171 chapitres, 703 citations) est traduit pour le moment ; il s'agit d'un premier jalon. Les livres 17 a 22 restent a traduire. La structure du div (oeuvre > section1 livre [n=16] > section2 chapitre > cit avec <bibl> d'attribution et <quote>) est integralement preservee ; les notes d'identification savante de l'editeur, qui ne font pas partie du texte de Vincentius lui-meme, ont ete exclues de la traduction, de meme que pour l'extraction du texte latin source. Le Speculum naturale cite abondamment des autorites deja traduites dans le corpus zoomathia (Aristote, Pline, Isidore, Ambroise et tout particulierement Thomas Cantimpratensis, cite sous "Ex libro de natura rerum" a travers tout ce livre) ; chaque passage a neanmoins fait l'objet d'une traduction propre, le texte latin cite differant toujours legerement d'une source a l'autre. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante. Correspond au texte latin deja present dans le corpus sous zoo68/1l (source Sourcencyme/IRHT).

div.head: DE OPERA QUINTE DIEI ID EST DE FORMATIONE VOLATILIUM ET NATATILIUM

cit.quote: On the fifth day God adorned the air with winged creatures and the water with swimming creatures. Both of these arose from the waters: for the passage from water into air is easy, by thinning, and from air into water, by thickening. Moses calls fish 'creeping things,' because they hurl their whole body forward with a certain rush, like serpents. They are not carried on feet, like wild beasts: to these God gave this blessing: Increase and multiply, etc. The reason is clear why the adornment of air and water was made on the same day, namely because these two elements hold a nature midway between the luminous body, that is the heavens or fire, and the opaque, that is the earth. Whence they agree in this, that each is receptive of light and darkness, each is capable of being rarefied and thickened, and each is also easily converted into the other, as has been said. Therefore the adornment of both was produced from one source, namely from water both winged and swimming creatures, and not winged creatures from the air, although they are the adornment of the air, because in its upper part, next to the fiery region, the air is clear and pure and so fine or subtle that nothing living could breathe or draw breath there, and thus could not live, as is evident on Mount Olympus: for this reason the air, as regards that part of itself, is not adorned with animals, since they could not live there, nor could it even support the bodies of birds, as this lower air can, thick and moist, which, receiving moist exhalations and stirred by winds, condenses into clouds and pours forth rain. This air, then, is adorned with its own animals, that is winged creatures, which can breathe from it because of the thickness of its moisture, and whose bodies it can support, just as water supports fish, while birds rely on it with their wings in flying, just as fish rely on water with their fins in swimming. And because this air, by reason of the moisture with which it is woven, being fine, is assigned to the moist nature, that is to water, it is therefore said that water is the common productive source of both, when it is said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things, etc. Moreover, for the coming-to-be of both, air and water agree, joined with the other elements, which are the extremes, namely fire and earth. And since water tends toward material nature, air toward active nature, while in winged creatures the active dominates over the material, and in fish the reverse, therefore winged creatures fittingly hold the air as the place of their dwelling, but fish the water. Whence too the flesh of fish is generative of cold humor, but that of winged creatures, of hot humor, according to their kind. Rightly, then, is water called the common productive source of both, because from waters raised into vapors of clouds comes the matter of winged creatures, but from waters growing rich below comes the matter of fish.

Isidore, in book 12 of the Etymologies: birds [aves] are so called because they do not have fixed paths, but run through pathless places [avia] wherever. They are called 'alites,' moreover, because they stretch their wings [alis] high and rise to lofty heights by the oarage of their wings. They are called 'volucres' from flying [volando]. For whence we say 'to fly,' from there we also say 'to walk.' Now 'vola' is said of the middle part of the foot or hand. In birds, then, the middle part of the wings is called the 'vola,' by whose movement the feathers are stirred, whence they are also called 'volucres.'

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: birds differ from one another by more or less in their limbs. All have feathers, or scales, or bark-like coverings, and wings, and a beak, and for the most part the neck matches the legs, namely long with long, short with short - except in birds having webbing between the toes. And their neck is like a fisherman's rod, but their beak like a hook for catching food. They have passages of the nose not clearly divided near the mouth, for the sake of breathing. And since they are curved and winged, they have little weight in the head and a narrow body. They have only two feet, since in the place of front feet they have wings. All birds, moreover, have a sharp and fleshy chest. Sharp indeed, because if it were broad, it would move much air and flight would be heavy - the sharper it is, then, the better they fly. Fleshy, however, because what is sharp is weak, unless it has a covering of much flesh, and is injured by the pressure of the air in flying. Birds have no teeth, but beaks in place of teeth. They have membranous eyelids, not fleshy ones, as quadrupeds do. They necessarily have sharp sight, since they see things from afar. They close their eye only by the lower eyelid, whereas walking creatures close by the upper. But the lizard kind does not close its eyes at all. Birds have a hollow lung, resembling foam, and small. They also have a navel at the time of birth, like other animals, but it is hidden as they grow. Birds do not urinate, however, because they drink little, and what remains of moisture passes into feather. It is proper to the kinds of birds to lack lips and teeth. Nor do they have ears or a nose, but they have other organs of these senses. The passage of the nose is in the beak, the passage of hearing is in the head. And none of these has hair or scales, but only feathers. In the front part of certain birds there is a crop, as in the cock and the partridge and the dove. For since a bird does not have a suitable organ for grinding food with teeth, it has this kind of organ to do this work. Its formation is from a large, deep skin, and in it is undigested food, and in these birds the gullet is found.

From the book On the Nature of Things: birds need much sight for the governance of their life. And those that close their eyes close them only by the lower eyelid, because of the hardness of the skin that covers the head. They nest in thorny places, and make their nests round, rough outside, soft within. Having lost their chicks, they grieve, and yet rebuild in the same places; struck, they raise themselves up high. And when they rise from the ground, they turn to face the wind, and steer themselves with their tails, and break through the air with their feathers by flying.

Ambrose: there is one name for birds, but their kinds are diverse. For there are those that live on flesh, those that feed on found seed, others on varied and chance food. There is also a diversity of pairings: those intent on plunder, like hawks and eagles, lack them. But, on the contrary, cranes and doves delight in the joining of very many. Some too are untamed, others migratory, some submit to the hand and grow accustomed to their master's table and are soothed by touch, others shrink away; some too delight in the same dwellings as men, others frequent the wilderness and compensate, by their love of freedom, for the difficulty of seeking their own food; some are noisy, others sing - the dove simple, the partridge cunning, the cock more boastful, the peacock more splendid. Again, some love to take counsel together and, joining their strength, to tend a kind of commonwealth and live as if under a king. Others love to look out for themselves, refuse rule, and, if captured, wish to escape unworthy servitude. Birds having hooked claws do not gather together at all, and each preys for itself. Some, however, fly in flocks; nature denies certain kinds even to certain places, just as with kinds of crops or shrubs.

Isidore, in the same place: just as birds differ in appearance, so too in the diversity of their nature. For some are simple, like the dove; some cunning, like the partridge; some submit to the hand, like hawks. Some shrink away, like the garamantes. Some delight in the company of men, like the swallow; others love a secluded life in the wilderness, like the turtledove. Some live on found seed alone, like the goose; others eat flesh and live by plunder, like the kite. Some are untamed, remaining always in their own places, like ostriches; others are migratory, returning at their proper seasons, like storks and swallows; others fly in flocks, like starlings and crows; others are solitary, for the sake of ambushing prey, like eagles and hawks; some are noisy in voice, like the swallow; others give forth most sweet songs, like the swan and the blackbird; others imitate the words and voices of men, like the parrot and the magpie.

Aristotle: some animals have kings and obey them, like cranes and bees. The manner of birds, too, differs according to their activities and the governance of their life. Some live on flesh, some on grain, some on both. Some rub themselves in ash upon the ground, some frequently swim, some do neither, and some rub themselves in ash and also wash themselves.

From the book On the Nature of Things: among birds, then, there is manifold difference. For some of them are wild, some domestic; some govern themselves, some live under direction, like cranes. There is also great difference of voices and even of character. The cock is wanton, the peacock careful, the dove lustful, the partridge cunning, and the domestic hen jealous.

Pliny, book 14: the first distinction of birds rests mostly on their feet. For they either have hooked claws, or toes, or are web-footed, like geese and nearly all water birds. And of those with hooked claws, some are diurnal, like hawks and eagles, some nocturnal, like the owl, the eagle-owl, and screech-owls. Some of these, too, live on flesh alone, like the hawk and sparrowhawk. Some not on flesh alone but on other food too, like the crow and the raven. Of these hook-clawed birds, however, more will be said fully below. The second kind, that is, those having toes, is divided into two species, namely into songbirds, that is, singing ones, and 'alites' [large birds]. For the former group, song of the mouth made the distinction; for the latter, size. Among these songbirds is the kind of the peacock. For the peacock sings, and the cock, geese and cranes, storks and swans, quails and swallows, the 'glutis' and the 'citramus,' the blackbird and the 'ochus,' the turtledove and the thrush and the starling and the like. Some of these are year-round, like the dove; some are here for three months, like the swallow. Some for three months, like thrushes and turtledoves; some remain in their places, some, like blackbirds and thrushes and starlings, go to nearby regions, where they seek winter pasture; others too, like turtledoves and wood-pigeons, depart, and where to is uncertain. There is also great wonder concerning the 'alites': some change their color and voice with the season of the year and suddenly become different, which, among the larger kind of alites, only cranes do, for in old age they turn black. The blackbird and the nightingale change color and voice. The thrush, color. The 'meanthe' has fixed days of hiding at the rising of Sirius, and comes forth at its setting, which we marvel at on those very days. The 'clarion,' too, which is entirely shining, comes forth around the solstices, and is not seen in winter. Of the web-footed, moreover, which is the third kind of winged creatures, it will be spoken below, where the feet of birds are treated.

div.head: DE MUTATIONE IN COLORE ET PLUMIS ET VOCE ET LOCO ET TEMPORE

cit.quote: Aristotle, in the same place: the colors and voices of certain birds also differ in winter and summer. The 'baharon' hisses with a sweet sound in summer, and its voice is poor in winter. In cranes, the color of the feather in youth is ash-grey, in old age it blackens. The 'kyke,' moreover, is a bird that cries with various voices and changes its voice nearly every day. Turtledoves do not appear except in summer, since they hide in the nest in winter. Likewise the kite and the swallow either hide in the hollows of trees or move themselves to warm places. The 'lehe' bird stays in summer in a place facing south and in shade, but in winter stays where the sun abounds. Furthermore, what birds hunt in summer is different from what they hunt in winter.

From the book On the Nature of Things: many birds, too weak for much flight, dreading winter, flee to the valleys in warm places, but before their departure fortify themselves, so as to eat much and grow fat, and thus better endure the want of hunger in winter. For most of them lie through the whole winter in the warm caves and hollows of the valleys, as if half-dead, huddled together, and live without food for a long time, their numbers contributing to the warmth. After winter, however, they come gradually, according to their strength.

[Of birds:] and owls are said to hide for few days, whose kind is not found on the island of Crete, and if any is brought there, it dies. The 'bodos' has no eagle. Partridges do not fly across the borders of Boeotia into Attica. In the territory of Fidenae, near the city, storks make neither chicks nor a nest. Songbirds, moreover, change color and voice. The blackbird, too, turns from black to reddish. The nightingale sings with a sweet melody in summer; soon, as the heat increases, its voice becomes altogether different, no longer modulated or varied, and its color too changes. Finally, in winter, it is not seen at all. Fig-peckers, too, and hoopoes change both form and color.

The Philosopher: a bird having white feathers does not change to black, though the reverse can happen. Noble birds, as is known, are changed [in molting] in cages made of twigs. Some, however, shed their old feathers only with laborious effort. To these help is given thus: a serpent is cooked for a long time in grain, and a hen fed with this grain, and that bird refreshed with it, thus changes fittingly.

Ambrose, in the same place: birds intent on plunder lack pairing. For, because of their eagerness for prey or their watchfulness in lying in ambush, they do not even agree among themselves, and so avoid mating; for avarice shuns the company of many. To these, then, nothing serves as a bond except the union of a single pair, whereas doves delight in the joining of many.

Aristotle, in the same place: a bird of prey is of sharp sight, since it needs to see its food from afar. But a bird that stays on the ground, like the hen, does not need sharp sight. In birds of prey, moreover, the feathers fall out most and return to vigor. The eagle and the other birds of prey produce only two chicks, or only once a year, and if they produce more, they cast them out. Likewise, what birds hunt in summer is different, as already said above, from what they hunt in winter. It is not proper to birds of one kind that they eat one another. The sparrow and many similar little birds feed on worms. Flesh-eating and hook-clawed birds are of good flight, having indeed many feathers and large, strong wings.

From the book On the Nature of Things: all predatory birds hunt prey of another kind than their own species, and in this they differ from fish. The sparrowhawk alone is without this mercy. Birds of this kind, that is, flesh-eating and predatory ones, when they take flight, are called back with leashes.

Aristotle, in the same place: birds do not have a nose, because their beaks do not have two separate openings, and so, since they need food and vigor, they have beaks made, as it were, of a bony nature. Nor do they have passages of smell except in the beak. In place of nose, lips, and teeth, then, they have beaks, both for food and for defense. These differ, moreover, according to the manner of need and use. For flesh-eating birds, the beaks are hooked, so that they can hold what they grasp. But the beaks of small birds are fine, suited to taking grain. Those, too, that eat worms and have webbing between their toes also spend much time in water. Some also have broad beaks, fit for digging, just as the pig, among animals, has an added tool for digging the earth. For they eat roots and have a life similar to pigs'. The shape of the beak, then, corresponds to what suits the acquiring of food: curved in birds of prey, for tearing; long in marsh-dwellers, for drawing things out of the depths; short and straight, for taking grain; broad, for taking herbs and roots and the like. In birds not having webbing between their toes, the measure of the beak is proportional to the measure of the legs. For if the legs are long, the beak is long; if short, short. In fishing birds, the neck is like a fishing rod, that is, the fisherman's line; the beak is like the hook. The vulture, when it grows old, has its beak lengthened above and curved.

Isidore, book 12: the feather [penna] is so called from 'hanging' [pendendo], that is, flying. For winged creatures are moved by the aid of feathers, when they commit themselves to the air. Down [pluma] is as if 'piluma,' because, just as hair is in quadrupeds, so is down in birds. There are also feathers arranged in order that serve for covering, so called because with these birds nourish and warm their young close to them.

Aristotle, in the same place: birds do not urinate for this reason, that they drink little, and what remains of moisture passes into feather. All feathers, moreover, have hollow roots, like reeds. The color of the feathers of certain birds changes according to the change of seasons, as in cranes the color of the feather is ash-grey in youth, and blackens in old age. In birds of prey, moreover, the feathers fall out most and return to vigor. Other birds pluck the feathers of the eagle-owl. Flesh-eating and hook-clawed birds, moreover, have many feathers and large, strong wings. Some water birds, too, have down covering their bodies that reaches to the feet. And this is suited to swimming, since it is like oars, as fins are to fish. The ostrich, too, has much down in the lower part of its body, like a bird. A bird that does not fly, because of the weight of its body, has this down passing into the thickness of skin, and for this reason closes its eyes by the lower eyelid. The swallow and birds similar to it have good wings and small or weak feet. There is also a kind of bird having something prominent in the middle of the head, made of down, like a helmet. Nesting birds shed their feathers, and the cause of this is the diminishing of hot, rich humor. For this same reason, conversely, the leaves of trees, in which there is rich sap, do not fall. In old age, too, the down of birds hardens, just as the bark or hide of animals, because of the diminishing of heat and the passing of moisture along with heat, for cold hardens and thickens the body, but heat rarefies it. There are two wings in birds, in the place of the two hands in man and the two front feet in quadrupeds. Birds of good flight have small bodies and large wings. Birds of poor flight, on the contrary, have this, or, if they have large wings, they are weak. The sicknesses of birds are known from the wings, when their position is disturbed. The partridge, in the manner of a hen, broods over its chicks and gathers them beneath its wings. The crane, sleeping, rests its head beneath its wing, and certain other birds likewise; the vulture stuns what it hunts, or fights with, by striking with its wings. The ostrich has no wings, but the shapes of wings, and these are fine like hairs.
Pliny, book 10: the feathers of eagles, mixed with the feathers of other birds, consume them.
[a fragmentary attribution to Avicenna:] of hens

Isidore, on birds, in the same place: we find, moreover, that the feet of birds that live on flesh are, as it were, curved and hooked, as if prepared for seizing prey. But those that have the habit and practice of swimming have broad feet, and a certain membrane joining and connecting their toes. In which the wondrous reasoning of nature is evident, that the former are equipped with a use suited to flying or to seizing food, and the latter have fitting aids for swimming, by which they may better float upon the waters and, with their feet, as if with a kind of oar, by the extension of that broader membrane, drive forward the flow of the waters.

Of birds, moreover, some are toed, some web-footed, some between the two, the breadth reduced. But all have four toes, three in front and one at the heel, though this is lacking in some with long legs.

Aristotle, in the same place: rightly, as has been said, a bird has only two feet, since it has two wings in the place of front feet. Few kinds of birds have only two toes, on the front part of the feet, and two behind, like the eagle-owl. Some, however, have a spur on the lower part of the feet, and such are of heavy flight, nor does any hook-clawed bird share this. Some, like the swallow and birds like it, have good wings and poor feet. Birds have long legs, and the cause of this is the weakness of their life. For nature gives an instrument according to the activity for which it is needed, and does not prepare the activity for the instrument, but the instrument for the activity. And so, for the kind of birds that neither stand nor swim in water, nature did not place skin between the toes of their feet. And because their dwelling is on land, they have long toes. Since, then, they are of poor flight, the food that would pass to the rear of the chest passes instead into the legs, and for this reason it accumulates there and they become large. And so, when this kind flies, it uses its feet in place of the rear of the chest and tail, and flies with its feet extended behind, and according to this manner the formation of the legs suited to it came about. Some birds, however, have short feet and legs, and when they fly they draw these in against the belly, lest they be hindered in flight by them. The feet of hook-clawed birds are suited to hunting and preying. And all long-footed birds have a thick and stout neck, and fly with the neck extended. But if they have a long and weak neck, they bend it in flying. All birds have haunches, though some think otherwise. And the haunches are near the vent, so that they can raise the body. In the legs of birds there is no flesh, for the same reason as in the tail, nor is there in the feet of quadrupeds. Also, in each foot of birds there are four toes, except in the ostrich, which is thought not to be of the kind of birds, because of the difference in its formation. And this bird has three toes on each foot, because of its wings and because of its weight, and because of what happens to long-legged birds. The ostrich indeed has two feet like a bird, but a cloven hoof like a quadruped.

[From the book On the Nature of Things:] winged creatures indeed have toes, some joined, like the goose, some separate, like the eagle-owl or the magpie. All birds that swim in water, having webbing on the toes of their feet, walk in flocks. Every bird having long legs also has a long neck. But those with short legs have a short neck, except those that have webbing between the toes, like the goose.

Pliny, book 10: birds having hooked claws do not gather together at all, and each preys for itself. Nearly all of these are high-flying, except the nocturnal ones and the larger kind. All those with large wings and a small body walk with difficulty. They rarely settle on rocks, the curvature of their claws preventing this; for the most part they live on flesh alone. The crow and the raven live not on flesh alone but on other food too. There are also certain nocturnal, hook-clawed birds, like the owl, the eagle-owl, screech-owls. All of these have dull eyes by day. The woodpecker, too, is hook-clawed. These same birds are also unfruitful. Nature has granted this generally to birds, that the more timid among them should be the more fertile, rather than the strong.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: hook-clawed birds are of good flight; but those that have a claw on the leg, like the cock, are of poor and weak flight. Likewise, hook-clawed birds have shorter necks and shorter tongues. Finally, birds of this kind, for the most part, have few eggs.

Aristotle, in the same place: a hook-clawed bird is of sharp sight, because it sees its food from a distant place. The feet of birds of this kind, moreover, are suited to hunting and preying. Heavy-bodied birds do not have curved claws, since these would harm them, for they would become entangled in whatever they walked over. For this reason, indeed, a hook-clawed bird does not walk, or walks poorly, nor does it sit on stones, since the nature of its claws is contrary to hard things. Finally, the bodies of hook-clawed birds are small and fine because of their wings, since food passes into the wings, which are their vigor and their weapons. But birds that are of poor flight, because of the weight of the body, and stay on the ground, have a straight claw. For a curved hook impedes walking. Some, in place of the help of wings, have claws on the legs suited to fighting, being fixed while walking on the ground. No bird has claws on both feet and legs, since nature does nothing superfluously. The ostrich has a cloven hoof, like quadrupeds. Likewise hook-clawed birds cannot be sociable, nor do they mate much, nor do they drink water at all, except a few, and these drink little. Nor does it remain long on stones, since the hardness of stones harms the curvature of the claws. Likewise the eagle, and all hook-clawed birds, as soon as they see that their young can fly, strike them with their wings and cast them from the nest, except for these, that is the crow, which cares for its young even after they fly. Hook-clawed birds have shorter necks and a thick tongue. Some birds of prey, however, migrate for only a few days, like the kite and the 'glutis.' Hook-clawed birds have fixed and strong feet and thick legs and sharp sight, for the governance of their life.

Aristotle, in the same place: birds have more flesh in front than behind, for all have a fleshy chest, since, being sharp, it would, for the reason stated above, be weak, and be injured by the pressure of the air in flying, unless it had a covering of much flesh.

The flesh of a bird is altogether drier than that of a quadruped. The flesh of chicks dries out with excessive heat, unless it is acidic. The flesh of large birds, geese, and kites is thick. The flesh of water ducks is of exceeding moisture, in this close to the flesh of sheep. All large water birds having long necks, like the peacock and the kite, and those of which there is a great abundance, have melancholic flesh. But the wings of large, active birds are of good digestion. Likewise, the flesh of large birds tends to bring on fevers. The flesh of birds, roasted or not, constipates the bowels.
[on] birds, and in their throat, especially cocks' - the skin

Isaac the Jew: winged creatures are finer and lighter than all flesh-bearing creatures generally, and more digestible than all walking creatures, but less nourishing. But wild ones are less moist than domestic ones and have more tender flesh, and are also easier to digest. The cause is the sparseness of their flesh from the excess of their exertion and the dryness of the air. Domestic birds, however, nourish more and are more temperate because of their moisture and the moderation of their exertion, and generate praiseworthy blood. Domestic birds inhabiting fields are better than those eating in a coop, because of their movement and because they receive food suited to their nature. Again, among flying creatures generally, the starling is finer, and the chicks of partridges and of the domestic hen, after these the partridge, the pheasant, and the hen. The rest of the birds, however, are harder and thicker: cranes, peacocks. But these should not be eaten unless they have first remained dead for a day in summer or three days in winter, so that their flesh becomes tender. More moist than the rest are the goose, the duck, and the starling, and dove-chicks especially if raised in a coop. For this reason they are thick and hard to digest, especially if they have inhabited marshes and lakes. Dove-chicks, however, are better. The goose, then, the starling, and the like are more harmful to the stomach, for they burden and putrefy it because of their excessive moisture. Nothing in them is of use except the wings and the neck. For the rest are unlike them, being easy to digest and far removed from corruption, because of the excess of their exertion and movement. The neck, nonetheless, shares in their exertion. Indeed, winged creatures do not have limbs as refined as the neck and wings. Land birds are better than water birds, and among water birds, ducks are the worst of all. Of all birds, turtledoves are the driest, and sparrows and other small birds the hottest of all. They are, then, astringent and stimulate the blood. Galen attests that the extremities of winged creatures are to the whole body what the internal organs of animals are to the working of their body. The stomach of all winged creatures is muscular, hard to digest, but if digested, gives much nourishment. Of all stomachs, the goose's is the most praiseworthy, because of the abundance of moisture in this animal, after this the hen's. Likewise the liver of the goose is more nourishing and more suitable than others. Of the wings and neck it has been said above. The necks of the goose and the hen are the best of all birds. Likewise castrated winged creatures are better than all walking creatures, like castrated cocks. For they generate more praiseworthy nourishment and perfect blood.

Pliny, in the same place: for all animals there is a fixed and single manner of movement proper to each in its kind. Birds, however, alone are carried in varied paths, on land and in the air. Some walk, like crows; some hop, like blackbirds, sparrows; others run, like the corncrake and partridges; others cast their feet before them, like storks and cranes; others spread their wings and, hovering, beat them at rare intervals, others more often, but only the first feathers; others spread the whole side. Some, for the greater part, fly with their wings drawn close and struck only once. Others, too, are carried through the air with a double stroke, or hurl themselves through the enclosed air, pressing upward, straight, downward - you would think some were being driven, or falling from a height, others leaping. Some raise themselves straight up at once and make for the sky in a single track, like ducks and those of this kind. The heavier ones, however, do not fly except from a running start or launched from a higher mound, like the vulture. Others are guided by the tail, others look about, others bend their necks. Some feed on what they have seized with their feet. Some do not fly without a cry, others are silent in flight. Some fly upright, some prone, some sideways, obliquely; some are even carried on their backs, facing upward.

Ambrose: there is a certain kinship between all birds and fish, in that the practice of flying is a kind of swimming, of swimming through the water and cutting through the air with swift flight, and for both kinds the oarage of tail and wings serves in advancing and directing their course. For indeed by the tail birds either raise themselves to the heights or plunge to the depths.

Aristotle, in the same place: a bird having hooked claws does not walk, but sits on trees. Some birds, in flying, draw their feet in against the belly, some spread them out. Some birds are of good flight, like those that eat flesh and are hook-clawed, and for this reason have feathers and large and also strong wings. To others, too, nature gave goodness of flight because of their leaping, and because they are transferred from one region to another. Some, however, are of poor flight because of the weight of the body, and because their life is from the ground. A winged creature, too, that has a spur on the foot is of heavy flight. Birds, as said above, of good flight have small bodies and large wings. Birds of poor flight, on the contrary, either have this, or, if they have large wings, are nevertheless weak.

Ambrose: [some birds are] settled, which always remain in their own places. Others, however, are migratory, which go off to other regions and return once winter is over. There are also others which migrate from us in summer and return in winter, either because in wintertime they betake themselves to warmer places, or because most of them, in turn, spend the summer in these places which they know to be more pleasant. Let us also consider the various birds of the sea, how, at the approach of a stirring of the winds, they betake themselves to safer and, at that time, sweeter waters, and search out, in the hidden recesses of the lands, foods unknown to them.

Aristotle: birds having webbing between their toes stay in the water. Those, however, having separate toes, stay near the water and take their food from the land; weak birds, in cold winter, flee to the valleys, seeking warmth. And in summer they return to the mountain-tops for the heat. All that are fat, before the change from cold to warm places, and indeed in spring, hasten mating more, and then move from warm to cold places. Likewise wild birds change the places of their dwelling according to what suits their life and the escape of their young, and some stay in lakes, some among rocks and crevices, and some in mountainous places, some appear at night and flee by day. Some too stay in shade and in places facing away from the wind. In winter, however, they stay where the sun abounds. Nature has given to some, as said, goodness of flight for their safety, since they are transferred from one region to another. Some, however, are of poor flight because of the weight of their bodies, since their dwelling is on the ground. Their food is grain and what is on the ground.

The Ordinary Gloss: birds, then, know their own seasons, so that they know when, hastening to warm places, they must avoid the harshness of winter, and, at the start of spring, return to their accustomed regions. Whence it is written: the kite in the sky has known its season, the turtledove and the swallow and the stork have known the time of their coming, etc.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: of each of these kinds, moreover, it will be spoken individually below.
Ambrose, in the same place: winged creatures, as has been said, live on flesh, some on found seed, others on varied and chance food.

Aristotle: some birds eat flesh, some grain, some both; some, however, eat their own particular delicacy, as bees feed on honey; some seek their food at night, like the eagle-owl, some by day. All hook-clawed birds feed on flesh; some, too, eat flesh and yet are not hook-clawed. Some, however, eat worms, like the sparrow. Some do not live on living creatures, but fall upon thorns and feed from them. Some birds, too, live on fruit, like wood-pigeons and turtledoves. Some live on the shores of waters, lakes, or the sea, and feed from these. Those, moreover, whose toes have, as it were, skin between them, dwell in waters and live from them; hook-clawed birds eat all creatures they can hunt, and live on blood. But they do not eat one another, as fish do. Hook-clawed birds do not drink at all, except a few. Rainy weather harms birds, since they do not make much use of drink.

[birds drink] as other creatures do. But those with long necks do so intermittently, from within, and with the head thrown back, as if pouring the water into themselves. The purple gallinule alone drinks by biting, and, touching every food with water in turn, brings it to its beak with its foot as if with a hand. The heavier birds all feed on grain, the high-flying ones on flesh alone; among water birds, divers are accustomed to swallow what the others bring back up.

Ambrose: birds that live on flesh have rough claws, a curved and sharp mouth, and are of swift flight, since they live by plunder, so that they can easily seize the prey they pursue, and disembowel it with their beak or claws.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania, on birds: the falling sickness happens to no bird or quail more than to those that eat henbane.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: birds eat their own particular delicacy, as bees eat honey and a few sweet things. Flesh-eating birds lay eggs only once a year, except swallows, which lay twice. Male flesh-eating birds, at certain hours, bring food to their mates as they warm the chicks in the nest. But since these mates, being of greater strength, are feared, they come to them chirping, as if announcing their arrival, with the flesh, and, once the food is received from the mother, flee. Birds, as has been said, do not urinate, because they are very dry, and much of their moisture passes into feathers and is consumed by flight, whence they also have no bladder.

The Philosopher: birds having a long neck drink and raise the head until the water descends into the stomach. All birds, moreover, take a long draught in drinking, except the cock and the swallow and birds that dwell in water. Hook-clawed birds do not drink water for this reason, that they eat flesh, which is moister than the food of other birds. Birds love clear and running waters, and do not descend upon a foul carcass unless it has a good taste, for then they do not avoid the stench. Hook-clawed birds live on flesh. The rest, however, feed on fruits and worms and reptiles.

Ambrose, in the same place: of winged creatures, some are noisy only in voice, others are melodious and delight with sweet modulation. Some by nature, some by training, speak the differences of various voices, so that when a bird has spoken, you would think a man had spoken. How distinct is the parrot's voice, how sweet the blackbird's - the song itself of winged creatures is for us a great incentive to rouse devotion. For what man, possessing human sense, would not blush to close the day without the celebration of psalms, when even the tiniest birds attend the risings of days and nights with solemn devotion and sweet song? Different birds find their own bird-haunt in the evening and, in their hiding-places, bring the day's setting with them, attending it with melodious song, lest they be found exempt from the gratitude with which every creature praises its Creator together. Night, too, has its own songs, with which it is accustomed to soothe the vigils of men; finally, whether the nocturnal or diurnal time has run its course or is just beginning, they render praises to their Creator.

Goldfinches - Pliny, book 10: goldfinches, smallest of birds, do what is commanded them, not only by voice, but with their feet and mouth in place of hands. There is one that imitates the lowing of cattle, a bird called the 'bull' in the territory of Arles, otherwise small. There is one that imitates the neighing of horses, called by the name 'anthus,' driven from its pasture-herb by their approach, avenging itself in this manner. Above all, however, the parrot renders human voices. It greets emperors and pronounces the words it receives, wanton especially after wine. The starling, too, renders human voices, and the nightingale, the raven; some, however, like swallows, learn nothing, but are untrainable; some do not fly without a cry, others are always silent in flight.

The same, in book 2: the more talkative birds are the smaller ones, and especially around mating. Some have a voice in fighting, like quails, others before fighting, like partridges, others when they have won, like domestic cocks: these have their own voice, that is, proper to the males; others have the same voice for females too, as in the kind of nightingales. Some sing the whole year, some at fixed times.

Aristotle, in the same place: many small birds have much vocalization, so that they recognize one another's intentions in turn, and this all birds recognize to a greater or lesser degree. Some birds, too, learn certain calls from others. The vocalization of birds, moreover, is greater at mating time. The cock cries out after battle and victory. The vulture, too, is noisy. The 'kyke' is a bird that cries with various voices and changes its voice nearly every day. The voices and colors of certain birds also change and differ in summer and winter. The 'ioabam' is a bird that, by imitating a horse's voice, stuns it and forces it to flee. The 'kolkis' is a bird at whose death the birds cry out with a sweet, sorrowful lament. The buzzing of bees and cicadas is not a voice, since they do not breathe, but it occurs from the rubbing together of certain parts. The female 'cubeth,' hearing the male's voice and smelling him, is filled with eggs. Among birds, that which has a broad, small tongue speaks; and likewise that which has a fine tongue. And in certain kinds the male and female cry out in one manner, in others differently. In some, the males give voice and the females do not, like the cock and the male quail. Some sing sweetly, both male and female, like the 'hardon,' and the female falls silent when brooding eggs. Small birds vocalize and speak more than large ones, and especially, as has been said, at mating time.
[Isidore, listing birds that live long or short lives:] cranes, the raven, the swan, the peacock, the kite, the owl, the cuckoo, the jackdaw

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is evident, moreover, by a certain wondrous natural skill, that winged creatures excel in building nests, in raising their young, in guarding against ambushes, in detecting and recognizing changes of air and weather. Also in applying remedies for illnesses and the like; for example, as said above, some, fighting one another, apply wild oregano to their wounds as a remedy. The swallow, as is read, is most skillful in building nests, and, having a certain foreknowledge, abandons roofs about to fall, flying in winding circuits, and is never made prey by other birds; when her chicks are struck with blindness, she restores their sight with a certain remedy. Having stayed across the sea in winter, she knows how to announce, by her arrival, the beginning of spring.
Swallows - the celandine. Pliny, book 8: the celandine, most wholesome for sight. The stork heals itself with oregano in illness.

The same, in the book on ravens: their favor is attested even by the indignation of the Roman people, not merely as a private matter. Under the emperor Tiberius, a young raven born in a brood above the temple of Castor flew down into a shoemaker's shop opposite, and was even commended, out of a kind of piety, to the shop's owner. Trained early to speech, it would fly out every morning toward the camp, toward the Forum, and, facing Tiberius, then Germanicus and Drusus Caesar, would greet them by name, and then greet the Roman people passing by. Afterward, returning to the shop, it earned merit through years of constant service. It is worth recording that it was seen, driven by thirst, gathering stones and dropping them into a bucket at a monument in which much water stood but could not be reached, so afraid was it to go down, and thus, by such a heap, raised the water enough to drink. Nor should it be omitted, when we discuss the intelligence of creatures, that among birds swallows are untrainable, just as among land creatures mice are.

The same, in the same place: birds have varied talents, especially regarding feeding. For the nightjar flies by night to the udders of goats for the sake of the milk's moisture. Some, as has been said, do what is commanded, not only by voice, but with feet and mouth in place of hands, like goldfinches, smallest of birds. Some also imitate the voices of men, some of animals, like horses and cattle.
Alexander Neckam: a bird avoids snares if it betakes itself to the heights and flies over the earth below. For in the heights no one stretches nets, no one hides snares.

Aristotle, in the same place: some birds also fight against one another, whose strength and weapons are their wings and claws. And so some of them, as has been said, have curved claws on their feet, suited to hunting and preying, while others have claws on their legs suited to fighting while walking, fixed on the ground, namely like the cock. It is not proper to birds of one kind that they eat one another. The raven and the eagle-owl are hostile to one another over their nests. Many kinds of birds, too, hate the eagle-owl, and these also strip its feathers. The raven is a friend of the fox and helps it against its enemy, namely the 'ascelon.' For the ascelon is a bird that fights with the fox, strips its feathers, harms it, and kills its cubs. Likewise the black raven fights with the ass and the bull, and, flying above them, pricks their eyes with its beak. Wood-pigeons naturally love one another, yet fight over their nests. Birds, when they fight among themselves, apply wild oregano to their wounds.

[a listing of hostile pairs of creatures:] swans and eagles, the raven and the 'cloreus,' seeking each other's eggs by night. In similar fashion the raven and the kite, the latter snatching food from the former; crows and owls, the eagle and the wren - if we believe it, since it is called the king of birds. The owl and other smaller birds; likewise, among land creatures, the weasel and the crow and the turtledove and the moth, ichneumons and wasps, spiders and their prey. Among water birds, ducks and gulls; the harpy-eagle and the buzzard, the hawk. Shrews and little herons lying in wait for each other's young. The tiny 'egythus' bird fights with the ass, for, rubbing itself against thorn-bushes to scratch itself, it scatters its nests, which it dreads so much that, hearing its braying voice at all, it casts out its eggs, and its chicks fall from fear. It [the egythus] then flies to it and pecks at its sores with its beak: foxes and kites. The 'escelon' is a small bird, breaking the raven's eggs, whose own chicks are troubled by foxes; in turn this bird plucks at the fox's cubs and the vixen itself, which, when the ravens see it, they help against, as against a common enemy. And the 'achantis' lives among thorns; for this reason it too hates asses, which devour the flowers of the thorn.
The same, in book 2: of birds, as has been said, some have a voice in fighting, like quails; others before fighting, like partridges; others when they have won, like cocks.

div.head: DE NOMINIBUS ET NATURIS AVIUM SECUNDUM ALPHABETUM ET PRIMO DE ACCIPITRE

cit.quote: Isidore, in the same place: the hawk is a bird armed more with spirit than with claws, bearing greater strength in a smaller body. It is named from 'seizing' [accipiendo], because it is eager to seize other birds.

Ambrose, in the same place: for hawks nothing serves as a bond for conjugal union, because of their eagerness for plunder and their watchfulness in lying in ambush. For avarice shuns the company of many. Hawks are said to bear a harsh severity toward their own young, in that, when they notice them attempting the beginnings of flight, they cast them out of their nests and at once banish them. But if they linger, they drive them off with their wings and cast them down, beat them with their feathers, and force them to dare what they dread, and afterward bring them no gift of nourishment. But in this they seem rather to be training their tender young for prey, and briefly, than to be disowning their offspring. For they take care lest, in tender age, they grow lazy, be undone by comforts, waste away in idleness, or learn to wait for food rather than seek it.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the wild hawk is allowed to fast a great deal, and thus grows tame. Whoever wishes to keep his hawk fat should give it beef or pork, and this from males. To keep it lean, give it young hens soaked in water. To keep it in balance, old hens. To keep it quick in hunting, give it a good throat-pouch, and shut it in darkness with only a little light, and hunt it on alternate days. From the blood of tender young birds the hawk also takes much strength, and boldness, and eagerness for hunting. Let it perch on willow or fir wood, and be given a bath of cold water. Do not handle its wings too much, unless they droop unevenly. If you wish the hawk to catch a hare or rabbit, teach it this in its youth, and tie rings on its legs near its feet, a hand's-breadth apart, and thus it will catch it without injury.

Aristotle: the hawk nests on the highest mountains and eats the hearts of the birds it catches. Meeting the bird called the 'kokie,' it is defeated by it; yet it does not begin the fight itself. It has gall only in the liver and intestine, as does the kite; both brood for twenty days. Hawk chicks are fat and of very good flesh. The vulture is said to mate with the male hawk. The spleen is small in birds of a hot stomach, as in the hawk and the dove and the kite.

When quails come across the sea, the hawk seizes the first one nearing land. But the kestrel defends doves from the hawk, for it terrifies hawks by a natural power, so much so that they flee its voice and sight. Once a hawk's voice is heard, the eggs being brooded are spoiled. Elsewhere, however, a kind of hawk is honored at table.
The same, book 11: in the hawk the gall is joined to the intestine, as in doves and moray eels.
The same, book 20: hawks, scratching at lettuce and staining their eyes with its juice, dispel darkness when they sense it.
The same, book 25: Theophrastus relates that the herb centaury, called by the name 'triorchis,' is defended by the hawk-kind called 'triorches,' and that those who gather it are attacked by it.
The kind of hawk called the chameleon-hawk is said to draw down to itself anything flying above it, and to offer it willingly to be torn apart by other animals.

The Ordinary Gloss, on Leviticus: those are likened to the hawk who seem tame, but strive to seize prey along with the powerful and rapacious. For this reason the hawk is forbidden to be eaten in the Law.

The Ordinary Gloss, on John: the ostrich indeed has a huge body and sparse feathers. The gerfalcon and hawk, on the contrary, surpass the other birds in speed. The hawk sheds its old feather every year when the south wind blows, a new one growing. Whence it is written: does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom? etc.

Aristotle: the hawk holds under its feet, the whole night, whatever bird chance offers it against the night. But at sunrise, hungry, it lets it fly away. And even if it encounters the same bird again while hunting elsewhere, it does not pursue it. The hawk changes the color of its eyes and its beak. Bread kills it, according to Augustine.

Pliny, book 10: the kinds of hawks are distinguished by their manner of hunting. Some seize a bird only from the ground, others only near trees, others one perched high, others one flying in the open. In all, we find sixteen kinds of hawks. Among these, the 'circus,' lame in one foot, also called 'triorches' from the number of its testicles - the Romans call this the buzzard, the Greeks the 'epyleon' - this alone appears at every season. The others, indeed, depart in winter. The nocturnal hawk is called the 'cymindis,' rare even in its own woods and seeing less well by day. It wages a war of extermination with the eagle, and, grappling together, they are often caught. The cuckoo, too, seems to be produced from a kind of hawk.

From the Aviary of Hugh of Fouilloy: there are two kinds of hawk, the domestic and the wild. Yet the same hawk can, at different times, be wild and domestic. The wild one is accustomed to seize domestic birds, the domestic one wild birds. The wild one devours at once what it seizes. The domestic one keeps what it catches for its master, who opens their bellies and gives the hearts to the hawk as food, and casts out the belly's inner parts along with the dung, which, remaining within, would breed a putrid stench of decaying flesh. The hawk is tied by a leash to a perch, which it is accustomed to have like fetters on its feet, so that it cannot fly away when it wishes. It is usually carried on the left hand, so that it may fly to the right to catch something. But as the blessed Gregory says: it is the custom of wild hawks that, when the south wind blows, they spread their wings, so that their limbs, in the season of wind, grow warm enough to loosen their old feathers. But when there is no wind, they warm themselves by spreading and beating their wings against the sun's rays. And thus, the pores opened, either the old feathers fall out or the new ones grow in. Domestic hawks, however, so that they may molt better, seek out sheltered and warm places.
From the Aviary: the wild hawk is accustomed to seize domestic birds, and, once caught, kills them and extracts and eats their hearts.

Aristotle, in the same place: there are three kinds of hawks. Some do not strike doves except on the ground. Some only near trees. Others only while flying in the air. Doves, recognizing all these, when they see one of these kinds, move themselves to a place where that kind does not strike.

From the book On the Nature of Things: there are four kinds of hawks. The first is large in body, very tamable, with variegated, translucent eyes, a cheerful expression, a thick foot, long claws, delicate in eating; it attacks all birds and fears none. The second kind is smaller than the first, which we may call the 'osprey,' having thick wings, short in proportion to its body, and thick claws and large, dark eyes; it does not tame quickly, and so is hateful to many. In the first year of taming it is of little worth, in the second more; in the third, by imitation, it hunts quite well. The third kind is the sparrowhawk, small indeed compared to the others, but nevertheless swift; it tames quickly and wishes to be delicately nourished, and hunts easily. The fourth kind is the merlin, which we call tame, much smaller indeed, but similar in color, as the sparrowhawk is similar to the hawk in its disposition and coloring. This bird tames quickly and wishes to be delicately nourished, and hunts easily, swift in flight.
The hawk, cooked in rose oil, is thought most effective as an ointment for all ailments occurring in the eyes; likewise the ash of its dung with Attic honey.
The same, in the same place: the dung of the 'cenchris,' a kind of hawk, with honey, thins white films on the eyes and gives clarity to the eyes; the Greeks call this condition 'argema.'
Aesculapius: if hawk's [dung] is ground in oil, an ointment made from this also removes clouding of the eyes.

The 'acanthis' [linnet] is a small but fertile bird, for it produces twelve chicks at once; it is nourished on the food of plants, and for this reason hates horses, which, when it sees them coming upon it as it grazes and tearing up the plants, it flees, and avenges itself as it can, imitating and mocking their neighing with its own voice.
The acanthis hates the 'egithus' bird so much that they are believed not to let their blood mingle.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'acanthis,' according to Isidore, is the same bird that among us is called the goldfinch, of which more will be said below.
Isidore: the 'acredula' is the same as the nightingale, of which, indeed, more will be said below.

The 'aeriophylon,' named as if 'lover of the air,' is commonly called 'aelion.' It is the noblest of birds, a little larger than the eagle, mighty in flight and swiftest in its wings; it has reddish feathers and a long tail, claws, and a very large beak and legs. It dwells in the clear open sky, so much that it scarcely ever, or only briefly, settles or rests on the ground. It is also often raised above the clouds, so that it cannot be seen by man, and takes its food in the air, and this too in the manner of birds of prey. If a bird crosses its path in the air, it is at once seized by it and cast down from the highest air to the ground. Nor can it be seen by man who has struck it down, killed, from the air. This bird, while still a fledgling and not yet self-aware, is caught by men and tamed and trained for hunting. And its nature is so changed from its wild alienation that it thinks its condition to be nowhere but among men and in houses, where it was raised, whence it happens that, contrary to the custom of other noble birds, it remains without tethers in porches and in houses. They fly sociably, two together, and divide the prey they have caught. This bird catches roe-kids and fawns, by tearing with its claws, first gouging out the beast's eyes, and thus, its brain pierced through, killing it.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the 'agochiles' is called in Arabic, in Latin, the goatsucker. It is a large eastern bird, which lays two or three eggs. It seeks out goats full of milk, placing itself beneath their udders, with a broad beak created for this purpose. It sucks milk from them like a kid, but from then on the milk in them is destroyed and their udders dry up. Pliny also says that from this same sucking the goats lose their sight.
The lark is a small bird known to all for the melody of its song. In summer it begins at dawn, as if announcing the rising of the day. In winter, however, it is caught, especially in time of snow.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the lark is named 'from praise' [a laude], because with wondrous delight, its wings spread in the air, it rejoices with the melody of its voice in the breeze of a more joyful season. For under a clouded or rainy sky it scarcely or never sings. It announces the day coming at dawn with a jubilant voice. Sitting on the ground it scarcely or never sings. But it sings while ascending: it ascends gradually, but descends suddenly like a falling stone; in ascending it draws its wings to its body and steers itself with a light motion of the tail. It fears the hawk so much that, when attacked by it, it flies, pressed to the ground, into a man's bosom, or offers itself to be caught by his hand, well aware that man is more likely to pity it than the hawk. It never feeds on impure things. The rising of dawn, even a hastened one, never deceives it. The crested lark, also called the 'cyrrita,' is, as Alexander [Neckam] says, to be preferred to other larks in the sharp distinctions of its song-patterns - for 'systema,' according to musicians, is a portion of the voice.
Rhazes, in the Almansor: the flesh of the crested lark constricts the belly, and its broth makes the belly flow.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'alieetus' [sea-eagle], according to Pliny, is the sixth kind of eagle, as will be said more fully below. According to others, however, it is a second kind of hawk, as said a little above. And it is an unclean bird according to the Law, as is read in Leviticus.

[Pliny:] the sea-eagle, moreover, striking even its still-unfeathered chicks, forces them repeatedly to gaze, turned away, at the sun's rays, and if it notices any of them blinking or moistening - that is, weeping - it casts that one out of the nest as if illegitimate and degenerate. But the one whose gaze has stood firm against the sun, it raises. The sea-eagle, moreover, is a bird of the sharpest keenness of eye, balancing itself from on high, and, having spotted a fish in the sea, plunges headlong upon it, seizing it with its breast, the waters scattered. Sea-eagles have no proper kind of their own, but are born from the varied mating of eagles. What is born from these has, in turn, the kind of the 'ossifrage,' from which the smaller vultures are bred, and from these the larger ones, which do not breed at all.
Radulphus of Flaix, on Leviticus: the sea-eagle feeds on plunder, but, since it lacks strength, is hostile only to smaller birds, over which it has the advantage.

Ambrose: the halcyon is a sea bird, accustomed to bring forth its young on the shores. For it lays its eggs in the sand, in the middle of winter nearly, when the sea rises highest and the waves crash most violently against the shores; and while it broods there, the sea suddenly grows calm and all the storms of the winds subside. It broods the eggs for seven days, then brings forth its chicks, which it nourishes for another seven days. Whence sailors observe these fourteen days of presumed calm, which they call the 'halcyon days': because, while the halcyon broods or nourishes its young, no disturbance of storms is feared.

Aristotle: the halcyon's nest resembles a pine cone, except in color, since its color leans toward red. Its shape resembles a bladder having a long neck. In the middle it is a hard cavity, so much so that it cannot easily be cut even with a sharp iron. Its entrance is very small, and so seawater does not enter it. Its depth resembles the depth of a sponge, and it is uncertain what that nest is made from. There is, however, an opinion that it is composed of the sharp spines of the needlefish. This bird begins to mate after four months, and mates throughout its whole life.

The halcyon is a bird a little larger than a sparrow, of a sky-blue color, though for the greater part its feathers are mixed with purple and white, with a slender and long neck. It is most rarely seen, and only at the setting of the Pleiades and around the solstices; for seven days before midwinter they build nests, and lay eggs for as many following days. The days of their breeding are called the halcyon days, the sea being calm and navigable during them, especially the Sicilian sea; in other regions, indeed, it is milder. There is another kind of them, distinguished by size, and smaller ones sing among the reed-beds; they live on fish and lay five eggs. Their nests are a marvel, shaped like a ball, slightly raised, with a very narrow opening, resembling large sponges, and cannot be cut through with iron, but are broken by a strong blow, like dry sea-foam, and what they are made of cannot be discovered.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the halcyon is a very tiny bird dwelling in the sea and rearing its young there. Certain domestic birds, like the hen and the dove, breed at indiscriminate times, since they are safe from the harshness of winter. This bird alone, however, among wild birds, breeds in wintertime. Its nest cannot be cut with iron, but is broken only by a strong blow, and it cannot be discovered what it is made from. It is called 'alcyon,' as if 'bird of the ocean,' because in winter it makes its nest and raises its young in the pools of the ocean.
Isidore: the duck [anas] took its fitting name from its constant swimming [natandi]. Of this kind, some are called 'germane,' because they nourish [their young] more than the rest.

Pliny, in the same place: birds hurl themselves through the air upward, straight, downward. You would think some were being driven, or, again, falling from a height, others leaping. Ducks alone, of the same kind, rise straight up at once and make for the sky in a single track. And so, having fallen into pits dug for hunting wild beasts, they alone escape.
The same, book [unspecified]: ducks and the 'margus,' and other water birds, cleaning their feathers with their beak, foretell wind.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the duck is a bird somewhat larger than a cock. The male has a head and neck of green color, a broad beak, and wings marked with white, green, and black. It has a white ring around its neck, and red and broad feet, with which it paddles in the water. For it delights in river waters and can scarcely live without them, especially since dry food chokes it more quickly. The males, sometimes when many are together, are carried by such madness of lust that, mating one after another in rivalry, they kill the single female. Their young, as soon as they leave the egg, are so agile that, even should their mother die or be lost, they can live without a nurse.

div.head: DE CIBO ET MEDICINA EX ANATE

cit.quote: Duck, cooked, is better in the breast than in the neck, of which Martial says thus: let the whole duck be served, but only the breast and neck please; give the rest back to the cook.
Duck's flesh has many superfluities and causes more distaste, and is of greater heat, yet nourishes no more than hen's flesh.
The blood of ducks is thickened, kept, and diluted with wine, against harmful medicines.

Avicenna: the duck is hotter than all domestic birds, and some say that it warms cold conditions. Once heated, however, it causes fever. It clarifies the voice. It increases desire in mating and multiplies the seed. Its fat is greatest in soothing pain and likewise a gnawing sensation deep in the body. And it is better than the fat of other birds. It also clarifies the complexion. Its flesh fattens and breaks up flatulence. It is slow in the stomach, however, and heavy, and properly so the goose's too, but what is lighter and better in it is the wings. When the flesh of the duck and goose is digested, it is more nourishing than all other bird flesh.

The same: duck's flesh is of vehement moisture and much nourishment, but not as good as hen's flesh and the like. Their sexual organs are pleasant, and their livers good and pleasant to eat, and of good humor.
The same: the wing of the fattened duck, that is, duck's flesh applied like a plaster, is good for swollen sinews. The fat of a fattened duck, smeared on cloth, is beneficial.
The same: the fatty liver of the duck, like that of the hen, is healthier than others; its brain is used in medicines for abscesses of the anus.
Some think the female duck more effective. Likewise its blood, poured onto a flowing wound of the brain, is effective, and likewise its fat cooked with rose oil.

The same, in the same book: the blood of male ducks also stops the bowels. It is a marvel, moreover, that is related, that in colic a duck applied causes the illness of the belly to pass into it, and the duck itself to die.

[Isidore:] gave [the name 'anser'] by derivation, or from resemblance, or because it has this same frequency of swimming; it attests to nighttime vigils by the constancy of its cry: for no animal senses the scent of man as the goose does, whence by its cry the ascent of the Gauls onto the Capitol was detected.

Ambrose: rightly, Rome, do you owe to geese the power by which you rule; your gods were sleeping and geese were watching; you ought rather to have sacrificed to them than to Jupiter. For your gods yield to the geese, by whom they know themselves to have been defended, lest they too be captured by the enemy.

Geese mate in water, and give birth in spring, or, if in midwinter, after the solstice. At most sixteen eggs, at least seven. The females alone brood, for thirty days. But if they are somewhat warmer, contact with nettle is deadly to their chicks, and no less is their greed harmful, sometimes through excessive satiety, sometimes when, having seized a root by its own strength with their bite, they often break their own necks trying to pull it up. The remedy against nettle, however, is a root placed in the straw beneath the brooding bird. Geese do not hatch eggs not their own. It is most useful, in brooding, to set nine or eleven eggs beneath them. In Germany geese are white, but the smaller ones are called 'ganze'; the price of their down is five denarii per pound, and luxury has advanced so far that without this, in straw, not even men's necks can now bear to rest. Female geese conceive by mutual imagination of desire with one another, or by dust: it is a marvel, this love in such a bird, and our people, wiser than others, have recognized in it the goodness of the liver, which grows to great size.
Geese, with continuous untimely honking, foretell dread storms.

Aristotle: geese are modest and watchful creatures. Large and small geese, which walk like a flock, are found near rivers and lakes. Small geese, moreover, fly in flocks; among geese, too, there are wind-eggs.

[From the book On the Nature of Things:] the goose is a bird the size of an eagle. Of this kind, those that are wild and of their own freedom are of a bluish-grey color and seek the high air. They fly like cranes, in orderly formation, and direct their flights according to the blowing of the winds. When the north wind blows, they seek the south, well aware that colder weather threatens; they scarcely rest from flight unless, feeding as they go, they graze meanwhile. For flight is so delightful to them that they rarely sleep. But, on the contrary, for domestic geese flight is burdensome; grazing is their chief occupation, resting and sleeping their special pleasure; they announce the hours of the night and betray thieves with their cry. In the Alpine mountains there is a kind of goose, the largest among birds except the ostrich, but so heavy that it is caught by hand, immobile on the ground. Ducks and geese and other birds purge themselves with the herb sideritis.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: geese, indeed, mate in spring, or, if in midwinter, after the solstice. If someone steals their eggs, they keep laying until exhausted, but do not hatch eggs not their own. In brooding it is most useful to set nine or eleven beneath them. Sometimes, too, they lay without mating, but these are eggs without chicks; they hiss to defend their young. They bathe more often before rain. Their flesh is hard to digest. When shut in for fattening, if a single one is left, deprived of company, it scarcely fattens further, from the sadness of solitude. A goose shut in for fattening reaches the limit of its fattening within nine days, beyond which it makes no further progress, even if kept shut in for many more days.
Aristotle: geese lay eggs even without mating. They swim in water, so that wind-eggs form in them.

Palladius: the goose, indeed, cannot easily be sustained without water or grass. It is hostile to cultivated places, since it harms crops both by biting and by its dung; it provides chicks and feathers, which may be plucked both in autumn and in spring. Three females suffice for one male. White ones are more fertile, spotted or dark ones less so, since they passed from a wild to a domestic kind. They brood from the first of March until the summer solstice. They will bear more young if you set their eggs under hens, and the mothers, once free of the last brood, are allowed to raise it. Under hens, peacock eggs as well as goose eggs should be set, but beneath the goose eggs, so they are not harmed, nettle should be placed. The chicks should be fed indoors for the first ten days, and afterward can be brought out in clear weather, where there is no nettle, whose stings they dread. At four months they are well fattened, for they fatten better in tender age. Barley-meal is given to them three times a day, and generous freedom to swim is forbidden. They should be shut in a dark and warm place. Thus the larger ones fatten even by the second month. For the smallest are often fattened by the thirtieth day, if soaked millet is given to satiety. Among legumes, any can be offered to geese except bitter vetch. Care must be taken, however, that their chicks do not swallow bristles.

div.head: DE CIBO ET MEDICINA EX ANSERE

cit.quote: Avicenna: goose flesh is thick. Its fat is good for baldness and effective for cracks of the face and lips. It also soothes ear pain and benefits the womb. Its wings are of good digestion and nourishment, and are light only because of the abundance of its movement and exertion. Its nourishment is not increased except by the abundance of flesh that is in it.

[Goose fat,] applied with honey, is effective against the bite of a rabid dog. Its blood is useful against the venom of the sea-hare and against all harmful medicines. Goose fat, in a bronze vessel with cinnamon and cassia and white pepper and the herb called 'commagene' and reed, buried in much snow and steeped in icy cold, is taken for the use of a famous medicine, called 'commagenum.' It is also pleasant in smell, most useful as a remedy, and for rubbing on convulsions or other sudden pains, being both an ointment and a medicine. The same fat with butter stops bleeding. Goose fat also heals holy fire, and by it carbuncles are cured. Likewise the fat heals ulcers of the tongue and lips and clears the skin of the face; it soothes pain and heaviness of the ears. Goose fat, cooked with rose oil, is effective for a flowing wound of the brain, and likewise its blood, poured on. Goose gall is beneficial for bruised eyes, so that afterward they are anointed with hyssop and honey. For those with celiac disease, it is beneficial to take the tongues of three geese as food.
Aesculapius, in the same place: goose fat dissolves all hardness. The same, dropped in with onion juice, expels water that has entered the ear.
Dioscorides: goose fat is exceedingly marvelous for the sweetness of its richness. It heals cracks of the lips and cracks of the whole face caused by cold most excellently, and ear pains.

Isidore: the eagle is named from the sharpness [acumine] of its eyes. For its gaze is said to be so powerful that, when it is carried on motionless wing over the seas, beyond the reach of human sight, it can see little fish swimming from such a height, and, descending like a missile, drags the seized prey with its wings to the shore. For it is said not to bend its gaze even against the sun's ray. Whence it holds its young up by their claws against the sun's rays, and those it sees keeping a steady gaze it preserves as worthy of their kind, but those it sees turning their gaze aside it casts out as degenerate.

Ambrose: the eagle's cast-off chick is taken up by the coot, called in Greek 'ceophes' or 'phene,' which joins it with its own brood, and feeds and nourishes it with the same maternal devotion as its own young. This same eagle, being of very sharp sight, forces its young, before their wings are fully grown, to look at the sun. And if the eyes of any of them water, it sometimes kills that one. The eagle, moreover, does not return to the surplus or remains of its hunt, so that the young might eat any of it.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the eagle is a great, royal bird, of which it is said that, wherever it sees a serpent from on high, it seizes it with its claws, crushing it with a great shriek, and, once it has torn out and stripped away the deadly venoms from its entrails, still devours the wounded creature, extinguishing the poison that was in it, the venom cooked away by heat; and by this trial too it is either saddened or made glorious: they always keep one dwelling and one nest.
Aristotle: the females of eagles are of larger body than the males.

Pliny, book 10: eagles do not carry off what they have seized at once, but first set it down and, having tested its weight, then finally depart; they die not of old age or sickness, but of hunger, the upper part of the beak growing so much that its hook cannot be opened. They are active from midday and fly in the early hours of the day, until the marketplaces of men fill with crowds, then sit idle. The feathers of eagles, mixed with the feathers of other birds, consume them. It is said that this bird alone is never struck lifeless by lightning, and for this reason custom has judged it the armor-bearer of Jupiter.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the eagle has straight and extended wings, but curved at the tip; a right foot larger than the left; it gladly sits turned toward the sun. Sitting, it always looks at its claws, lest they have grown too curved. Nor does it sit long on a stone, lest their sharpness be blunted. This alone among birds is never struck by lightning. All noble birds, at the sight of it, grow greatly afraid, and lose their boldness that day, nor can they easily fly to hunt prey. Of the gerfalcon alone is it said that it catches the eagle, and in this its boldness is blamed as if guilty of treason, for injuring the queen of birds. The eagle does not carry off captured prey at once, but first sets it down and, having tested its weight, goes off according to its strength. It shares its prey with other birds and allows them to eat with it. But if the food placed before it is not enough, it seizes one of the birds feeding with it and eats it. The crow pursues the eagle, but when the eagle has long ignored it, it at last seizes it with its claws. The eagle is also said, by its imperious cry alone, to check the movement of other birds. Its long fasting is compensated by taking a great quantity of food at once. That the feathers of eagles, joined to the feathers of other birds, corrode them, has often been tested with feathered arrows, when these feathers and those of other birds are placed together in a quiver.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the eagle, then, flies loftily and dwells among rocks. It sharpens its beak, they say, on rock. It is the king of birds, as the lion is of wild beasts and the ox of beasts of burden. It hunts doves and other small or middling birds. It fasts until midday, and then flies to hunt. It places a gem in its nest, to defend its young from serpents. Alone among birds it gazes at the sun in its full circle. It also brings its young to the sun's ray: it tests their blood, licks its wings, renews itself, fishes for fish, and, when it stands, looks at its claws; it is tawny outside, like the kite. It is noisy, and lives by plunder. Whence the verse: it flies high, dwells on rocks, sharpens its beak, is king, hunts, fasts, has a gem, the wheel of the sun; it tests its young by the sun, licks, a spring renews its wings; tawny, watching its claws, it preys on fish, its voice resounds.

Pliny: among the birds we know, the eagle has the greatest honor and the greatest power. There are six kinds of these.
