The 'melenetos,' otherwise called 'melenotes' by the Greeks, and the same in Valeria - smallest in size but preeminent in strength, blackish in color. Alone among eagles it nourishes its own young. For the others, as we shall say, drive them off. Alone it is without cry or murmur. It dwells, moreover, in the mountains. Of the second kind is the 'pygargus,' in towns and fields, with a whitening tail. The third, called 'morphos' by Homer, and 'percnos,' some also call it 'plancus' and the 'duck-eagle,' whose life is near lakes, second in size and strength: Phemonoe, said to be Apollo's daughter, reported it to have teeth, and otherwise to be mute and lacking a tongue. This same one is the blackest of eagles, with a more prominent tail. Boethius agrees too. It has the trick of breaking seized tortoises by dropping them from a height, and this fate killed the poet Aeschylus, foretold, they say, by fate as the ruin of that day, though he trusted in the secure safety of the open sky. Likewise, of the fourth kind is the 'percnopterus,' which likewise dwells around lakes, of vulture-like appearance, with very small wings but excelling the rest in size, but unwarlike and degenerate, since indeed it is beaten by the crow. This same one is always of a hungry greediness and a plaintive murmuring; alone among eagles it strikes lifeless bodies. For the others, when they kill, settle upon them. It does not do as the fifth kind does, which is called the 'genesion,' truly and alone of unspoiled origin, of middling size, of a reddish hue, rarely seen. There remains the one with the clearest keenness of eye, balancing itself from on high, and, having spotted a fish in the sea, plunges headlong upon it and, spreading the waters with its breast, seizes it. The one we made third seeks out water birds around ponds, plunging repeatedly until it seizes them, drowsy and tired. A struggle worth watching is that of the bird making for the refuge of the shores, especially if the reeds are dense, and the eagle, in its swoop, driving it off, and, when it dives into the lakes, falling too, and, as it swims beneath the water, showing its shadow from the shore; and again the bird, emerging in a different spot, where it believes it least expected to be seen. This is the reason birds swim in flocks, because many together are not attacked, the enemy being blinded by a spray of feathers. Often even eagles themselves, unable to bear the weight seized, are drowned together with it. The sea-eagle, moreover, striking even its still-unfeathered chicks, forces them repeatedly to gaze against the sun's rays. And if it notices one blinking and weeping, it casts it out of the nest as if illegitimate and degenerate. But the one whose gaze has stood firm against the sun, it raises. Sea-eagles have no proper kind of their own, but are born from the varied mating of eagles. What is born from these has the kind of the 'ossifrage,' from which the smaller vultures are bred, and from these the larger ones, which do not breed at all. Some add a kind of eagle they call the 'bearded' one, but the Etruscans call it the 'ossifrage.' In the nests of the first three kinds and the fifth kind of eagle, the stone 'aetites' is built in, which some have called 'gagates,' useful for many remedies, losing nothing to fire. This stone, moreover, is pregnant, with something sounding inside when you shake it, as if in another womb. But that medicinal power exists only in stones taken from the nest. The first and second kinds prey not only on smaller quadrupeds, but even do battle with stags. And, gathering much dust by rolling in it, it shakes it, settling on the stag's antlers, into its eyes, beating its face with its wings, until it drives it over a cliff. Its fight with the dragon is fiercer, and much more uncertain if it takes place in the air: here the dragon, with malicious greed, pursues the eagle's eggs. But the eagle, for this reason, seizes it wherever it sees it. And the dragon binds its wings in a manifold coil, entangling itself so that they fall together.

The same, in the same book: eagles nest on rocks and in trees, and lay three eggs, hatching two chicks - sometimes even three have been seen - and drive out the other, weary of raising it. For at that time nature has denied them food, foreseeing that otherwise the young of all wild creatures would be seized. Their claws, too, are turned inward during these days; their feathers whiten from want of food, so that they rightly come to hate their own offspring; but the cast-out young are taken up and raised, along with their own, by the kindred kind of the ossifrage. But the parent still pursues even the grown young and drives them far off, as rivals for prey. Otherwise a single pair of eagles, needing a great range to plunder for their fill, would go hungry: they mark out their own territory, then, and do not prey nearby.

Aristotle: the eagle broods its eggs for thirty days, and is so burdened in the nest that it cannot hunt. And so it can feed no more than two chicks. Whence it casts out the third egg or the third chick. But as soon as it sees that its young can fly, it strikes them with its wings and casts them from the nest.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: [a fragmentary note attributed to Juba, on] the young: [it places] amethyst in its nest, and by it drives away venom from them.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the eagle builds its nest in the highest trees, where an evil beast cannot reach, and, carefully guarding its young, does not abandon them until they know how and are able to protect themselves. And so, against a dragon or a man or another animal, if it wishes to trouble or seize them, it fights with wondrous spirit and exposes itself to the danger of death for their sake, and even lifts them on its shoulders, so as to encourage them to fly. It is also said to have a certain foreknowledge, so that, however far it is from its young, it senses their enemies approaching. It also teaches them to lick blood. It has the stone 'aetites' in its nest, which, as if pregnant, has within it a small offspring-stone that sounds; and this it has against the excessive heat which the eagle naturally has in its nest, so that the eggs are not spoiled by being cooked in too much heat, for the heat of fire cannot harm this stone. Other philosophers say too that it places two precious stones called 'indi' in its nest, without which it cannot give birth. The eagle fasts for many days; it drives off its grown young, chasing them far away as rivals for prey. There is also a most wicked kind of eagle, which expels its young before their time, weary of raising them. The reason, according to Aristotle, is that after brooding it becomes so weakened that it cannot hunt; even its claws become curved, so that it cannot hold prey; its wings whiten and grow heavy, so that it can scarcely fly. Eagle chicks are without cry or murmur. There is a large eagle dwelling in the north, which always lays two eggs, as Pliny says, suspended among the tops of branches, and, having caught a hare or a fox, strips off its hide little by little and wraps its eggs in that fur and places them under the warmth of the sun; and thus, leaving them, it does not brood them, but waits until they break open by natural ripeness. It returns, however, when the young are about to walk, and then nourishes them until full strength.

Aristotle: because of its own heat, the eagle places very cold stones next to its eggs, lest the eggs be spoiled by its heat. Its young, held up on high to the sun's rays, which cannot bear it, it casts out as degenerate; nature, however, provides them what is necessary: it carefully carries its young, perched on its back, and interposes its own body between them and the archer, like a shield, so that, if necessary, it takes the blow itself.

[Augustine on] eagles: the eagle is said, when weighed down by old age, to be unable, because of the excessive hooked growth of its beak, to open its mouth and take food, and so grows weak from this; but by a certain natural method it strikes its beak against a rock and shakes off the excess of the beak, and thus returns to feeding, and everything is restored to it, so that it becomes young again, whence it is said: your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's.
The Ordinary Gloss: the eagle, indeed, queen of birds, at a certain time, having lost its feathers, remains featherless. Whence the prophet says: extend your baldness like the eagle's.
The Ordinary Gloss, on Ezekiel: for when the eagle is afflicted by old age, it loses the feathers and wings with which it was accustomed to go hunting.

From Papias: the Physiologus says the eagle has this nature: when it grows old, its wings grow heavy and a mist covers its eyes; then it seeks a spring of living water and flies up against it, high into the ether of the sun. And there it burns its wings, and at the same time burns away the mist of its eyes from the sun's rays. Then finally, descending, it plunges into the spring and is at once entirely renewed, so that, in vigor of wing and brightness of eye, it is renewed for the better.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: the eagle, its feathers aging and its sight dimmed, rising up three times, sharpens its sight and wings against the sun, and, descending each time, plunges into the spring 'semoth' and sharpens its beak on a rock. And thus, three times, its sight, feathers, and beak are restored. If it attempts this a fourth time, then it dies.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the eagle is a great and most noble bird, being the queen of birds, which, when weighed down by old age, flies up high above all the clouds, and, from the sun's heat, the mist of its eyes is consumed, and soon, descending swiftly with the very heat's onset, plunges three times into the coldest waters. And rising from these, it at once seeks its nest and, among its now grown young, gripped as if by a kind of fever from the imbalance of cold and heat as it hunts for prey, sheds its feathers with a certain sweat, and is warmed by its own young and fed, until, recovering its feathers and down, it is renewed.
Aesculapius: eagle's gall, mixed with honey, heals suffused eyes.
Pliny, book [unspecified]: they say that clarity of sight is restored by eagle's brain or gall mixed with Attic honey.
The same, in the same book: eagle's gall, which we said the young are tested with by gazing at the sun, mixed with Attic honey, is applied to films, clouding, and suffusions of the eyes.

The same, book 30: for pain of the loins, an eagle's feet, torn off at the joint, are bound on - the right for pains of the right side, the left likewise; besides this, eagle's brain in three cups of wine resists jaundice.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: moreover, as said above, according to Pliny, in the nests of certain kinds of eagles the stone 'aetites' is built, useful for many medicinal remedies, losing nothing to fire. Yet this medicinal power exists only in stones taken from the nest. Let the reader seek more on this stone above, in the treatise on the more notable stones. Now let us proceed, in order, through the other birds according to the alphabet, as we have begun.

div.head: DE ARDEA ET ARDEOLA ET ASALON ET ASIDA

cit.quote: [Isidore:] the heron is named as if 'ardua' [steep], because of its steep flights. Whence Lucan: and the heron, that dared to fly. When it flies higher, it signifies a storm. Many call this bird the 'tantalus.'
Ambrose: the heron, accustomed to keep to the marshes, abandons its known haunts and, dreading rain, flies above the clouds, so as not to feel the storms of rain.
Pliny, book 18: the heron, when it stands sadly amid the sands, foretells dread storms.

From the book On the Nature of Things: though the heron seeks its food in the waters, it nevertheless places its nest in woods and tall trees. It is said, moreover, that it strives to defend its young with wondrous firmness. The hawk is hostile to them, but the heron turns its rear toward it and discharges its dung, at whose touch the hawk's feathers rot. They have a single intestine, like the stork, and most of them have an ash-grey color, though some are white. There is a certain kind of these whose males are distressed in mating with great cries, and pour forth blood from their eyes in pain; nor do the females suffer less in giving birth. There is also a kind of heron differing from the rest only by the size of its beak, which is indeed half a cubit in the front part and more than three fingers in breadth, and seems to have been created for this alone, that it may seek its livelihood more conveniently from it; this bird lives on fish, which, once every effort to escape is foiled, it seizes with its beak and swallows. There is also a kind of these, as Pliny says, that has only one eye, with which it can see; from this it happens that it can be caught more quickly by the fowler.

There are three kinds of little herons, namely the 'leucon,' the 'asterias,' the 'pellos': these are distressed in mating. For the males, in mating, with a great cry, even pour forth blood from their eyes; nor do the pregnant females suffer less in giving birth. Shrews and little herons are at odds with one another, each lying in wait for the other's young.
[Pliny says] of the kinds of little herons, that the one called the 'leucos' is said to lack one eye.

The merlin is a small bird, which breaks the raven's eggs; its chicks are troubled by foxes. But it in turn plucks at the fox cubs and the vixen itself, which, when the raven sees it, it helps the fox against, as against a common enemy. This bird lives among thorns, and for this reason hates asses, which devour the flowers and leaves of thorn-bushes. This name is found varied in different manuscripts. For sometimes it is 'asalon,' as here, sometimes 'assalon,' sometimes 'aschelon,' sometimes 'esolon,' and perhaps such variety arose by the error and fault of scribes.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'asida,' according to the Physiologus, is the ostrich itself, of which more will be said below.

div.head: DE ATHACO ET AVIBUS PARADISI ET AURIFRIGIO

cit.quote: Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'athacus,' of which one reads in Leviticus, is a bird unknown even to Jewish experts.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: birds of paradise are so commonly named, not because they are from paradise, but because of their remarkable beauty; for they are of such splendor and glory that no color is believed lacking to them. Their size is that of a goose. Their voice is so sweet and gentle that it can stir devotion and joy in a man. If it is ever caught and ensnared, it groans and does not cease lamenting until restored to freedom. It gladly dwells along the river Nile and is rarely found elsewhere. There are also other birds in the same regions, called by the same name, of a dark and somewhat reddish color, smaller than jackdaws. They are called birds of paradise because it is not known whence they come or whither they go. For their mating is never seen, but at certain times, gathered together, they leave the lands they had inhabited before crossing over, and thus depart. The 'auriphrygius' is a bird so called, as if 'following the Phrygian breeze.' They have one foot with hooked claws for hunting, but the other broad, for swimming. It makes manifold circles in the air, now as if playing, now as if lying in wait, until, spotting prey in the waters, it descends violently, seizing the prey with one foot, while the other, swimming, helps it seize.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the 'bartlathes' are birds growing from wood, which the common people call 'bernacas' [barnacle geese]. It is said, indeed, that when fir wood falls into the waters of the sea, in the course of time, when it begins to rot, it gives off a thick moisture, from which, thickened, small forms of birds are shaped, the size of larks. At first they are bare, then, ripening, they grow feathers and, hanging by their beaks to the wood, float on the sea until maturity, until, stirring themselves, they break free, and so grow and become strong up to their proper form. We ourselves have seen many of these, and trustworthy men who testified they had seen them still hanging. They are smaller than geese, of an ash-grey and black color. Their feet are like a duck's, but black. Of these, Bishop James of Acre, speaking in his history of the East, says that there are trees along the shores of the sea, from which these are produced, hanging with their beaks fixed to the trees. But at the time of maturity they fall from the trees and, growing by stages, begin to fly like other birds. Yet unless, once fallen, they quickly find water, they cannot live, since in the waters is their nourishment and their life. It should be noted, moreover, that they hang not at the tops of the branches, but on the bark and trunks of the trees. They grow, moreover, by the tree's moisture and the infusion of dew, until, having feathers and the strength of life, they break away from the bark. Of these, then, it is certain that in our part of the world, around Germany, they neither breed by mating nor are bred by mating. Nor has any man among us seen their mating. Whence some, even Christians, in our own age, in places where there is an abundance of such birds, have been accustomed to eat their flesh during Lent. But Pope Innocent III, at the general Lateran Council, forbade this to be done any further. These birds live on grasses and herbage, like geese. But they cannot at all forgo drink when eating dry food.
The Philosopher: the barnacle goose, which is born from a tree, is also found in certain parts of Flanders. This bird has no bodily waste, just as trees do not.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the bustard is a bird the size of an eagle, which, slow in flight, makes two or three leaps on the ground before it rises into the sky, whence indeed it is said to have its name. It has claws like an eagle's and a hooked beak; it feeds on flesh, yet does not seize prey in flight, but if it finds a sheep or another defenseless animal anywhere, several of them gather and cast down and kill what they find, and thus are sated on its flesh; it also feeds most gladly on carcasses. It is almost the only one, among flesh-eating birds, that also grazes on plants. It has white on the wings and tail; in the rest of its coloring it resembles the eagle. It does not lay its eggs in trees, since it cannot fly high, but lays them on the ground and broods them there while the crop is still standing. The 'bonosa' is a bird in the regions of Germany, having flesh black outside, white within, delicate, close to the taste of the partridge. It has the size of a pheasant. And when the season arouses mating, the male runs with open mouth, until it foams at the mouth; then the female comes and receives the foam in her mouth, and from this conceives and lays eggs.

Isidore: the eagle-owl has a name composed from the sound of its voice, a deathly bird, indeed burdened with feathers. But, always held by heavy sluggishness, it frequents tombs by night and day, always dwelling in caves. Of it [the poet says]: an ill-omened bird, herald of coming grief, the sluggish eagle-owl, a dire omen for mortals. Finally, among augurs it is said to portend evil. For when it is seen in a city, they say solitude is signified.

Pliny, book 10: the eagle-owl, funereal and abhorred, especially in public auspices, dwells in deserted places, and not only desolate ones but dire and inaccessible ones, a monster of the night, with no melodious song, but a groan. And so, seen in cities, or at all in daylight, it is a dire portent; I know very many cases where it lay in wait around private houses without being funereal. It never flies in a straight line, but is carried sideways. The eagle-owl, moreover, has hooked claws, like the owl and the screech-owl. And the eyes of all of these are dull by day. Illaphus relates that the eagle-owl, the owl, and the woodpecker hollow out trees.
The same, book 11: among feathered creatures, only the eagle-owl and the 'otus' have feathers like ears; the rest have hollows for hearing.

Radulphus of Flaix, on Leviticus: the eagle-owl hides by day and comes out by night, since it fears the other birds. For it is hateful to all, so that, once seen, it is at once mobbed by all with cries, or even torn apart.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the eagle-owl has its name from the sound of its voice; it flees the light, dwells in churches and drinks oil from the lamps, yet befouls them with its droppings; it also drinks doves' eggs; it hunts mice, and by this too other birds are caught. But when it is attacked by those birds that dwell in the light, it defends itself lying on its back with the claws of its feet. For Pliny says it comes out of the egg tail-first, because the weight of the head makes the mother apply the rear part of the body to be warmed.

Aristotle: the eagle-owl, like the bat, gets its food at night, and, with few kinds of birds, has only two toes on the front part of the feet and two behind. It turns one toe backward, and has a large tongue and large claws like an eagle's, and cries out loudly. The jackdaw fights with the eagle-owl, because the eagle-owl has weak sight at midday. And so the raven seizes and eats the eagle-owl's eggs, for the raven is indeed stronger by day and the eagle-owl by night. And so the eagle-owl and the raven are hostile to each other over their nests. The raven eats the eagle-owl's eggs at midday, and the eagle-owl eats the raven's eggs at night. The other birds, too, fly around the eagle-owl and strip its feathers. For many kinds of birds hate it.
Avicenna: the blood of the eagle-owl greatly benefits asthma, and likewise its broth and flesh.
Physiologus: if the eagle-owl's heart is placed on the left side of a sleeping woman, she will, it is said, tell everything she has done.
Pliny, book [unspecified]: the burnt feet of the eagle-owl with the herb pennyroyal help against serpents. The ash of its eyes, mixed into an eye-salve, is said to give clarity to the eyes.
The same, book 30: the ash of the eagle-owl's eyes is also applied to the frenzied.

The buzzard is of the hawk kind, but a little darker and quite slow and sluggish in flight; it lives on prey, however, which it can catch through cunning or by some weakness or sluggishness holding it back. This bird is most sweet in taste. The bittern is a bird so named from the sound of its voice; it has long legs, an extended neck, and a long, sharp beak, like the heron's, though differing from it in color, for it is most similar to the earth. It dwells around fishponds, eager for food, and even eats frogs and venomous things. This alone, in springtime, gives out a horrible cry instead of a song. And it is said to be unable to do this unless it plunges its head into the water, so that the density of the element within it renders its captured voice resonant, like a kind of thundering. On the shore, in the heat of the sun, in a place it knows fish frequent, it stands so still that it appears as if dead, whence it happens that it is less suspected by wary fish. But though it has a long neck, it makes it short by curving it, so that, when fish, unwary, approach it as if it were thinking of nothing, it draws them to itself by extending its neck. And when it knows it is caught in a snare, it feigns stillness, and when the approaching fowler thinks to catch it by hand, it, seizing him unexpectedly with the weapon of its beak, which it uses with great power, wounds him by piercing. This same bird, too, sleeping and waking, always keeps its long and very sharp beak raised to defend itself, and when the hawk tries to seize it, rushes onto its beak to its death. Its flesh, when roasted at the fire, gives off a marvelous smell, and for this reason it is often served at the tables of the rich. Its fat, then, is said to be useful for remedies.

Physiologus: the bittern is named as if 'bootaurus,' because it seems to imitate the bellowing, that is, the lowing, of a bull. For it fixes its beak in the marshy ground and gives forth cries like a bull's. Once hatched, the mother at once places her chicks beneath her armpits, one under one side and the other under the other. But the chicks, clinging to the mother's body, project their beaks near the tips of her wings. And the mother, warming her chicks beneath her wings, sweetly offers food to the projecting beaks of her young.
Vincentius Belvacensis: [see] the pelican [onocrotalus, cross-referenced below].

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the caladrius, as is said, is unclean according to the Law. The Physiologus says it is a bird entirely white, having no black part, whose inner droppings cure clouding of the eyes. It is found in the courts of kings; through it one knows of a sick man whether he will live or die. For if he is sick unto death, as soon as it sees him, it turns its face away from him. But if not unto death, it fixes its gaze upon him and takes on all his illnesses and disperses them, and the sick man is healed.

Aristotle: the caladrius does not look at a sick man if he must die, but if he can recover, and wishes to see him, it draws all his illness to itself. And so he is made well and the bird sick, so much so that it often dies in his place. This bird has one thick bone in the leg, whose marrow, if applied to clouded eyes, makes them clear and of good sight.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the caladrius is a white bird, which, if brought to a sick man to heal him, gathers all his illnesses into itself and, flying into the air, burns them up there and disperses them. The inner part of its thigh removes clouding from the eyes. These birds are said to have been found by Alexander in Persia. The crested lark is a small bird, nearly similar to the lark, dusky in color, unremarkable in feather, but gladdens its hearers with the wondrous modulation of its voice. It also imitates, distinctly, the voices of all birds. And so, when caught and shut in a cage, forgetful there too of its captivity and misfortune, it scarcely lets an hour of the day pass without song, and delights so much in wandering through the varied songs of birds that it is not even anxious for food.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the capon is called a castrated cock or domestic fowl, of which indeed more will be said below; these are castrated so that they may fatten more easily and be eaten more tender.

Dioscorides: live capons, opened and applied, counter venomous bites, if changed frequently. Capon's brain is better than others'. Taken in wine, it checks the flow of blood. The dried, pounded, and drunk skin of its gizzard is good for the stomach with wine. A light broth of it, simply prepared, soothes lesser inflammations of the stomach; but a stronger, more elaborately prepared broth softens the belly, and expels raw humors, that is, black bile. It is useful for periodic fevers and typhoid illnesses, tremors, and inflations of the stomach, and is a singular remedy for arthritic pain. The gall of a white capon is of great power, being good for discharge of the eyes and for clouding and roughness of the eyelids.

Goatsuckers are called larger-looking blackbirds; they are nocturnal thieves, for by day they lack sight; they enter shepherds' stables and fly to the udders of goats for the sake of sucking their milk, by which injury indeed the udder withers, and blindness arises in the goats they have thus milked.
Vincentius Belvacensis: the goatsucker is the same bird that Aristotle calls the 'agochiles,' of which more has been said above.

Aristotle: it is a mountain bird, a little larger than a blackbird, of cunning habit, rarely seen by day, nor does it see well then, but its sight sharpens by night; it sucks milk from the udders of goats. Whence it is called 'agochiles,' that is, one who sucks the milk of goats. It lives by night, and stays among stones by day.

div.head: DE CHARADRIO ET CARDULE ET CARISTA

cit.quote: Radulphus of Flaix, on Leviticus: the 'charadrius' is a chattering bird, of which it is read in Leviticus that it is unclean according to the Law.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: this is the same bird spoken of above as the crested lark; those are mistaken who think this is the caladrius, as the interlinear gloss says on Deuteronomy.

Isidore: the goldfinch [carduelis] is so called because it feeds on thorns and thistles [carduis]. Whence among the Greeks it is called 'acanthis,' from 'acanthae,' that is, the thorns on which it feeds. Augurs, moreover, say that signs are set in the bearing, movement, and flight of birds.

Pliny: goldfinches, smallest of birds, do what is commanded, not only by voice, but with their feet and mouth in place of hands. There is one that imitates the lowing of cattle, called the 'bull' in the territory of Arles. There is one, called by the name 'anthus,' that imitates the neighing of horses, driven from its pasture-herb by their approach, avenging itself in this manner.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the goldfinch is a small bird, black and saffron on the body, adorned with a red color on the head. It seems marvelous that this little bird feeds on the sharp thorns of thistles. In this, then, appears a marvel of nature, which gave it a cunning that it was unwilling to grant to the ox or the ass, great animals, namely that, enclosed in a cage, it draws to itself with its beak water placed below by a thread hung from a little vessel, and, its foot sometimes also placed on the thread, when it reaches the vessel, quenches its thirst with drink. Caryatid birds, as Solinus says, are birds that fly into flames unharmed, so that neither their feathers nor their flesh yield at all to the flames of fire.

Isidore: storks [ciconiae], as if 'cicaniae,' are so named from the sound they make by clacking, which sound, it is agreed, comes from the mouth rather than the voice, since they make it by beating their beak. These, heralds of spring, companions in society, enemies of serpents, fly across the seas, and travel to Asia in a gathered column. Crows go before them as leaders, and follow them as if an army.

You would think storks in flight an army marching with its standards, so entirely do they all keep an order of traveling and accompanying. Crows, moreover, lead and direct them and press close around them, so much so that they are believed to help them in battling against enemy birds and to take up others' wars at their own peril. For, returning even wounded, they speak to the others by the clear evidence of their blood and other signs, that they have undergone the conflict of grave battles.

Solinus: they say storks have no tongue, and it is agreed that the sound they make by clacking comes from the mouth rather than the voice; they consider it wrong to harm them, everywhere indeed, but especially in Thessaly, where there is a monstrous abundance of serpents, which, while storks pursue them for food, they draw off a great deal of harm from the regions of Thessaly.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: so great is the honor given to storks in Thessaly for the destruction of serpents that it was a capital offense to kill a stork, as also a man, for they lie in wait for serpents in many ways and eat them and other venomous things, yet do not die. But they eat a toad only in great hunger, in which the natural evil of the toad is noted. The stork, moreover, seems to have a head very prone to catarrh, since its beak is a remedy against venomous things. They return to their nests yearly, and cast down one of their young, feathered, to the master of the place where they breed, as a kind of tribute, it is said. But perhaps the cause is more weariness of raising it. Preparing to depart, as Solinus says, they gather in a certain place, so that none of their kind is left behind except as a captive. In Asia there is a field where, gathered together, they murmur among themselves, and tear apart the one that arrives last, and thus depart. The stork divides the hours of the day by its clacking; it knows how to purge its bowels with its beak, whence, in imitation of it, Galen invented the enema. In winter it hides in the waters; in spring it rises onto dry land.

Pliny, in the same place: from what place storks come, or to what place they return, is still unknown. That they come from afar is not doubted, in the same way as cranes, the latter being winter migrants, the former summer ones. No one has seen either the departing or the arriving column; both happen at night. Storks return to the same nests, and in turn nourish the old age of their parents.
The same, in the same book: the stork, too, heals itself with oregano.
The same, book 29: it is said that whoever has eaten a stork chick does not suffer bleary eyes for the following years. The stork's stomach, too, is effective against all poisons.
The same, same book: the stork's stomach, boiled in wine.
Dioscorides: stork's dung, given to drink with water, cures epileptics.

Ambrose: the devotion and mercy of storks, too, is to be considered. For, once the father's limbs, stripped of feathers by long old age, are set down, the offspring standing around warm him with their own feathers. And what shall I say? They feed him with gathered food, when they even repair nature's very losses, so that, lifting the old one from side to side, they train him, with the support of their wings, to fly, so as to bring his unaccustomed limbs back to their former use. Which of us would not shrink from lifting a sick father? Which of us would place an aged brother on his own shoulders? But for birds, what is full of devotion is not burdensome. Whence this bird, by Roman custom, is called the devoted bird.

[Isidore, on storks:] their young, their nests, their chicks. For by their constant sitting they shed their feathers, and for as long a time as they spend raising their young, for that same time they in turn are nourished by their chicks.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the stork is called the devoted bird, for when the older storks, their feathers gone, cannot obtain their own food, the younger ones, warming their parents' cold limbs, provide for their feeding until their wing regains its strength. Nor is there doubt that they are devoted followers of chastity and keep the bond of marriage faithfully with one another. Whence it is said that a pair of storks dwelt in a high place of a certain house, and that, while the male often withdrew to feed, another male, coming, would defile the female with adulterous union. But she would at once plunge herself into a distant pool, and thus, washing away the crime of adultery with water, deceive her own mate. The master of the house often noticed this happening, and one day, after the adultery, kept her from the pool so that she could not wash. Without delay her mate, returning from feeding, discovered the crime of adultery upon his mate, and, concealing it for the time, went away. And returning the next day, he brought with him a great multitude of storks, which, attacking her one by one, tore the wretched adulteress apart in a cruel death.

Isidore: the swan is called 'cygnus' in Greek, 'olor' in Latin, because it is entirely white in feather; for 'holon' in Greek means 'whole.' 'Cygnus,' moreover, is named from singing, because it pours forth the sweetness of song in modulated tones. And they say it sings sweetly for this reason, that it has a long and bending neck, and the voice, struggling through such a long and winding passage, must necessarily produce varied modulations. They say that in the Hyperborean regions, at the leading song of the lyre-players, very many swans fly up and sing in fitting harmony. Sailors, moreover, say this bird makes a good omen for them, as Aemilius says: the swan, in the auspices, is always the most joyful bird; sailors wish for it, because it does not drown in the waves.

Aristotle: the swan is of the kind of birds having webbing between their toes. It stays on the shores of lakes and in places of many trees. It is of good life and nature and good old age; birds of this kind do not begin to fight against the hawk. But if the hawk begins to fight with them, they fight against it and defeat it.
Pliny: it is related, by false accounts I believe, that swans sing mournfully at death; the same swans feed on one another's flesh.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: the swan bird does not delight in the least in sweet song, but when it sings most sweetly, this signifies that it draws nearer to its death.

Ambrose: the swan's songs delight under the grave terror of imminent death. It gives forth natural melodies of song with which the marshes resound with most sweet gentleness. The swan has a rather long neck, so that, since it is somewhat sluggish in body and cannot easily penetrate the depths of the waters, it extends its neck for prey and seizes it from the depths.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the swan has white feathers but black flesh, its strength in its wings; it is of choleric temperament, and therefore prone to anger. It has very tiny teeth in its beak, with which it cuts its food; it is impatient of burdens and does not fly gladly, but delights in resting on ponds; it swims with one foot and steers itself with the other like a rudder; raised among fish, it is harmless to them. It nests over the water, attentive in raising its young; at mating time male and female caress one another and bend their heads, that is their necks, alternately, as if for an embrace. Without delay, once they have mated, the male, aware of having hurt the female, flees from her. But she, impatient, pursues the fleeing male; yet that resentment does not persist long; indeed, the hurt ceasing, her mind is calmed, and, ceasing to pursue the male, after mating she purifies herself, plunging into the water with frequent motion of tail and beak. Swans, when about to migrate to another place for food, gather and travel in such swimming formation that they are carried by the thrust of their beaks, so as more easily to cleave the air than if they pushed with their foreheads. From the rear they gradually spread out, and the flock is drawn out in a wedge; they rest their necks on those in front, and, when the leader tires, they take him up at the rear. A swan struck on the head dies easily, though it can endure many other injuries. When death is imminent, it fixes a feather in its brain and thus sings sweetly, for it naturally precedes its own death with a song of joy and rejoicing.

Fulgentius, book 2 of the Mythologies: the Physiologists relate that this bird is so full of reproaches that, when it cries, the other birds present fall silent. Whence it is called 'olor,' as if from 'hyperbole,' which in Latin means 'insult.'

div.head: DE CYNOMULGO ET CYPSETO ET CITRAMO

cit.quote: Isidore: the cinnamon-bird [cinomulgus] is a bird of Arabia, so named because it weaves its nest, in high groves, out of cinnamon shrubs. And because men cannot climb there, on account of the height and fragility of the branches, they bring down these same nests with lead-weighted darts and take that cinnamon and sell it at higher prices, since merchants judge that cinnamon better than the rest.
[Pliny:] the bird called the cinnamon-bird nests in sprigs of cinnamon, and so they bring these down with lead-weighted arrows, for the sake of this unworthy merchandise.

Aristotle: the cinnamon-bird is a little larger than a sparrow, and its color is sky-blue mixed with yellow, and these colors are distinct in it. Its beak is long, inclining to yellow; on tall trees, made of cinnamon, as is said, it builds its nest spherically, having a small entrance.

Pliny: swifts, also called 'apodes' because they lack the use of feet, fly the most, resembling swallows; they nest in cliffs; these are seen over the whole sea. And ships never depart so long or so continuous a course from land that swifts do not fly around them. Other kinds settle and rest; for these there is no rest except in the nest; they either hang or lie, and their skills for feeding are equally varied.

Aristotle: the kind of bird that has no feet appears at every season; this bird is long, slender, and of little breadth, resembling the swallow. Nor is it easily distinguished from those; it nests in summer, and this behind stones, so as to avoid animals and men.
Pliny: the 'citramus' urges on its companion birds as they return, and perseveres steadily to reach the lands awaited for it, and, even at night, rouses them, reminding them of the journey.
Aristotle: the 'eokeramamor' bird cries out to the other birds by night, and hunters, hearing this, know that the birds will not remain in their places.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the 'citramus' is a bird of Asia which, as winter approaches, accompanying the departing swallows and storks, perseveres more swiftly and, going ahead, urges them on.

The cuckoo seems to be produced from a hawk, changing its shape with the season of the year. For at that time the other hawks do not appear, except for a few days. This bird, too, seen for only a short part of summer, is afterward not seen at all. It is, moreover, neither hook-clawed like hawks alone, nor similar to them in head, nor in anything but color and sight; it is more like a dove in head and claws. Indeed it is consumed by the hawk, if they ever appear together, the only bird among all destroyed by its own kind. It also changes its voice; it comes forth in spring, hides at the rising of the Dog Star; and it always lays, for the most part, single eggs, in the nests of others, especially of wood-pigeons - which no other bird does, though rarely two. The reason for placing its young there is thought to be that it knows itself hated by all birds. For even the tiny ones attack it, and so it supposes its offspring will not be safe unless it deceives them; for this reason it makes no nest, being otherwise a fearful creature; it raises, then, an adulterated brood placed in another's nest. That chick, greedy by nature, snatches food from the other chicks; and so it grows fat and sleek, and turns the foster-mother to itself. She, indeed, rejoices in its appearance and marvels at herself for having borne such a creature, and condemns her own chicks by comparison with it, as if they were strangers. She even allows her own to be destroyed while she watches, until it seizes her too, once able to fly. Yet no bird's flesh compares to it in sweetness.
Aristotle: the cuckoo has few eggs, one or two, since its nature is very cold.

Isidore: doves are so named because their necks change color at each turn. They are gentle birds, dwelling among crowds of men, and without gall, which the ancients called 'birds of Venus,' because they frequent their nests and conceive love through a kiss.

The Ordinary Gloss: the dove is without gall, does not harm with its beak, nests in the caves of rocks, nourishes the young of others, stays near flowing waters, chooses the better grains, gives a moan instead of a song, flies in flocks, defends itself with its wings, recovers its sight.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the dove, as is read, sits over the waters, so as, seeing the hawk's shadow beforehand in the water, to avoid it.

Physiologus: [the dove and] the dragon. It says doves are of various colors: white, black, red, sky-blue, ash-grey, golden, reddish. There is, moreover, a tree in India called in Greek 'peridexion,' in Latin 'around the right,' whose fruit is exceedingly sweet and pleasant. Doves delight in this tree, since they are both refreshed by its fruit and rest in its shade and are sheltered by its branches. There is, moreover, a cruel dragon, enemy of doves. But it so avoids and fears that tree that it does not dare even approach its shadow. But if its shadow falls on the right side, the dragon stands on the left, and vice versa, so that if it sees a dove even slightly or lightly separated from the tree, it seizes and devours it. But the doves, knowing its hatred, gather there in the tree.

Pliny: doves and turtledoves, when they drink, do not tilt their neck back, and drink freely, in the manner of beasts of burden. Doves and turtledoves, moreover, live eight years, and, seeing a hawk, either sit still or fly up against it, helping themselves against its nature. For some hawks seize a bird only from the ground; others only while flying near trees; others one sitting high; others one flying in the open.

Aristotle: in birds of a hot stomach the spleen is very small and hidden from sight, as in the dove and the hawk. Likewise some birds rub themselves in ash and wash themselves, like the sparrow and doves. The dove, like the quail and swallow, has its gall attached to the intestine. Doves, like turtledoves, when drinking, do not raise their head until they have had enough. They kiss before mating. They recognize the different kinds of hawks and guard against them in different ways, as said above.

The dove, as Bede says, lacks gall. Yet Aristotle says it has gall, not in the place other animals have it, but in the intestine. It does not live on carrion, but on pure grain; it recovers its sight nine times. It nests high, where an evil beast cannot reach; it gladly rests over the waters, so as to quench its thirst and watch for the shadow of an approaching hawk in the water. But sometimes it sits alone, admiring its varied colors around its neck, and smooths its little feathers with the applause of its wings and beak, and arranges its plumage for the governance of flight and finer grooming. Then the sparrowhawk, watching in secret, seizes it as it delights in its own glory. Doves are of the hottest nature and eat small stones for the tempering of the stomach; they also have very hot dung, which they cast out of the nest and teach their young to cast out too. With raised feathers they fight, and when they see a stray dove, they gather it to themselves. James says that across the sea, toward the East, there are doves which, performing the office of messengers, carry the letters of their masters under their wings over great distances in a short time. And so they are very necessary, especially when, through enemy lands, other messengers dare not pass. It is a peculiarity of the dove among birds not to raise its head when drinking, until it has had enough.

Palladius, in the same place: for a dovecote, a single lofty tower, set within the manor grounds, with smoothed and whitened walls, in which doves may be received and nourished, is suitable, and beneath its chamber two rooms should be made: one small and nearly dark, in which turtledoves can be kept, which are very easy to raise; the other should nourish thrushes. Of these two, indeed, more will be said fully in appropriate places below. In dovecotes, on all four sides, very small windows should be made, so as to allow only the doves entry and exit; the nests too should be shaped inside, and made safe from weasels, if old savory is thrown among them. Their wings grow in if they are constantly fed cumin, or if their bristling wings are touched with balsam liquid. Sprigs of rue should be hung in many places against harmful animals.

Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans: a 'zab,' that is, an ancient human skull, if placed in a dove-tower, doves dwell in it and rest there. But also, if the milk of a woman nursing her own daughter from two years old, kept in an earthen vessel, is hung in the tower at the entrance and exit of the doves, they dwell there and multiply.

Pliny, book [unspecified]: doves have a certain understanding of glory, so that you would believe they know their own colors and the arrangement of their variety, which are even believed, in flight, to be displayed and traced in varied patterns in the sky. In this display, as if offering themselves defeated to the hawk, their wings tangle with a rustling sound, which is struck out only from the very joints of the wings. Otherwise the thief, hidden in the foliage, watches for one much swifter than in its usual flight, and seizes it as it delights in its very glory. For this reason the bird called the kestrel should be kept with them, which defends them by terrifying hawks by a natural power, so that they flee its sight and voice. For this reason doves have a special love for these; and it is said that if kestrels are buried at the four corners of the dovecote in new, sealed pots, the doves, otherwise wandering birds, do not change their dwelling. For it is their art to charm one another and corrupt others, and return more accompanied by theft. Indeed, they have even served as messengers in great matters: letters attached to their feet were sent, during the siege of Modena, into the camp of the consuls by Decimus Brutus. What good did the rampart and the watches' siege-works, and even nets stretched across the river, do against Antony, when the message went by way of the sky?

The same: chastity is the first virtue of doves, so that they do not violate the faith of marriage; they also keep a common home. Unless single or widowed, a dove does not leave home. Love for the offspring is equal in both. Often, too, for this reason, there is correction when the female is slow to return to her chicks. In labor, comfort and service come from the male; the parents spit, into the chicks' mouths, from their throat, earth gathered more salted, preparing seasoning for the food. Doves kiss with their own beak before mating; they lay generally two eggs, nature so moderating it, that for some the brood is more frequent, for others more numerous.

The dove, it is said, having lost its bodily mate, goes about alone and no longer seeks bodily union. It is certain, however, that there are some doves that have never known a male, and others that, having had one and lost him, remain widows. The wood-pigeon is a kind of dove which, having lost its bodily mate, goes about alone and no longer seeks conjugal union, nor does it even seek any green place to rest. And indeed those that remain single or widowed avoid the company or home of the others, lest they be troubled by the disturbances of the males, and flee, and dwell among ruined walls.

Pliny, in the same place, and also from the book On the Nature of Things: females endure even unjust males. For there is suspicion of adultery, although this is not their nature; then the throat is full of complaint, and cruel blows from the beak; but soon, in reconciliation, there is kissing, and, around mating, entreaties, and flattery with frequent circling of the feet.

From the book On the Nature of Things: doves rear two chicks, always bearing a male first, and after three days a female. Male and female brood in turns, since love for the offspring is often equal in both. The female broods after midday, until morning; the male the rest of the time; and on the eighteenth day they hatch. Among the chicks, eggs are often also found; and while some fly off, others are just hatching; these chicks themselves breed at three months. The dove is greatly burdened in laying eggs, and if she is slow to lay, she is struck by the male. The male drives grown chicks from the nest, but first mates with them.
Palladius, in the same place: doves breed more if they often eat roasted barley, or beans, or bitter vetch.

Aristotle: doves lay eggs and breed throughout the year, if the dwelling place is warm and food ready; otherwise only in summer. Their chicks are better in spring and autumn, worse in winter and summer. The male mates with the female after one year of age. Dove eggs are white in color, like the partridge's. There are also wind-eggs among doves, as among hens and partridges and peacocks and geese; heavy birds of good flight, then, are of much breeding, like doves. Wood-pigeons and turtledoves lay eggs twice a year, but doves ten times. An old dove cannot mate, but only kisses. The female dove, too, mounts another female, if there is no male, and they kiss each other, and from that mating indeed they produce eggs, but do not breed chicks. Doves and other birds of much mating produce more eggs than others; among these are two yolks, from the joining of two seeds from two matings of the dove; the male broods the eggs by day, the female by night; yet the female is more anxious about the chicks. Likewise, when the dove wishes to drive its chicks from the nest, it mates with them. Finally, the dove and the partridge live and breed for fifteen years.

Dioscorides: flying doves are of lighter digestion and better taste than dove-chicks. But in chicks that cannot yet fly, there is heat and also thickness, because of excessive moisture. Dove eggs, however, are of poor taste and very hot.
From the book On the Nature of Things: dove-chicks are healthier in autumn and spring, since at these times they live mostly on grain.
Rhazes, in the same place: doves, like sparrows, are of vehement heat, and inflame the blood and cause fever.
Avicenna: in dove-chicks that cannot fly there is heat and excessive moisture, and those that can fly are lighter.

Isaac the Jew: dove-chicks are hot and abundantly moist, for which reason they give thick nourishment, which their heaviness for flight attests; but once they begin to fly, they lose this heaviness, and so their flesh becomes lighter and more acceptable for digestion. It is, however, suitable for the phlegmatic, unsuitable for the choleric and those hot by nature. Young and old doves, however, are of hard digestion. They produce a poor nourishment, harmful in generative respects.

Aesculapius: a dove, killed and applied warm, helps against every bite. Its blood, poured into congested eyes, is effective, especially when drawn from beneath the wing. Its dung dissolves all pains and dries humors.
Dioscorides: dove's blood stops bleeding of the nose that comes from the membrane of the brain. The same, warm, is dropped onto a crushed and painful abrasion.

Fresh dove's flesh helps against serpents. Wild dove's dung is effective against a draught of quicksilver. Male blood, drawn from the vein cut beneath the wing, is exceedingly beneficial for eyes suffused with blood.

Dove's dung heals bruises and discoloration. The same dung, with vinegar, removes scars. It soothes the pains of those with celiac disease, roasted and drunk, and, applied with honey, stops the bowels. The same, again with honey, removes warts. It has a dispersing power by itself, or applied with barley or oat flour. With this dung a carbuncle is dispelled, applied alone or with flaxseed in vinegar-honey. Dove's blood also stops bleeding from the nostrils; for this reason it is kept dried, to be applied to the forehead.

Avicenna: dove's blood is beneficial for gout. Dove's dung is the hottest of dungs used in medicine, among those from birds kept in houses. It is lessened by the dung of those that graze in fields. It is reddening, and, with barley flour, dispersing. It is good for joint pains and effective for skin eruptions. With honey and flaxseed, it is useful for treating shingles and burns from fire. Likewise, with rocket seed, it is effective for the malady called 'galea'; and it is among the medicines that produce a good complexion. It also benefits colic pain when administered in an enema.

Haly Abbas, in the second part of the Royal Book, second discourse: dove's blood benefits eye-spots and nosebleeds if dropped in; its dung, applied as a poultice with vinegar, cures every kind of dropsy from cold.

From the book On the Nature of Things: fresh dove's flesh, plucked together with that of swallows, is effective against serpents. Its blood, taken from the right wing, applied, heals the eye; for it is sharp and has the power to dissolve.
From the book On the Nature of Things: the 'coredulus' [heart-eater] is so named as if 'eating the heart'; for, living on flesh and prey, it especially longs to be sated on the heart.

Isidore: the crow is named among the Latins for its longevity. Augurs say it directs men's cares by its signs, reveals the paths of ambushes, foretells the future - a great wickedness, to believe that God entrusts his counsels to crows; among many auguries, they attribute to these the foretelling of rain by their cries. Whence that saying: then the shameless crow, gorged, calls for rain with its voice.

Ambrose: crows delight in the joining of many. They lead and direct storks passing through their regions, and help them against enemy birds. A proof of this is that none are found remaining in those places for even a short time. And, returning wounded, they testify, by the clear evidence of their blood, that they have undergone grave battles. Let men learn to love their children from the practice and devotion of crows, which, flying beside their young, follow them doubly in company, and, anxious lest the tender ones by chance fail, bring food and do not abandon their duties of nourishing for a long time; let men also learn from birds to keep the laws of hospitality, since crows, along with storks, are not accustomed to refuse their own dangers.

Crows eat flesh and other food, and, flying up with a nut whose hardness resists their beak, throw it onto rocks or tiles, again and again, until they can break through its shell. This bird is of ill-omened chattering. This alone, among flying creatures, still feeds its flying young for some time. All others of the same kind drive the chicks from the nest and force them to fly, as ravens do too. When the crow is brooding, the male feeds her. This kind of bird, too, is said to come out of the egg tail-first, because the weight of the head makes the reversed eggs apply the rear part of the body to be warmed by the mother. There was in the city of Rome a crow of a remarkably wondrous black color, uttering many connected words and constantly learning new ones.
When land birds, and especially the crow, cry out toward the water, they foretell rain, since they will be drenched by it.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the crow is seized by sickness at the solstice; it gladly feeds on nuts; these noble birds attack it as if it were their enemy, but they, having often long tolerated its attacks, at last, overcome by impatience, tear the troublesome bird apart. The crow foretells rain with much cries. It lies in wait for the dove's egg, to break it open and suck it out.
[a fragmentary note:] of the crow
They think it most useful for long illnesses to eat crow's flesh and to smear the nest.

Isidore: the raven, or 'corax,' has its name from the sound of its throat, because it makes the sound 'coracino.' This bird is said not to give full food to its hatched chicks before it recognizes, by the blackness of their feathers, a resemblance to its own color. But once it has seen them black in feather, fully recognized, it feeds them more abundantly; this bird seeks out the eye first in carcasses.

Pliny, book 10: ravens drive their chicks from the nest and force them to fly; they lay at most five eggs. The common people believe they conceive or mate through the mouth; Aristotle denies this. They breed before the solstice; they suffer illness for sixty days, mostly from thirst.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: the raven conceives through the mouth. And since its chicks are not recognized by their parents before their blackness is complete, they cry continually after their parents, whence moisture and foam is produced in their mouths. When flies and gnats settle on this to feed, they catch and eat them. Ravens, when hunting, having eaten the eyes of animals, afterward extract and eat the brain with their chicks.
The Ordinary Gloss, on the Psalm: raven chicks are said to feed on the dew of heaven, and, through the kindness of their youth, are ignorant of their parents' food, that is, the stench of carcasses.

Gregory, in the Moralia: raven chicks, it is said, before they turn black, are neglected somewhat by their parents, and, afflicted by hunger, wander here and there in the nest and seek the aid of food with open mouth. Whence it is written: who prepares food for the raven, etc. But once they begin to turn black, the raven seeks food for them all the more eagerly, the longer it has delayed feeding them.

Aristotle: ravens always appear and do not change their places. The raven, like the eagle, casts out the egg or chick if more than two occur. And similarly there is a bird that nourishes its cast-out chick. The raven kind is of little mating and little breeding. Its feathers change color, however, because of the change of season toward cold, as also happens with sparrows and swallows, which change from black, tending somewhat toward white. For a sparrowhawk, a sparrow, and a white raven have already been seen, which does not happen from the time of their breeding.
Ambrose: ravens too delight in the joining of many.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the raven is a noisy bird, knowing how to make no other sound but 'cras, cras'; yet it forms various voices, namely six hundred and four, as Fulgentius says. It sometimes mates in flight; it always breeds more than two chicks. It is said to become pregnant if it happens to eat a raven's egg. They are said to conceive and give birth through the mouth. The females of ravens brood their eggs alone, and the males bring them food. Raven chicks are said to remain for seven days without any nourishment of food; but on the seventh day they turn black, and some of these are cast out, weary of raising them. The raven is stronger by day, the eagle-owl by night, and they eat each other's eggs in turn. Ravens mate little, but kiss each other much, and some think that they do not mate in any other way, but this is false. The raven feeds on carrion and, it is said, abstains from drink as long as it can glory in the sweetness of its fig's fruit. Whence Ovid: and while a milky fig hangs for you on the tree, you will drink no water from any cold spring.

The goose and the raven are said to be afflicted with illness from summer into autumn. A raven's egg, mixed and smeared in a bronze vessel on a shaved head, brings blackness to the hair, but oil must be kept in the mouth until it dries, lest the teeth turn black too. And this must be done in the shade, and not washed off before three days. Some also use its blood and brain with black wine against baldness.

The same, book 30: raven's dung, too, bound in wool, heals infants' cough, and it is said that pigs follow the one from whom they received raven's brain. It is agreed that pregnant women should avoid raven's eggs, since eating them is said to cause miscarriage.
Aesculapius: raven's brain, poured into a hollow tooth, breaks and wondrously removes pain.
Pliny: the raven, having killed the chameleon-hawk, which even harms its victor, extinguishes the harmful venom with laurel.

The same, book 12: it is worth recording that a raven was seen, driven by thirst, gathering stones and dropping them into a monument's bucket in which rainwater stood but could not be reached, so afraid was it to go down, and thus, by such a heap, raised the water enough to drink.
The same, book 18: ravens, croaking with a kind of sobbing and shaking themselves, foretell a storm, if indeed they continue. But if they swallow back their voice in bursts, they signal windy rain.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the raven seems skilled with a wondrous cunning. For even if it finds money anywhere, it is said to take it secretly and, as it were, stealthily with its beak, and hide it carefully, and give it to whomever it wishes.

Aristotle: ravens fight with the ass and the bull, and, flying above them, prick their eyes with their beak. The black raven is a friend of the fox and defends it against its enemy, the 'aschelon.' It is hostile, however, to the eagle-owl. Whence a certain kind of raven eats the eagle-owl's eggs at midday, and the eagle-owl eats the raven's eggs at night.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: there is a kind of raven in the East that fights with the ass and the bull, and, as they flee, flies above them and thus, with force, pierces their eyes, and, when it can, blinding them, renders them useless to their masters. And so, consequently, once killed, they are skinned, and their bodies carried off by birds, and thus strong animals are overcome by a base bird. The raven inhabits towers and nests there; it is most swift, a messenger of changes in the weather, and by one voice of its cawing prophesies calm air, by another a storm. A long-lived raven quickly becomes tame, and holds and lures wild ravens against their will.

Isidore: quails are named from the sound of their voice; the Greeks call them 'ortygiae,' because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They have their season for coming; for once summer is over, they cross the seas. The 'ortygometra,' however, is the bird said to lead the flock, and, as it nears land, the hawk, watching, seizes it; and for this reason all of them take care to enlist a leader of a foreign kind, through whom they may avoid the first dangers. Their most pleasing food is the seeds of poisonous plants; for this reason the ancients forbade eating them, for this creature alone, like man, suffers the falling sickness.
Ambrose, book 3: the learned say hellebore is the quail's food, since by a certain natural temperament of their body they avoid the harm of this noxious plant.

Solinus: quails, once summer is over, when crossing the seas, wait for favorable winds, and, fearing the length of the crossing, husband their strength by delaying. But when they sense land, they gather in troops, then, massed together, hasten more violently. This haste often brings destruction to sailors. For it happens at night that they fall upon the sails and, the ropes overloaded, sink the ships. They never set out with the south wind. For they fear the force of the more swollen wind, and generally trust themselves to the north winds, so that a drier and stronger breeze may more easily carry their somewhat plump and therefore slower bodies.

The quail is a small bird, and when it comes to us, more a land-bird than a high-flier. It always, even before, comes heavily and not without danger to sailors, when they near land. For often at night they tear the sails and sink the ships. Their journey is through fixed resting-places. Quails do not fly with the south wind, that is, the more humid and heavier wind. They wish, however, to be carried by a breeze, because of the weight of their bodies and their small strength. With the north wind, then, they fly most, with the 'ortygometra' as their leader. The males fight among themselves out of desire for the females.
Peter Comestor: the quail is nourished especially in the bosom of Arabia, and is a royal bird, which we commonly call 'curelium,' from 'curing' [curendo].

From the book On the Nature of Things: the quail is a bird we commonly call 'quiscula'; they have the 'ortygometra' as leader, which, as they cross the sea and near land, that is, a sea port, hawks, watching, seize; and for this reason it is the concern of all of them to enlist a leader of a foreign kind, namely the crow, through whom they may avoid the first dangers. Among the kind of birds, they have very rare females, as scallops do among the kind of fish. But among mankind, fewer males are born than females.
The Philosopher: quails have their gall attached to the intestine, like swallows and doves; these have a voice in fighting.
Avicenna: from eating quail flesh, spasm and tetanus are to be feared.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the wren is called, in Italy, the king of birds; it is indeed the smallest of all, but the smaller it is, the swifter, so spirited that it even dares to make attempts against the eagle. It also deceives men, for when it offers itself nearby as if to be caught by hand, it escapes, tireless, the man's effort and labor in vain. It feeds on spiders, and is fertile in chicks, for it produces very many at one brood; many gather together in one den or cave in winter, so that the warmth, small in such tiny bodies, may be increased by the crowd contributing to it.

Aristotle: the 'cubeth' is a lustful bird, whose male, if he finds his female's eggs, breaks them, so that the female is not anxious over them; the female, however, hides them. She lays suddenly, by smell or by hearing, whether she mates or not. Likewise, if they sense the male coming, they run to meet him and mate. The male, indeed, approaches the female cautiously, without noise, lest other males notice and fight with him and not allow the mating. Likewise the males fight one another, and the victor mates with the defeated one, and, conversely, if the victor is defeated. They mate, however, solitarily and secretly, the victor choosing the place for this and the defeated one following. The male and female are often caught in their pleasure and fall into the hands of hunters. And though this bird is lustful, each male nevertheless takes a single female. The 'cubeth' makes two rows of eggs, and the female broods one, the male the other. But even when the shells have cracked, both are anxious about their chicks. And since its mating is of a greater kind, like the hen's, it has larger testicles, and does not have a nest like other birds, but makes its dwelling in flat places, where birds do not nest, out of thorns and other material, because of the hawk and the vulture, and for warmth. It casts out the hatched chicks suddenly, since it cannot fly well to bring them food. It lays no fewer than ten eggs, and perhaps twelve. It is, however, of bad and cunning habits. Birds that cannot fly well, but stay on the ground, like the hen and the 'cubeth,' rub themselves in ash. Likewise heavy-bodied birds that are not of good flight have much surplus, mate much, and are of many eggs, like the 'cubeth' and the ostrich and the hen.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'cubeth' seems to be the same as the partridge, for what is said here of it will be said, nearly the same, of the partridge below - which perhaps escaped the translator's notice.

Isidore: cuckoos are named from their own call; they too have their season for coming, carried on the shoulders of kites because of their short and small flights, lest, exhausted by the long stretches of the sky, they fail; their saliva breeds cicadas. They eat sparrows' eggs found in the nest and put in their own instead. Afterward they brood and nourish these; these are called by another name, 'tuci.'

From the book On the Nature of Things: the cuckoo is a base bird, which does not change its voice in singing, but repeats the same one. It is a most sluggish bird and unstable in its dwelling. It has nearly the color of the turtledove; in winter it is said to be stripped of its feathers, and enters a burrow in the ground or the hollows of trees, gathering there in summer what it lives on in winter. It lays its eggs in the nest of a smaller little bird, and removes as many from that bird's eggs, lest, finding a surplus in number, she reject them as foreign. The cuckoo, warmed and raised by a foreign mother along with her own chicks, while it still sits weak in the nest, nevertheless, by a certain natural greediness, snatches food from the other chicks, and by this cunning grows fatter and sleeker than the rest. The foster-mother, charmed by its elegance, delights in its form and marvels at herself for having borne such a creature, so foolish that she does not distinguish the chick by size from her smaller chicks, but condemns all her own chicks by comparison with it. But once she has raised it and nourished it to the strength of flight, it, in turn, rises up against its foster-mother and kills her as she follows it.
[a fragmentary attribution to Pliny:] on the cuckoo

The same, book 13: there is a certain marvel told of the cuckoo, that in the place where one first hears that bird, if the right foot's outline is traced and the footprint dug up, fleas will not be bred wherever it is scattered.
The same, book 28: cuckoo's dung, boiled in wine and drunk, helps against a rabid dog's bite.

Aristotle: the cuckoo broods its own eggs, but, placing one egg in the coot's nest, sucks out that bird's eggs. She, ignorant of what is to come, broods the egg as a devoted foster-mother. But once the cuckoo hatches and later grows up, the foster-mother is sometimes said to be killed by it. In summer it flies and is playful, always repeating the same song; in winter it lies languishing, featherless, and resembling the eagle-owl.

Isidore: the Diomedean birds are named from the companions of Diomedes, whom fables say were changed into these same birds: in form similar to the coot, in size to swans, white in color, with hard and large beaks. They are found around Apulia, on the island of Diomedes, flying among the rocks and cliffs of the shore. They judge, moreover, between their own people and strangers. For if a Greek approaches, they draw near and flatter him. If a foreigner, they bite and wound him, lamenting with tearful cries, as it were, either their own transformation or the death of their king. For Diomedes was killed by the Illyrians. These birds are called, in Latin, 'diomedeae.' The Greeks, however, call them 'herodii.'

Nor shall I pass over the Diomedean birds. Juba calls them 'cataractae,' and reports that they have teeth and fiery-colored eyes, otherwise white. They always have two leaders: one to lead the column, the other to drive it on. They hollow out pits with their beak, then line them with wicker and cover them with earth that had earlier been dug out; in these they breed, with two doors for each pit. One faces east, by which they go out to pasture; the other faces west, by which they return. About to relieve their bowels, they fly up above and against the wind. These are seen in only one place of the whole world, on the island we have called famous for the mound and shrine of Diomedes, opposite Apulia, resembling coots. They attack barbarian strangers with their cries. To the Greeks alone they show affection, by a wondrous discernment, as if attributing this to the kinship of Diomedes. And every day they wash and purify his shrine, their throats full and their feathers dripping. Whence arose the fable of Diomedes's companions being changed into their likeness.

Solinus: the island that faces the shore of Apulia, marked by the mound and shrine of Diomedes, alone produces the Diomedean birds, which are white in color, with fiery eyes and toothed mouths; they fly gathered together, and there are two leaders. One of these goes before the column, to direct its course by leading; the other follows, to press the slow ones on by its insistence. When the breeding season is at hand, it hollows out pits with its beak, and, twigs placed crosswise, they cover the hollowed space beneath; and lest coverings be lacking, if by chance the wind carries off the frail wood, they press down this pile with the earth they had dug out. Thus they build their nests with a two-fold entrance: the entrance leading out to pasture faces east; the one that receives them on their return faces west, so that the light may both rouse those who linger and not deny them their return. They celebrate the sacred shrine with such devotion every day, drenching their feathers in water and, their wings heavily wetted, gathering, dripping, and thus purify the shrine by shaking off the moisture. Then they applaud with their wings and, as if the rite were completed, depart. For this reason they are said to have been made from Diomedes's companions. About to relieve their bowels, they fly up against opposing winds, so that the discharge may be carried farther away.

div.head: DE EGYTHO ET EMERIA ET ERCINIA

cit.quote: Pliny, book 10: the tiny 'egythus' bird fights with the ass. For the ass, rubbing itself against thorn-bushes to scratch itself, scatters its nests. This little bird so dreads it that, hearing its braying voice at all, it casts out its eggs, and its chicks fall from fear. And so, flying to it, it pecks at its sores with its beak. Furthermore the 'acanthis' hates the 'egythus' so much that they are believed not to let their blood mingle.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: [the 'emeria' are] birds that, flying by night, light up the air because of the nature of their feathers, which shine more in darkness than in light; and thus they are betrayed and caught.

Isidore: the 'hercinian' birds are named from the Hercynian forest of Germany, where they are born, whose feathers shine so brightly through the darkness that, however densely the night is held in shadow, when thrown ahead they shine through, to aid in directing the journey, and the course of the path is made clear by the sign of their glowing feathers.
The same: it is called 'falco' because it has curved [falcatis] claws; in the Italian tongue this is called 'capus,' from seizing [capiendo].
Radulphus, in the same place: the 'herodius' is what we commonly call the falcon, swift and rapid in seizing prey.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the falcon is a most noble bird, most impetuous in flight, and less cautious in guarding itself. And so, when it is to be sent after prey, it is held back by its master, and the bird to be caught is not shown to it until it has first been given some distance, so that it may pursue the prey with a measured onset. In hunting the heron, two falcons are released together, one of which makes for the heights, the other flying near the ground, namely so that the one may knock the flying heron down by its impact, and the other may catch it as it falls.

Aristotle: the falcon has weak kidneys but a strong chest; it uses delicate foods. With a single motion it turns its neck in a circle, its chest remaining motionless, so much so that its two eyes seem, by reason of this natural discernment of sight, to answer equally, as if with the many eyes of Argus. It also keeps watchful care for prey that is behind it.

From the book On the Nature of Things: there are two kinds of falcons. One noble, which naturally catches a bird with little effort. The other ignoble and base, which does this only when trained through much labor and being reduced by hunger. This latter kind, when it has driven the heron to the ground and is on the point of catching it, the heron vomits up an eel or another fish it had recently swallowed, and then the baser falcon, letting it fly freely away, prefers the foul-smelling gift offered to it and gladly seizes it more quickly. The noble falcon does not do this, but, scorning the gift cast out, punishes the cunning bird more sternly. The falcon, moreover, has a sharp and hard bone in its chest, which nature, providing for it, gave for striking its prey. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion wrote a letter to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, in which they treated of noble birds and their medicines; of which it suffices here to recall only a little. There are eight kinds of falcons. The first is called the 'lanner,' and is divided into two kinds: one has a thick head and beak, feet like an eagle's, which is trained for hunting only with great labor; but once trained, it is excellent in flight in its second and third year. The other is of smaller stature and reckoned base.
