The second kind of falcon is called the 'peregrine,' and this for two reasons: one, that it always migrates from land to land; the second, according to falconers' belief, that its nest is unknown, since they build their nests on the highest crags of mountains, and there is no approach to the nest except from above, at the mountain's peak, a man let down by rope. The third kind is called the 'mountain falcon,' short and quite compact in body, and especially short and thick in the tail, with a very round and large chest, and strong, short legs in proportion to its body's size, knotted feet and strong claws, and it has this habit, that it often looks at its feet. It is ash-grey on the back and on the outside of the wings. This kind is wild, of bad habits and irascible, of inconstant anger. The fourth kind is blue-grey in feet and legs, whence it also gets its name; this is noble in its first and second year, but by the fifth year is most worthless. The fifth kind is slender and long in build, most excellent in flight. The sixth kind is called the 'supranicum,' which nearly resembles the eagle, except that in its feet, wings, and eyes it resembles the falcon in coloring. The seventh kind is the British kind, which holds the primacy among all hunting birds, so that no bird dares to hunt in its presence, or even fly, while it is flying overhead. This kind has knotted legs, thick feet, cruel claws, a terrible appearance, fiery eyes, a thick head and feet, and large 'iuga,' that is, wing-joints; it is most easily trained for flight and can fly much and long; it wishes to be fed most delicately, and eats almost as much as an eagle. We believe this kind to be the one we called above the 'aeriophylon.' The eighth kind is that called the 'herodius,' or commonly the 'gyrfalcon,' of which more will be said below; this kind is more common than the previous one and held dearer for the moderation of its food and life. Furthermore, the tercel, the smallest of hunting birds, but most ready by nature and sex for hunting, is joined to the kinds of falcons.

Albertus Magnus, in the book On Animals: the kind of falcons has four distinguishing features. First, the shape of the body. Second, color. Third, its proper activity. Fourth, the sound of its voice. The fitting shape is to have a thicker and round head, a shorter neck, a shorter beak, a larger chest with a sharp bone in the chest, longer wings, a more contracted tail, and legs shorter and stronger in proportion to its body. The fitting color is to have black spots on the face, on the jaws, white around the eye-sockets on both sides and on both sides of the beak, and to have black eyelashes, and an ash-grey or blackish hue on the crown, on the back, on the upper part of the neck and the outside of the wings, likewise on the outside of the tail, so that the wings are full of variety, as if descending in streaks, the streaks sometimes interrupted. And this variety always has blackness as one of its colors. The second color is a subdued, muted red, and, as it changes more and more often, it grows whiter and whiter. The color of the eyes is a yellowness, so that it approaches redness, and the pupils are black. And the best color of the feet is a yellow inclining much toward white, and the less white the feet, the less noble the falcon; and if it inclines toward a hyacinth or sapphire color, this is an ignoble color. Its proper activity is to be borne with force upon its prey. And so the falconer must take care not to show the prey to the falcon at once, but rather to release the falcon while the bird is still somewhat distant. The sound of its voice, generally, is thicker and more drawn out, proceeding from sharp to deeper. According to him there are ten kinds, distinguished as to their nobility. The first, the 'sacred' falcon, which Symmachus calls the British falcon, otherwise 'elium' or 'aeriophylum.' The second, the gerfalcon. The third, the mountain or 'montanarium' falcon. The fourth, the peregrine. The fifth, the 'gibbous' falcon, small in bodily size, but wondrous in boldness and strength - called 'gibbous' because, on account of the shortness of its neck, its head scarcely appears in front of its wing-joints. The sixth degree of nobility is held by the black falcon, somewhat shorter than the peregrine falcon, but similar to it in shape in every way. The seventh place is claimed by the white falcon, which comes from the north and the ocean sea, from the regions of Norway and Sweden and Estonia and the neighboring forests and mountains. The eighth degree is held by the red falcon, not that it is red all over, but because the spots that are white in others are, in this kind, red and black. The ninth kind is the one with hyacinth-blue and azure feet. The tenth, which is smallest in size, is commonly called the merlin. The training of falcons is divided into three. The first is the training of domestication, which is directed to two ends: one, that it grow accustomed to man's hand; the other, that it become bold and swift in catching birds. The second is the regimen of health, and consists especially in this, that it be fed the food, at the hour and in the quantity, by which and when it was accustomed to feed in the wild, and especially the light flesh of birds, still warm with the breath of life, and that it be kept midway between leanness and fatness. The third is the regimen for illness, concerning which, from the aforesaid letter of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion - Albertus, and the book On the Natures of Things - the following are recorded. If sickness grows in a bird's eyes, anoint its eyes with olive oil; if a white film grows on the eye, apply powder of fennel seed and warm woman's milk. If it has grown dim from old age, take a suitable piece of iron, heat it, and place it over the nostrils, where the crown of the head joins the eye to the nostrils. If it has blocked nostrils, take powder of pepper and stavesacre, and blow it into its nostrils through a small feather-quill, and afterward rub its palate with powder of stavesacre alone. If it has catarrh in the head, place rue near its nostrils and dip the flesh it eats in the juice of rue. Likewise put crushed garlic with wine into its nostrils, and let it sit a whole day in a dark place, and let it fast for one day. If it has trouble with its throat, take its tongue and rub it with powder of stavesacre mixed with honey; give it butter to eat if the aforesaid remedies do not work; powder of dried cabbage is likewise effective. If it is excessively noisy, take a bat, and place ground pepper inside it, and give it to the bird to eat; if you take another bird instead, it will work just as well; for one that cries too much is often full inside. If it has loss of appetite, have live shrews given to it, likewise a newborn puppy before it has opened its eyes. If it frequently vomits its food, take scammony to the weight of a quarter of an obol and as much cumin, and, having ground these, sprinkle their powder on fatty pork, and give it to the bird as food. But if it cannot eat, take egg white and put the said powder in it, and put it into its mouth. Likewise, for the same, if it throws up its food, take raw eggs and break them into goat's milk, then have this whole mixture cooked, and give it three times to the hawk to eat, and it will be saved. If it begins to molt, free it from all work, and give it food in abundance; for as often as it hungers, it will have that many breaks in its feathers, and in this a secret of nature is noted. Green turf placed beneath its feet is good for it, and the sun's warmth, unless great heat presses in. If it has fevers, give it juice of wormwood three or four times, and hen's flesh as food; or this: bind its right shin tightly, and in the middle of the leg a vein will appear, and bleed it very carefully. In its leg there are four veins: one in front, another below, another outside, another behind, above the larger claw. You can know whether a bird has a fever if its wings droop and it holds its head lowered, and trembles, and shows as it were cold in its feathers, or takes food reluctantly, or takes it eagerly but digests it poorly. If it is very thirsty, take powder of lovage stalk and dill and fennel reed, and cook these with wine, and mix in a spoonful of honey, and give it the strained liquid to drink, or put it into its mouth; or on one day give it flesh smeared with cold rose oil. If it suffers from the gall, sprinkle powder of willow flowers on its food. If its wings droop, take goose blood and fat; rub its wings with the blood in the sun, and give it fatty goose flesh to eat. Likewise, better: take pig's gall and anoint its wings with it, or dip its food in verbena juice; sage juice works the same. If its wings have gout, boil ground ivy in water, and its well-crushed leaves, and bind them around its wings, along the sides, and soak its food in that same water; likewise if it has gout in its feet. If moths eat its feathers, let it eat goat's flesh dipped in vinegar, and rub its wings often with warm vinegar and laurel oil. If you wish to remove a broken feather without pain, take the blood of the small creature called the 'galy,' or the blood of a rat, and anoint the place of the feather, and it will fall out; and afterward, from honey boiled to a thickness, make a little rod the shape of the hole where the feather stood, and insert it into the hole, and a new feather will emerge. Likewise anoint its feathers with the warm juice of the poppy, and dip its food in the same juice. If it has a broken bone in the leg or wing, bind warm aloe over it, and leave it for a day and a night. Likewise, chicken dung cooked in vinegar, bound over it. If the bird is restless on its perch or on the hand of the one carrying it, boil myrrh in water, and sprinkle its body with that water, and dip its food in it, up to nine times. If it suffers the sickness called 'ranna,' let its food be dipped in juice of wormwood. Likewise rub its feet with warm lamb's blood, or with warm wine in which nettles have been boiled, and dip its food in that same wine. If it cannot excrete, give it cock's gall to eat, or boiled white tortoises. If it is too loose, give it a little juice of henbane to drink, and dip its food in the same. If it has lice, take juice of wormwood or water boiled with wormwood, and, as it sits in the sun, pour this over its feathers and its whole body. If it has nurtured a stone in its belly, give it ointment and butter to eat. For the same, take aloe herb with celery powder, wrap it in the hearts of small birds, and give it to eat. Thus you will be able to more conveniently apply any medicine given to birds. But you will find much more on this matter recorded by Albertus in his book On Animals. These, and many other things about their medicines, are read in the aforesaid letter on noble birds.
Isidore: the pheasant is named from the island of Phasis, whence it was first brought.

Palladius, in the same place: young pheasants, hatched the previous year, should be prepared for breeding offspring. Old ones, however, cannot be fertile. They mate with the females in March or April, or produce broods once a year. The number laid is completed at about twenty eggs; hens brood these better. They should be kept from access to water, lest they contract catarrh. They are fattened with wheat or barley flour; this flour, made into very small pellets, sprinkled with oil, should be softened, and thus the pellets inserted into the throat, so that they do not sink beneath the lower part of the tongue - for if this happens, they will die at once. One male suffices for two females, since it does not match other birds in lustfulness.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the pheasant is a wild cock, a beautiful bird, with feathers shimmering, like fire, sometimes sky-blue and green, with a red brilliance interwoven with the feathers. It seems to have two ears on its head, feathers standing out, which it raises when it wishes and lowers. It lacks a crest on its head and spurs on its legs; yet, deprived of these weapons, it is spirited and bold. Knowing this, the fowler makes a shield from linen cloth, in the middle of which he places a small red patch, which redness against the white the cock gazes at intently and marvels at as unfamiliar. Then the fowler, seeing it transfixed by the sight, forces it to retreat backward by the effort of the shield, until he drives the captive bird into nets set up at a distance. This bird grows sad in rainy weather, and then hides in the brambles and woods. Around evening or dawn it comes out of the woods, and then is easily hunted. Fixing its beak in the ground, it hides its head, and thus believes itself entirely hidden. It sheds its feathers because of its fatness, and renews itself again. Its flesh is finer and lighter than that of other wild birds, except for the chicks of partridges.
In Colchis, pheasants lower and raise twin ears of down.
The same, book 11: in pheasants the gall is joined to the intestine only on one side of the kidneys.

Aristotle: pheasants dwell together only at mating time, but at other times separately, nor do they quickly grow reddened beards or spurs on their feet, like domestic cocks, but only with the passage of time. The pheasant is caught in this way: sometimes the fowler, covered with a cloth on which this bird is depicted, shows himself to the pheasant, which, following the covered figure that neither flees nor retreats, is at last entangled in a net by the fowler's companion lying hidden in ambush.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the 'fatator' is a bird in the East, which, naturally eager to produce offspring, anticipates the season of spring, in which other birds are accustomed to begin their conceiving. Whence it happens that the eggs it lays then are spoiled by cold, so that they have no effect of offspring; but again, in the following warm season, they lay, and then produce chicks - which is contrary to almost all wild birds, which lay and breed only once a year.

Isidore: the phoenix is a bird of Arabia, so called because it has a purple-red [phoeniceum] color, or because it is unique and singular in the whole world. For the Arabs believe the phoenix to be singular and unique: this bird, living more than five hundred years, when it sees that it has grown old, gathers together bundles of spices and builds itself a pyre, and, turned to face the sun's ray, feeds the fire it has willingly kindled by the beating of its wings, and thus rises again from the ashes.

Ambrose, book 5: the phoenix, when it perceives that the end of its life is at hand, makes itself a casket of frankincense and myrrh and other spices, into which, once the time of its life is fulfilled, it enters and dies; from the moisture of its flesh a worm arises, and gradually grows, and, in the course of the appointed time, puts on the rowing-oars of wings, and thus is restored to the appearance and form of the former bird. Let this bird, then, teach us by example to believe in the resurrection, since, without example and without the instruction of reason, it establishes for itself the marks of resurrection.

Solinus: among the Arabs the phoenix is born, a bird the size of an eagle, its head weighed down with feathers standing up like a crest, its throat crested with golden brilliance around the neck, purple in its hind part, except for the tail, in which a sky-blue brightness is interwoven with rose-colored feathers. In the consulship of Quintus Plautius and Sextus Papinius, the phoenix flew into Egypt, and, caught in the eight hundredth year from the founding of the city, was displayed by order of the Emperor Claudius in the comitium, which deed is also recorded in the city's public records.

Pliny, book 10: the senator Manilius, distinguished by the greatest learning, taught by no teacher, is the authority that no one has ever existed who saw it eating; that the phoenix is sacred to the sun in Arabia alone, living six hundred and sixty years; that, growing old, it builds a nest of cassia and sprigs of frankincense, fills it with spices, and dies upon it. From its bones and marrow, then, is born first, as it were, a small worm, then a chick is formed, and at the very start it is given the same funeral rites as its predecessor, and carries the whole nest to the city of the Sun near Panchaia, and deposits it there on an altar. Manilius reports, moreover, that the life of this bird reveals the completion of the Great Year, and that the same signs of the seasons and stars return again in this cycle; and that this begins around midday, on the day the sun enters the sign of Aries. He also states that this same year of its cycle, according to his own reckoning, fell in the consulship of Publius Licinius and Marcus Cornelius, the year 215. Cornelius Valerianus relates that a phoenix flew down into Egypt in the consulship of Quintus Plautius and Sextus Papinius, and was brought to the city in the eight hundredth year of the reign of the Emperor Claudius, and displayed in the comitium, as is attested in the public records - which no one doubts to be false.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the phoenix is a bird in the world living alone, without a father, for three hundred and forty years, its head weighed down, like a peacock's, and its tail of a sky-blue color, in which rose-colored feathers are interwoven with wondrous variety. And when, with the passage of its foreseeing age, it begins to grow heavy, in the highest regions of the East, on a most beautiful tree set above a most pleasant spring, it builds, as it were, a nest-altar from frankincense, myrrh, and cinnamon and other spices. Then, drawing the burning orbs of the sun into itself by the beating of its wings, it throws itself upon the pile, and, likewise set alight, a worm is born from its ash, which is reshaped into the original bird. Isidore says, moreover, that this bird entered the city of Heliopolis in Egypt in the month of April, its wings laden with various spices, and set alight the pile of brushwood that had been laid aside as a sacrifice by the priest, and burned itself there among those spices; on the first day following, the priest came and found the wood he had placed on the altar burnt, and, searching through the ash, found a small worm, fragrant with a most sweet smell, which on the second day appeared shaped into a bird, and on the third, in its own most perfect state, bade the priest farewell and flew away.

Isidore: fig-peckers are so named because they eat figs more than other food. This is expressed in that old little verse: since the fig loves me, since I am fed on sweet grapes, why did the grape not rather give me its name?
Pliny: fig-peckers change both their form and color at once; they have this name in autumn, but afterward are called 'melancoryphi.'
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'philomena' is a small, songful bird, known to all, called the nightingale, of which more will be said fully below.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the nightingale [philomena] is named from 'philos,' which means 'love,' and 'mene,' which means 'sweet.' For this bird gladdens its hearer with wondrous melody; it rejoices at the rising of the sun and precedes its coming with joy, yet sings only in springtime, never in winter. At the start of spring, moreover, it delights so much in the pleasantness of its own voice that it eats most rarely, and this in the greatest haste. And so they compete with one another so persistently that the defeated one often ends its life, its breath failing before its song; whence it is also named from 'philos,' which is 'love,' and 'mene,' which is 'failing,' as if 'failing from love.' We marvel, then, at so persistent a spirit in so small a little body; we marvel at its perfect knowledge of music. For a modulated sound is produced, and now it is drawn out long in one continuous breath, now varied by a bend, now broken off and joined together in a trill, deep, sharp, rapid, sustained, quivering, and sometimes indeed middling, highest, lowest. Younger nightingales, meanwhile, practice and learn songs at which we marvel; the attentive pupil listens and gives back the song in turn; it is understood, corrected, and in a manner reproved by the teacher. But as soon as it begins to mate, it loses the pleasantness of its voice, and, as Pliny says, its voice becomes different, and its color changes. For from the end of spring, as the heat increases, its voice becomes altogether different, and its color too changes. The thinness of their tongues is not like that of other birds.

Isidore: the coot is so named because its flesh tastes like hare's flesh, for 'lagos' means 'hare.' It is a pond-dwelling bird, having its nest in the middle of the water or on rocks surrounded by it, and always delights especially in the depths. When it senses a storm coming, it flees and plays in the shallows.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the coot, as is read, is a bird similar in size and color to the swan, with a large beak. It dwells among the rocks of the shore; the Latins call these 'diomedeae,' the Greeks 'herodii.'

Physiologus: the coot, most prudent among all birds, does not feed on carcasses, nor wander from place to place, but stays in one place until the end, and there gathers its food around itself and rests.
Pliny: nature has given the kind of coots a pleasing crest, set along the middle of the head from the beak.
The same, in the same book: coots foretell storms by their morning cry.

The Ordinary Gloss, on Psalm 103: the coot's home is strong, but not in the heights. Whence it is said: the coot's, or the heron's, home, etc. For the coot is a sea or pond-dwelling bird, whose home, that is nest, is a rock in the water, which, pounded by the waves, breaks them, but is not itself broken.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the coot, as Ambrose says, feeds and nourishes, along with its own chicks, with reverent mercy, the eagle's chicks cast from the nest, giving to rational men an example of how much mercy they ought to be moved to show toward strangers, the poor, and the afflicted.

The coot is a bird of good character, black, similar to a duck, except that it is smaller than a duck. It stays delightfully in ponds, content with food and peace. Whence, if it finds a place where it has peace and food, it does not leave.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the cock is a bird crested at the throat and head, armed with opposing spurs on the legs; hens too sometimes have spurs, but this by an error of nature rather than by its design. The cock crows more forcefully in the depth of night, more lightly at dawn. For its crowing is carried with the wind and heard farther off than can be estimated. And so, with its crowing, it calms horses, rouses camels, and is even said to drive away phantoms. It raises its tail and curves it like a half-circle. When it raises its feathers around its neck, shaking itself, it makes itself bolder; when about to sleep, it climbs high and rests on one foot; its image sits on church towers, and it turns its beak against the wind. Herbs that nourish the cock kill other animals; if several cocks are together in one enclosure, one rules over the rest, having defeated them, and struts proudly, and the end is often a fight to the death, both dying together. The cock is a terror to lions for this reason, that it is likened to the basilisk, as some hold; or rather, as we believe, a fear of the cock is naturally implanted in the lion. When the hens die, the cock, wasting away with grief, abstains from crowing out of sorrow. A cock, in decrepit old age, produces from itself an egg, from which the basilisk is bred. But in this generation many things must coincide. It lays the egg in warm, abundant dung, and there it is brooded in place of a father, and after a long time a chick emerges and grows strong as the chicks of ducks do. It has a tail like a snake's, but the rest of the body like a cock's. Those who testify they have seen the creation of this creature say that the egg has no shell at all, but a very tough skin, so tough that it can withstand the strongest blows. Some are of the opinion that a snake or a toad broods this egg of the cock, but this is uncertain; we have this much only in the writings of the ancients, that a certain kind of basilisk is bred from the egg of a decrepit cock. The cock announces the day with its crowing and rouses the sleepy. And it is said that it thus marks the hours by its crowing, because, from much heat, the humors in it come to a boil at certain hours, and from this arises a saltiness and thus an itching, from which arises a delight, by which it is roused to crow. In the longer nights it gives forth greater and stronger crowing, and, gazing at its own image in a mirror, exhausts its strength. With a light murmur it calls its hens to eat grain. Finally, among birds the male, not the female, gives voice, like the cock and the quail. The cock feeds the hen he has called, and then drives her to the labors of impregnation and childbirth.

Gregory, in the Moralia: the cock, herald of the day, dispels the hours of night and finally gives forth a voice of exhortation. And when it prepares to give its crow, it first shakes its wings and, striking itself, makes itself more alert.

Ambrose: the cock's crowing is sweet in the nights and useful, like a good companion rousing the sleeper and admonishing the anxious. It comforts the traveler, marking the night's progress: at its crowing the thief abandons his ambushes, at it the morning star itself, roused, rises and lights the sky; at its crowing the fearful sailor lays aside his sadness, and every storm and tempest, roused by the frequent evening blasts, grows calm; at it devoted affection leaps up to pray and takes up again the task of reading; at it, finally, Peter himself, the shepherd of the Church, washed away the guilt he had drawn upon himself before the cock's crow. At its crowing hope returns to all: the sick are relieved of their trouble, the pain of wounds is lessened, the burning of fevers is soothed, faith returns to the fallen. Jesus looks upon those who waver, corrects those who err.
The lion fears the cock, and especially the white one.

Aristotle: cocks have been seen that killed their own females. Then, anxious about their own chicks, they governed them and resembled the females in raising them, even in voice. And they were unwilling to mate, but even submitted to being mounted.

Cocks, the night's watchmen, whom nature made to rouse mortals to their work and to break off sleep, know the stars and mark the three-hour divisions of the day by their crowing. They go to roost with the sun, and at the fourth watch of the camp call men back to their tasks and labor. Nor do they let the sunrise creep up on the unwary, but announce the coming day with their crowing, and their crowing itself with the applause of their sides. When hens die, their mates have been seen taking their place in turn and doing the rest as the hen does, and abstaining from crowing. Next to the pheasant, they feel the greatest glory. They rule their own kind, and exercise their dominion in whatever house they are; they fight, moreover, among themselves as if with weapons attached to their legs. And the end is often only when both die together. But if victory falls to one, it at once crows in triumph and proclaims itself the ruler. The defeated one, however, is hidden away, silent, and bears its servitude with difficulty. And yet the common flock too struts just as proudly, with lofty neck, its crest raised high, alone among birds often looking to the sky, and raising its curved tail on high. And so they are a terror even to lions, the noblest of wild beasts. Castrated ones, too, cease to crow.

Isidore: the capon is named from castration. For among all other birds, this alone has its testicles removed. The ancients called castrated birds 'galli.' In the gizzards of capons a gem is found, called the 'alectorius,' of crystalline appearance, the size of a bean.

Pliny, in the same place: cocks, as has been said, cease to crow once castrated. This is done in two ways: by burning the loins with a hot iron, or by covering the lower legs, once wounded, with potter's clay; thus they fatten more easily. Male birds fight among themselves out of desire for the females, and the defeated one submits to being mounted. This indeed sometimes happens to the domestic cock too.
The same, in the same book: nature also gave capons a flexible crest, set along the middle from the beak, but most remarkably formed in the body, being neither flesh nor cartilage.
The same, book 22: if capons eat the flower of the vine, they do not touch the grapes. Catarrh of the capon kind is said to be healed by the herb savin.
The same, book 28: it is said that capons are not touched by foxes, if they eat a dried fox liver, or if a small skin from its neck is worn by the cock.
The same, book 29: the limbs of hens are poison to gold, and a capon itself, with a bronze ring added to its neck, does not crow.
The same, in the same book: weasel's ash, given to capons, protects them from weasels.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the domestic fowl, deprived of its testicles, is commonly called a capon. It is said to fatten more quickly, since it is kept from lust. It fattens among the hens, but never fertilizes them by impregnating them; it feeds with them, but does not defend them. It does not crow, nor does it distinguish the hours of day or night. It is thus useful for nothing but the kitchen. Whence a certain man, speaking rather aptly to the clergy in a synod recently, said: Shebna the scribe, he says, shall be carried off, like a capon, but nowhere indeed except to the devil's kitchen - and why? Because he neither breeds nor crows. Sometimes a cock is castrated after three years, and afterward allowed to live five or seven years more, and so in its liver the 'alectorius' stone is found by chance; once it has conceived this, it never afterward drinks. Whence if anyone holds this stone in his mouth, it quenches thirst. Sometimes the feathers of this bird's chest are plucked and burned bare with nettles, so that it may warm orphaned chicks in place of their mother, by the heat that it too gives them from its bared body. Thus, once it has found relief from cold and a remedy for the burning in the placement of the chicks beneath it, conceiving a maternal affection, it warms and feeds them, and forms sounds after the manner of hens, so as to call, with a broken voice, those wandering off.

Alexander Neckam: a capon, if well stung with nettles, will lead its chicks like a hen; but this, it is said, it does not do for the chicks' benefit, but for its own, so that from the chicks' warmth it may cause the nettle's venom to evaporate.

div.head: DE CIBO ET MEDICINA EX GALLO

cit.quote: From the book On the Nature of Things: cock's flesh is harder to digest and of less moisture than hen's or capon's. But the flesh of decrepit cocks is more tender than that of younger ones. The capon, however, has flesh stronger than all other winged creatures, generating good blood and excellent nourishment. Its flesh has some viscosity, but this dissolves in cooking.
[a fragmentary listing:] on the cock: dog, weasel, wolfsbane

Avicenna: of cocks, as Rufus says, the better one for food is that which does not yet crow; old ones are bad. The testicles of cocks are much praised, being of quick digestion. Cock's broth benefits stomach pain from flatulence; broth of an old cock, with polypody and dill, greatly benefits colic. Galen teaches, in preparing a decoction of old cocks, that after they have been fed, they should be tired out by making them run until they fall and are exhausted; then their bellies, emptied and filled with salt, should be boiled and cooked with twenty [measures of] water until reduced to three portions, and this broth drunk; it benefits asthma. It also benefits tremor and joint pain, but it must be cooked with polypody, dill, and salt. Likewise the aforesaid broth, with polypody, dissolves melancholy, and with cardamom dissolves phlegm. Sometimes it is cooked with astringent medicines for dysentery, and with milk for ulcers of the bladder. Cock's fat, like the stag's, is of more vehement heating power; hen's fat is less so. Split hens placed on their own heart, or a cock, placed on a spot injured by venomous worms, and changed every hour, prevent the harm of poisons. In poisons drunk, too, their decoction with dill and salt is drunk in and vomited up. The inner skin that is in the cock's stomach and throat, dried, ground, and drunk, benefits stomach pain.

Aesculapius: cock's brain, drunk with wine, undoes every bite and does many other wonderful things. Its blood, mixed with water, heals white spots of the eyes and scars. Its testicles, drunk with water, free epileptics, provided they abstain from wine for ten days. The inner skin of its stomach, ground with wine, benefits the ears, and, drunk, constricts the bowels, brings up phlegm, breaks stones, and expels them through urine. Its dung, mixed with vinegar, cures boils and dog bites.

Capon's flesh, applied warm, tames the venom of serpents; likewise its brain drunk in wine. The Parthians prefer to apply hen's brain to wounds. Its broth, too, drunk, is remarkably healing and marvelous for many other uses. For lions and panthers do not touch those anointed with it, especially if garlic has been cooked in with it; it loosens the bowels, more strongly from an old capon. It is beneficial also against long fevers, and for numb and trembling limbs and joint diseases and headaches, discharges, inflammations, loss of appetite, incipient tenesmus, the liver, kidneys, and bladder, against indigestion and sighing. And so there are precepts for preparing it: it is more effective cooked with rosemary, or with cabbage or capers or celery or mercury-herb or polypody or dill. It is most useful, moreover, in three measures of water reduced to three heminae with the above herbs, and given cooled in the open air at the right time, preceded by vomiting. Fresh capon's dung, applied, cures baldness. A white capon's gall is effective for suffusions of the eyes. Capon's dung, when red, is applied for night-blindness. Capon's gall is praised, but especially the fat, against pustules in the pupils; white dung too, in old oil, is kept in horn boxes for white films of the pupils. The gizzard's lining of capons, usually discarded, aged and ground in wine, is effective for suppurating ears.

The same, book 30: capon's broth heals dysentery and tenesmus, but the broth of an old capon, saltier, more strongly moves the bowels. Furthermore, roasted capon liver stops the bowels. Capon's dung with oil and soda heals warts of every kind. Capon's brain, applied to the forehead, stops bleeding from the nostrils.
Isidore: the hen is named from the cock [gallus], as the lioness from the lion. Some say the limbs of hens, if mixed into molten gold, consume it.

The good breeding of hens is shown by an erect and sometimes double comb, black feathers, a red mouth, sometimes uneven toes, and one crossed over the four. For divine ritual, those with yellow beak and feet are not thought suitable; black ones for secret rites. There is also a kind of dwarf hens among these, not sterile - unlike other bird kinds - but of certain, rare fertility, and their brooding harms the eggs.
The same, book 29: if the limbs of hens are mixed into molten gold, they consume it within themselves, so that it can be said that gold is poison to hens.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the hen has, on the domestic parts of its body, that is from the middle of the back upward and from the chest below downward, likewise a double feather growing from a single shaft. Catarrh is most hostile to hens, and this especially between harvest-time and vintage-time; the remedy is a feather inserted crosswise through the nostrils and moved every day, or garlic as food.

Aristotle: birds that stay on the ground and do not fly, like the hen and those similar to it, do not see with sharp sight and rub themselves in ash. Likewise those of greater mating have larger testicles, like the hen and the 'cubeth.' Likewise hens sometimes fight with cocks and defeat them; then they raise their necks and chests upward and crow, and mount on the males, and sometimes have small crests.

Palladius, in the same place: in raising hens, dung and dust and ash should be used, especially of black and yellow color; white ash should be avoided. They are often made to lay by half-cooked barley, and produce larger eggs. Catarrh is usual for them, which covers the tip of the tongue with a white membrane; this should be gently plucked with the nails, and the place touched with ash, and the cleaned wound sprinkled with crushed garlic. If they eat bitter lupine, seeds appear beneath the eyes, which, unless the membranes are gently opened with a needle and these removed, destroy the eyes. Then their eyes should be treated with purslane juice from outside and with a woman's milk, or with ammoniac salt mixed equally with honey and cumin. Stavesacre and roasted cumin, ground together equally with wine and the water of bitter lupine, kill their lice, if it penetrates the depths of the feathers.

Pliny, in the same place: catarrh is most hostile to every kind, and especially between harvest-time and vintage-time. The remedy is fasting and roosting in smoke, if this is made from laurel or salty herb; a feather inserted crosswise through the nostrils and moved every day; garlic as food with spelt, or water in which an owl has bathed, cooked with the seed of white bryony.

Aristotle: the hen, when she desires mating, sits before the cock; she mates, like the dove, throughout the year, except in the tropical months. After mating she shivers. These, and other birds of much mating, produce more than all others eggs with two yolks, because of the joining of two seeds. Some of these lay many eggs, perhaps two in a day, and die quickly. Wind-eggs, that is from those not yet mating, occur only in birds that lay many eggs, as in hens. A hen's egg is completed, for the most part, on the eleventh day after mating. Old hens lay at the start of spring, and the eggs of a young hen are of larger size. When they mate, they shake themselves with shivering. They often, too, carry straw with an ear of grain in their beak, and sometimes even do this while laying. Likewise heavy-bodied birds not yet of good flight, like hens, have much surplus; and so their males mate much, and the females have much matter [for eggs].
Pliny, book 10: farmyard hens, once they have laid an egg, shiver, shake themselves, and, turning around, purify themselves, or circle themselves and the eggs with a straw.

From the book On the Nature of Things: eggs are stolen daily from hens, and yet they do not cease laying for this; indeed, once they have laid in a hidden place, they betray it to thieves by clucking. But those exceeding the proper measure in laying die quickly. The eggs from which males will hatch, the hen carries in the right part of her belly; those from which females will hatch, in the left. Those rounder at the pointed end produce a female; but oblong ones, sharp at the end, produce males, and these are of more pleasant taste. The cock, calling the hen, feeds her, and then drives her to the labor of impregnation and childbirth. For she labors greatly in laying, and yet after laying she sings, seeking food; she turns over dust with her feet, and thus obtains her living. Many hens, and peacocks, and geese lay wind-eggs, that is eggs without mating, which are small and tasteless and moister than others. And if anyone sets one of these to brood, its condition will not change, but it will remain white and yellow. The egg first emerges from the wider end, and afterward from the pointed one. Pliny is the authority that on the day a hen lays an egg, she does not die from the bite of an asp; indeed, it is a medicine for those bitten. Some hens lay twin eggs and sometimes hatch twins.

The Philosopher: the hen lays at every season, except in the two tropical months. But while hens, enjoying the comfort of dust and its frequent sprinkling as if it were a bath, delight without mating, they lay eggs called 'apala,' so named as if 'without shell,' but they do not achieve the grace of offspring.

[Pliny, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham, and from the book On the Nature of Things:] eggs should always be set beneath hens in odd numbers, with the moon waxing, from the tenth to the fifteenth day. It is most useful to brood eggs laid within ten days; for old or too-fresh eggs are infertile; they must be set in odd numbers, however. On the fourth day after brooding begins, if, held up to the light in the hand at their tips, a pure and uniform color shines through, they are judged sterile, and others should be substituted for these. There is also a test in water: an empty egg, thrown into water, floats, but a full one sinks. They forbid shaking the eggs to be set as a test, since eggs whose vital veins have been disturbed do not hatch. Brooding begins after the eleventh day of the moon, because those begun earlier often fail and do not develop. The best are those to hatch before the spring equinox; those hatched after the solstice do not reach their proper size, and the later they hatch, the smaller they remain. Generally, if hens do not brood their own eggs, they become ill. And certain hens always produce twins, and one is always larger, the other smaller. A hen brooding in summer hatches her chicks more quickly than in winter; for in summer the eggs crack open in twelve days, in winter in thirty. Generally, however, if hens do not brood over their eggs, they become ill and are harmed. After they have brooded their eggs, signs of the chicks appear after three days. The hen, moreover, follows her chicks, as does the partridge.

Palladius, in the same place: as said above, peacock eggs, and likewise goose eggs, are suitably set beneath hens, but beneath goose eggs, so they are not harmed, nettle is placed. Chosen foster-mothers for peacocks are those that, from the first increase of the moon, have nine eggs set beneath them for nine days, namely five peacock eggs and the rest of their own kind; on the tenth day the hen's own eggs should be removed, and again as many fresh hen's eggs set as were removed, up to thirty. When thirty days of the moon are complete, they can be opened along with the peacock eggs. The peacock eggs set under the hen should often be turned by hand, since she will scarcely be able to do this herself. Larger hens, however, should be chosen; for smaller hens fewer eggs should be set. Hens will also brood pheasant eggs better, so that one foster-hen covers fifteen pheasant eggs. The rest of their own kind should be set as usual.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the hen, according to Augustine, and the females of other winged creatures, by brooding their eggs, warm them, and there the heat of the maternal body naturally cooperates, in its kind, to form the bodies of the chicks.

Pliny, in the same place, and from the book On the Nature of Things: in all eggs, in the middle of the yolk, there is a small, blood-like drop, which they believe to be the bird's heart, always supposing this to be produced first in every body. This drop leaps in the egg, and the creature itself pulses; and from all the rest of the liquid of the egg nothing is incorporated into the chick. Its food, however, is in the yolk; in all of them, before hatching, the head is larger than the head and the whole body. The eyes, pressed together, are larger than the head; as the chick grows, the white turns to the center, the yolk spreads around it, on the twentieth day. If the egg is moved, the voice of the now-living creature is heard within the shell. From that time it grows feathers, positioned so that it has its head above its right foot, and its right wing over its head; the yolk, meanwhile, gradually diminishes. The part that is pointed contains the head; the rounder part, the hindquarters of the chick. In Egypt men wrap eggs in dung and cover them with sand, and so, in due time, without a hen's brooding, they come to completion, and, once extracted, the shells crack open and the chicks emerge. Likewise, when a hen broods in warm summer, the shells of the eggs crack of themselves, so that the chicks emerge more quickly than in cold weather. Certain hens always produce twins, but one of them is small and the other large; and sometimes the small one, compressed by the larger, becomes deformed. In Gaul a chick was seen with two heads and one body; both took food and passed it into the one body; it had four feet, but two hung useless, and it ran on the others. Chicks are hatched more quickly in warm weather, and, contrary to other animals, all birds are born feet first. If it thunders suddenly, they often fail, and, hearing the hawk's voice, are also spoiled; the remedy against thunder is an iron nail placed beneath the straw of the eggs, or earth from a plough. The hen is most attentive around her chicks; she breaks crumbs of bread or grain for them and calls them with a broken voice, and sometimes proud chicks, fleeing her caressing wings, thus become prey for birds of prey.

[Augustine] likens himself to a hen, which has great affection for her chicks, so that, affected by their illness, she herself is made ill, and, what you will find more difficult in other animals, protecting her young with her wings, fights against the kite.

Vincentius Belvacensis: [these traits] of the hen are fitting for Christ, and are contained in these verses: the hen is a simple bird, domestic, gentle, rough-feathered, grows hoarse, wastes away with love, protects, grows sick, leads, feeds, fights, gathers, attends to her chicks, and after all this, freely climbs.

div.head: DE CIBO ET MEDICINA EX GALLINA

cit.quote: Aristotle: of hens, the better for food is one that has not yet laid eggs; old ones are poor. The fat of chicks is hotter than that of grown hens. Hen's flesh, too, clarifies the voice and, [for chicks,] calms inflammation of the stomach. Hen's brain prevents bleeding from the nostrils arising from the membranes of the brain. The flesh of young hens increases understanding. Among the wings of birds, hen's wings are the best for food.
The same: the liver of fat hens, like that of ducks, is healthier than others. Hen's blood, it is said, dropped warm on a crushed and painful abrasion, prevents an abscess from forming.

The same: cock's fat, like the stag's, is of more vehement heating power; hen's fat is less hot and benefits roughness of the tongue. All light fats, like the hen's and similar creatures', benefit pains of the womb; but old ones are bad for these. Hen's dung benefits colic; it has been proven to be an antidote for choking on mushrooms and causes thick humor to be spat up. Fresh hen's eggs are better than other eggs, and what is better in them is the yolk, which also benefits hot abscesses in the ear.

The Parthians apply hen's flesh to wounds. Its broth is marvelous for many uses. Fresh dung, applied, cures baldness. Its fat is poured into suppurating ears. Moreover, on the day someone eats hen, they are not killed by an asp; it is also very beneficial to apply hen's flesh, with tortoise blood, to those bitten by an asp.

Hen, cooked in oil and salt, given, soothes the pains of those with celiac disease; but both hen and man should abstain from grain beforehand. Hen's fat preserves the complexion of the face. It also heals ulcers of the lips and tongue. Hen's dung, too, heals all ulcers of the feet.

Dioscorides: hen's fat, like goose fat, is marvelous for the sweetness of its richness. It is usefully applied for women's ailments. It heals cracks of the lips and cracks of the whole face caused by cold most excellently, and ear pains.

Aesculapius: hen's egg is effective for every pain of the eyes; even the white, poured into the eyes, soothes stinging. A whole egg, burnt and drunk with wine or vinegar, stops all fluxes. Five egg yolks, drunk with three cups of wine, benefit those coughing blood. Hen's fat represses pustules of the eyes. The shins with feet, cooked with salt, oil, and vinegar, soothe pain of the neck. Its dung, applied, heals inflammations that arise in the nostrils.

Alexander Neckam: the gerfalcon comes from lands across the sea in a flock of many wild geese, driving one of them, by night, because of the cold, beneath its feet, and catching another by day for food.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the gerfalcon is said to be the same as the 'herodius,' of which more will be said fully below.

From the book On the Nature of Things: [the 'gosturdi'] are quite small birds, earth-colored, having a small crest of feathers on the head, and, not flying in the manner of other birds, imitate the waves of the sea, which, driven by the wind, now rise high, now sink low. Of these it is commonly told that their eggs, laid on the ground, are brooded by a toad, from which, once the chicks have hatched, the parents then, for the first time, care for them and bring them food, until they can attempt flight.

Isidore: the 'glottis' is a bird so named in Greek because it puts out a long tongue. This bird, as winter approaches and the swallows and storks depart, eagerly sets out on the journey with them, flattered by their company. But afterward, finding the labor of flight, is led to regret it, and, since it is loath to return unaccompanied, follows some birds, yet with such great reluctance and such short daily stages that winter overtakes it before its journey is complete. The 'citramus,' on the contrary, a bird of Asia, perseveres more hastily, and goes ahead of the other companion birds, and keeps them alert, and rouses the sleepy ones at night.
Aristotle: the bird called 'galator,' that is, 'large-tongued,' has a very prominent tongue, and this joins with the cranes and other birds on their return.

Pliny: the 'glottis' and the 'cithramus,' always returning from here, urge on their companions and depart together by their own signals. The 'glottis,' indeed, puts out a very long tongue, whence its name; this one, at first eagerly enticed by the migration, afterward regrets it, finding the flight laborious. It is loath to return unaccompanied and to follow; nor does it ever complete more than one day's journey, but abandons its lodging for the nearest one. But it is found again, the one it had followed having left it behind. The 'cenchramus,' more persistent, hastens even to reach the lands it seeks; and so, at night, it rouses them and reminds them of the journey.

Isidore: jackdaws are named from their chattering, not, as some hold, because they fly in flocks, since it is clear they are named from their voice. For it is the most talkative kind, and troublesome in voice.
The jackdaw too, like certain other birds, purges its annual distaste for food with laurel leaf.
The same, in the same book: jackdaws, leaving their feeding grounds late, foretell winter.

From the book On the Nature of Things: the jackdaw is a bird black over its whole body. It is of the crow kind, though smaller in body. It gladly nests in the highest places, and this in such numbers that often eight pairs of jackdaws build their nests in a single tree. For these birds get along remarkably well with one another. It is an exceedingly noisy bird, especially at mating time, which the spring season stirs. For love's sake, the male feeds the female. The flesh of its chicks is edible, especially if skinned. Some falsely think this bird is the same as the jay, but there is much difference between them. For the jackdaw, as said, is of a single color, while the jay is marked with varied feathers. It is named from chattering, for it moves chattering from one tree to another, nor can anyone pass by it without being chattered at. It is also said to imitate the voices or melodies of other birds not for the delight of joy, but only for chattering's sake. It is marked with such variety of feathers that no color of any other bird is said to be lacking to it. Caught in its youth, it is caged, so that it may be taught to speak articulate words, and, once it escapes, is all the more eager to chatter. And sometimes, while intent on its chattering and not watching out for itself, the sparrowhawk suddenly seizes it. It is often said to go mad, so much so that it usually hangs itself among the forked branches of trees.

Isidore: the griffin is so called because it is a feathered, four-footed creature; this kind of wild beast is born in the Hyperborean mountains. In every part of the body they are lions, similar to eagles in wings and face; they are exceedingly hostile to horses, and tear apart men they see.

Solinus: in Asian Scythia there are lands rich, yet uninhabitable. For though they abound in gold and gems, griffins, most fierce flying creatures, raging beyond all measure, hold them entirely, and, because of their monstrousness standing in the way, access there is rare for visitors. For they tear apart those they see, as if created to punish the rashness of avarice. The Arimaspians fight with these to seize the stones found there, among which are emerald, sapphire, and crystal.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the griffin is a four-footed bird, with a head and wings like an eagle's, but much larger; yet it places an agate stone in its nest, and there is no doubt this is for some remedy. These are most hostile to horses and men, and overcome and kill armed men in combat. Griffins are said to dig up gold and delight in gazing at what they have dug up.

Isidore: cranes took their name from their own voice, for they murmur with such a sound. As they travel, one follows another in orderly formation, like letters, of which Lucan says: and the crowd forms with feathers spread wide. Their color reveals their age, for they turn black in old age.

Aristotle: nature also gave cranes a pleasing crest, set along the middle of the head from the beak. Cranes have a king, and are obedient to him. A sleeping crane bows its head beneath its wing and stands on one foot. Cranes have a leader, who keeps watch, with head raised, while the rest sleep with heads tucked beneath their wings. Cranes fight one another, so much so that at the hour of their fighting they could be caught. In cranes the color of the feather is ash-grey in youth and blackens in old age.
Cranes, and similar birds, heal themselves with marsh rush.
Cranes hastening toward inland regions foretell a storm; cranes, however, flying silently on high, foretell fair weather.
Crane's fat effectively cures incipient carbuncles, swellings, and whatever needs softening.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is also read elsewhere that the crane, when it sees a bat, flees.

[From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham:] domestic cranes and other cranes have flesh heavier than other birds; whence a crane, killed, should be kept one day in summer, two in winter, before being eaten, so that its flesh becomes more digestible and tender.
Rhazes: crane's flesh is thick, digested slowly, and generates melancholic blood.
Haly Abbas: crane's gall, hot and subtle, if dropped into the nostrils with marjoram, benefits paralysis and causes a tingling sensation.

Isidore: cranes seek the highest places, so that they may more easily see the lands they make for. Their leader controls the voice that drives the flock, but when it grows hoarse, another succeeds. At night, moreover, they divide the watches and take turns keeping guard by shifts, holding little stones in raised claws, by which they may detect sleep, since their falling reveals what must be guarded against, the noise gives warning.

Aristotle: cranes leave their own regions chiefly after the autumn equinox, fleeing winter, and return after the spring equinox; one of them cries out among the others by night, and when hunters hear its voice, they know these birds will not remain in their places. Cranes fleeing to inland regions foretell a storm. When they move to other places, they first fly up in a long ascent, so as to gauge the evenness of the air toward which they intend to travel.

Ambrose, book 5: cranes love to migrate frequently. Among those remaining behind you may observe assigned watchers, for while some rest, others go about and keep watch lest an ambush be attempted from any quarter. When the time of the watch is complete, the one who has fulfilled this duty settles into sleep with a cry sent forth beforehand, to rouse the sleeping one to whom the turn of duty is to be passed, and that one, not unwillingly but readily and eagerly shaking off sleep, takes up the turn. And if anything should be guarded against or is seen, it is signaled to the others by this cry. They keep this same order in flight too, and by this discipline lighten all the labor, so that by turns they perform the office of leading; for one goes ahead for an appointed time, then turns back, and yields to the next the lot of leading the flock.

Solinus: it is well known that in winter cranes fly in great numbers to the northern region, and they go as if under a certain military standard. And lest, as they press toward their destination, the force of the winds resist them, they swallow sand and, having taken up small stones, are ballasted to a moderate weight, when about to cross the sea, they seize on narrow passages. And when they know they have come to the middle of the channel, they free their feet of the burden of pebbles: and thus sailors have reported that they are often drenched by a rain of stones from that occurrence; they do not disgorge the sand before they are secure in their own resting place. Their common concern for one another is such, when exhausted, that if any should fail, they all rush together and lift up the weary one, until its strength is restored by rest. Nor is their vigilance any less on land: they divide the night watches, so that a tenth of them stays awake as sentinels, holding little pebbles clasped in their claws, which, should they by chance fall, betray their sleep.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the crane, flying, sets itself against [the wind], and the one confident in its flight goes first among the flocks, which is now first in flight, at other times becomes last without resentment. And they all fly together under a kind of military standard, and because, when they sense they have come to the middle of the sea's channel, they free their feet of the burden of pebbles, hence it is that sailors have sometimes believed that showers of stones were falling. Cranes sometimes fly to the very ends of the earth, so as to find land suited to their constitution, and always in flying they set themselves against the wind. Aristotle says that in winter they come to the northern region beyond Egypt, where they are met by pygmy men, that is, men a cubit tall, and fight with them. The battle of the cranes is so fierce and stubborn that they can be caught by hand. When they foresee rain clouds, they cry out and clamor, while urging their leader to fly faster. But when they have come down onto the ground to eat, their leader raises its head high, as guard over them all, while the rest feed securely. When these cranes sleep, they stand on alternating feet. It is also reported that, flying after winter from the mountains of the East, they swallow golden sands and orichalcum stone, and afterward disgorge them in the lands across the sea. Whence those who have made trial of it have said that the stone which cranes disgorge passes into gold through the mediation of fire.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: harpies are said to be certain very large birds, which are never satisfied by eating.
Plautus, in the Aulularia: harpies sharpen their claws for prey, fly over the tables fearsome with their curved talons, and carry off what they touch, and defile what they leave.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the harpy is a bird of the wilderness by the Ionian sea, ravenous with hunger, almost always insatiable. It has hooked claws, always ready for seizing and tearing, but has the face of a man, though nothing of human virtue in itself. For it is hardened in ferocity beyond human measure. It is said to kill the first man it sees in the desert; and thereafter, when it has chanced upon waters and contemplated its own face in them, presently, perceiving that it has killed one like itself, it grieves immoderately, sometimes even unto death, and mourns the slain for all the time of its life. Though this bird lacks reason, yet sometimes, tame and taught, it speaks with a human voice.
Isidore: the Greeks call them 'herodii,' which the Latins call diomedean birds, of which mention has already been made above.
Gloss, on Psalm 103: the 'herodius' is a most rapacious bird, the greatest of all winged creatures, and it overcomes the eagle.
Gloss: the 'herodius' is commonly called the gerfalcon, and it seizes the eagle.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: as for what was said above about the falcon, that it is itself the 'herodius,' according to Radulphus this seems to have been a copyist's error, whereby, where 'gyrofalco' should have been written, the first syllable was dropped and 'falco' was written instead.

From the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the 'herodius,' also called the gerfalcon, as the gloss on Leviticus says, is the noblest bird of all, sky-blue in color, though for the most part of its body inclining to white, except on the breast and wings, where it more clearly imitates the color of the sky. It is so strong that it catches the eagle, and so bold besides that, once let loose after five cranes or any other birds flying in the air, it does not give up its pursuit of them until it has brought them all down to the ground in succession. There is also a dog trained and taught for this purpose, which, while the 'herodius' flies above, catches and kills the birds it has brought down. When the 'herodius' sees its prey, it shakes itself and rouses itself, and judges whether it is fit for capture. It rises up high indeed, and, descending with force, brings down its prey; flying toward the prey, it also draws its feet to its breast, and thus strikes the prey: which, if it does not catch on the first strike, it climbs up high again and, from indignation, scarcely returns to its handler's call. It does not eat raw meat that has been kept, but only fresh. There is a kind of gerfalcon called the 'sacred' one, and this is stronger and has a dark color. The 'herodius' is small of body in proportion to its wings.
Isidore: the ibis is a bird of the river Nile, which cleanses itself with its beak, pouring water into its anus; it feeds on the eggs of serpents, carrying this most welcome food to its nests.

Solinus: when the marshes of Arabia send out swarms of winged serpents, whose venom is so swift that death follows the bite before the pain does, the ibis birds, made keen by their instinct against these, all go out in formation before the foreign evil can lay waste to their native borders, meet them in the air in their pestilent hordes, and there devour the whole troop. For this reason they are rightly sacred, and give birth unharmed. And so they benefit not only within the borders of Egypt, while eating the eggs of serpents, whence the broods of harmful creatures become rare, but they also destroy the foreign evil as it approaches, as has been said; only those at Pelusium are black, the rest are white in their other parts.

Physiologus: the ibis walks by the shores night and day, seeking some carcass that has been cast up by the water, already putrid, avoiding the higher and purer waves, where clean fish dwell, since it does not know how to swim, nor does it take pains to learn, while it delights in carcasses.
Pliny, book 10, on serpents: the Egyptians invoke their ibises against the coming of serpents.

Gloss, on Isaiah 34: the ibis is indeed a water bird, hostile to serpents. Josephus relates that birds of this kind were brought by Moses into war against the Ethiopians, since serpents abound in that land, through which the way lay.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the ibis is a bird that rests upon the Nile, yet never enters the water, but eats cast-up carcasses. When it has become too full of food, it draws out indigestible foods from the secret parts of its nature with its beak. Those plainly lie who say that ibises are storks, unless perhaps they mean a kind of stork unknown in our world. For Pliny says the ibis has a hooked beak, which is certainly false of our storks, which have a long, straight beak, sharp at the tip. This bird gives birth through the mouth, and whoever eats its eggs dies.

Isidore: the swallow is a talkative bird, flying through winding circuits and twisting turns, most skillful in building nests and raising its chicks, having also a certain foreknowledge, so that it abandons roofs about to collapse and does not seek them out. It is called 'hirundo' because it does not settle to take its food, but eats it in the air. It is not attacked by other birds, nor is it ever prey. It flies across the seas and stays there in winter. This devoted bird knows how to announce, by the witness of its arrival, the beginning of spring.

Pliny, book 10, on swallows: swallows depart in the winter months; it is the only bird that feeds on flesh among those that do not have hooked claws. They are said not to enter under the roofs of Thebes, since that city has often been captured; nor at Bizye in Thrace, because of its crimes. Of all birds, the swallow alone has winding flight and swift speed. And so it is neither seized by other birds of prey, nor does it feed except in flight. Among birds, swallows are untrainable, just as mice are among land animals.
Pliny: the swallow flying near water, so that it often strikes the water with its wing, signals a storm.

Aristotle: the swallow, like the turtledove and the kite, appears only in summer; for in winter it moves to warmer places, or hides in its nest or in caves. Alone among flesh-bearing and flesh-eating animals it harms bees; it breeds twice a year and lays twice. For other flesh-eating birds lay eggs and breed only once a year. The swallow, like the quail and the dove, has a gall bladder attached to the intestine. It also has weak feet. For certain birds have weak or poor feet. And so they are said to have, as it were, no feet, like the swallow. Likewise small birds do not have a wide crop or stomach opening, but have a long belly, like the swallow and the sparrow. It happens to crows and sparrows and swallows that they change from black, tending somewhat toward whiteness. The swallow makes its nest from mud.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things, and Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the swallow is a very light bird, with a small beak, forked tail, pleasing shape, most becomingly black, white on the belly, reddish under the throat; it has little flesh, and black, many feathers and large wings, and so has swift flight; it announces the coming day, wakes the sleeping, and calls them to praise the creator. In winter it seeks sunny mountain retreats and there is found bare and featherless; it keeps the time of its own arrival, and by its arrival announces the beginning of spring. Some carry the swallow-stone in their liver; the chicks of these are recognized by this, if for a sign of peace they sit in the nest turned mouth to mouth. For the others, who do not have this, sit with their backs to one another. The swallow feeds in flight on gnats and flies and little bees. Swallow's dung, if it falls into the eyes, has a most potent power to blind.

Ambrose: let us take the swallow as a great example of a mother's devotion. The swallow is tiny in body, but distinguished by exceptional affection. In building its nest it is so wise that it entrusts its little ones to human dwellings, where nothing may attack them; it gathers straws with its beak and smears them with mud, so they may be able to stick together, but since it cannot carry mud with its feet, it soaks its feathers in water, so that dust may cling to them and become mire, with which it may gather the straws to itself and make them stick. And if any of its chicks should be afflicted with blindness, their eyes pricked, it has a certain kind of remedy, by which it restores light to their blocked sight.

Pliny: swallows build their nests of mud, strengthen them with straw. If ever there is a lack of mud, they sprinkle dust soaked with much water on their feathers. They also line the nest itself with soft feathers and down, to warm the eggs, and likewise so it is not hard for the tender chicks. In feeding, they alternate food with the utmost fairness. With notable cleanliness they carry out the chicks' excrement. They also teach the grown ones to turn around and release their waste, that is, dung, outside. There is a second kind of swallow, of the countryside, which rarely nests in houses, differing in shape, but making its nests of the same material, entirely rounded, with the opening drawn narrow, the interior capacious - wonderful with what skill they are suited for hiding the chicks and are soft for bedding them. There is a third kind of these that hollows out riverbanks and so nests in the earth; the chicks of these, burned to ash, heal the deadly disease of the throat and many other diseases of the human body. These do not build nests and migrate many days beforehand if a river is going to rise and reach them. The chicks of the swallow are blind at first, as are those of all birds with a more numerous brood. In the bellies of its chicks are found swallow-stones of white and reddish color.

Aristotle: swallows, as has been said, lay eggs twice a year, but the first eggs are sometimes ruined by the winter. The later ones, however, come to completion and produce chicks. Swallows and sparrows produce incomplete chicks and hatch many chicks; because of this, if a chick swallow's eye is removed while it is still small, it grows again.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book: the female swallow conceives from the mere image of desire, or from dust. Swallows revealed the herb celandine, as Pliny says, most healthful for sight, healing with it the afflicted eyes of their chicks. Some swallows nest in houses, some in glass windows, some in mountain crags. And these differ in kind and number. The chick swallow cries eagerly, both fasting and by night. If the eyes of chick swallows are removed, nature restores and recovers them. In its belly is found a stone useful for many purposes, namely one red and another white.

Dioscorides: opening a chick swallow at the very start of the failing moon, you will find in it two stones, one beneficial and the other harmful. But when you open it, take care it does not touch the ground; this, placed in the skin of a calf or a stag and bound to the neck or left arm of the sufferer, cures epilepsy, if this is done regularly. These, eaten, taste something like a fig-pecker. If larger swallows are burned, their ash mixed with honey and applied clears dimness of the eyes. It also benefits those with quinsy and eases swelling of the uvula and throat.

Aesculapius: burning of the swallow, or ash of its burned chicks, cures diseases of the throat, and heals wounds of the tongue and lips. Swallow cooked in mead purges the chest excellently. Its heart, if drunk, does the same.

Avicenna: swallow's ash, especially when well-burned, sharpens sight. And it is said that its brain with honey helps at the onset of dropsy. The palate is touched with its ash for quinsy, and it helps. Likewise, when salted and dried, it is drunk. He says, moreover...

Dioscorides: when the belly of a chick swallow is cut open, two stones are found in it, of which one has a single color, the other has many; placed in the skin of a calf not yet ready for mating, and hung on the neck of an epileptic, they are beneficial.
Avicenna: swallow's dung is effective for white spots of the eye, and I have myself found this to be marvelously true.

Haly Abbas: if a swallow is placed on spots where there is corrupted blood or a spreading sore, it sucks out that bad blood and clearly benefits them. Likewise the ash of burned swallows, if mixed with honey and applied as a poultice to the throat, benefits quinsy sufferers and other abscesses of the throat. Moreover, if mixed with honey and used as an eye-salve, they sharpen sight. If dried after being split open and drunk ground up, they cure suffocation.
Pliny: swallow's dung, boiled and drunk, benefits the bite of a rabid dog.

Pliny, book 29: fresh swallow's flesh, cut up, helps against serpents. Their burned chicks help against the bite of a rabid dog. Likewise a small lump from a swallow's nest applied with vinegar. The ash of the chicks with milk of spurge is also said to produce eyelashes. Chick swallows are blinded at the full moon and, once their sight is restored, their heads are burned, and the ashes, with honey, are used for clarity of the eyes, and for pains and inflammations, and for blows.

Pliny, book 30: swallows cooked in mead heal ulcers of the tongue and lips. Swelling of the uvula and pain of the throat are eased by swallow's ash with honey. Swallows kept in the sun are drunk for quinsy, which ailment their nests, drunk, are also said to cure. The falling sickness is helped by fresh swallow's blood or heart eaten with frankincense. Moreover, a small stone placed from their nest is said to draw out immediately and, bound on, to protect forever. Likewise hairs are plucked out with swallow's blood or gall.

The kikes is a bird that cries out with various voices and changes its voice almost every day; it nests in trees and gathers sufficient food for itself from acorns when they are ripe. Once its chicks are raised and strengthened for flight, they feed their parents in old age and make them stay in the nests without any labor. The kokis is a bird at whose death, as said above, other birds cry out with a sorrowful and sweet lament. Also, all birds of hooked claws, once they see their chicks able to fly, strike them and cast them from the nests, and afterward are not concerned about them once they are grown, except the kokis, which for a long time is concerned for its chicks and flies with them as they fly and gives them food to eat.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the same is said elsewhere of the crow, whence I judge this bird to be the crow.

div.head: DE LAGO ET LARO ET LUCIDIO

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, king of Mauretania: the 'lagus' is a water bird, in some ways opposite in habits to the diver-bird; for as the diver-bird flees a sea-storm, so the 'lagus' rejoices and plays in a storm.
Hesychius of Jerusalem: the 'lagus' is a creature living both on land and in water, for it flies and swims.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: it is a bird, so reported, commonly called 'rasse.'

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'lucidii' are so called as if 'giving light.' For the feathers of these birds shine in the dark at night. Whence those who have them, when they wish, having cast the shining feathers ahead, direct their course by their favor. This bird lives in the Hercynian forest of Germany.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the nightingale is itself the 'philomena,' as is read in Papias.
Isidore: the nightingale is so called as if 'lucinia,' since it is accustomed to signal by its song the rising of the dawning day; Cicero also calls the same bird 'acredula.'

Ambrose: the nightingale, a watchful guardian, warming her eggs in a certain fold and lap of her body, eases the sleepless labor of the long night with the sweetness of her song, so that she can, it seems to me, animate the eggs she warms no less by sweet melodies than by the warmth of her body.

Pliny: nightingales sing continuously, chattering, for fifteen days and nights without a break, as the buds of leaves grow thick, a bird worthy of wonder. First, so great a voice in so small a little body, and so persistent a breath. Then, in one bird, a perfect knowledge of music, a modulated sound is produced, and now it is drawn out long in continuous breath, now varied by an inflection, now marked off by being cut short, joined in a trill, brought forth, called back, darkened unexpectedly, and sometimes it even murmurs to itself, full, deep, sharp, rapid, sustained: where it seems fit, quavering, highest, middle, lowest, and briefly all the things that human art has devised with such elaborate torments of flutes, achieved in such tiny throats. And it is not the same song for all, but each has its own song. They compete with one another, and there is an open, spirited rivalry; the loser often ends her life in defeat, her breath failing before her song does. Younger ones practice and receive verses to imitate. The pupil listens with great attention and repeats, and they take turns falling silent. For a given correction is understood, and, in the one teaching, a kind of reproof. And so Caesar's young men had nightingales trained to sing in Greek and Latin speech. Moreover, practicing daily and constantly saying new things. It has often been observed that, bidden, they began to sing and alternated with an accompaniment. But these so great and so skillful subtleties gradually cease after fifteen days, so that you could not say they are either tired or satisfied. Then, as the heat increases, the voice changes entirely into something else, neither modulated nor varied, and even their color changes. Finally, in winter itself, the bird is not seen: the thinness of their tongues is not, at first, what it is in other birds; they lay in early spring, mostly six eggs.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'linachus' is a bird of very sharp sight, which strikes its own chicks even before their wings are fully grown and forces them to look at the sun, and if any one's eye waters, it kills that one, but nourishes the others; this bird also feeds on sea birds, and sometimes, lifted up in the air above them, watches them swimming, and when they see it, they submerge themselves. But it descends near the water, forces them to stay submerged to the point of suffocation, and then, once they are brought by their feathers to the surface of the water, seizes them.

[Thomas Cantimpratensis]: a sea bird larger than a duck, of ashen color, having a short neck and legs, grey-blue eyes, a beak partly saffron-colored and partly red, named from the sound of its voice, for it always cries out. It is most greedy for carcasses, and human ones at that: and so, when a storm is approaching, it cries out most, as if already exulting at having found a feast of carcasses, and it seeks out the eye first in a carcass.

Isidore: Egyptian birds, named from the place where Memnon perished. For they are said to fly in flocks from Egypt to Ilium, near the tomb of Memnon. For every fifth year they come there, and when they have circled around for two days, on the third day, entering battle, they tear at one another in turn with claws and beaks.
