Pliny: authorities say that every year the Memnon-birds fly from Ethiopia to Ilium and do battle at Memnon's tomb. Cremutius reports that he had ascertained that they do this same thing also every fifth year in Ethiopia around Memnon's royal seat.

Isidore: the diver-bird [mergus] is named from its constant diving. These often, with head submerged in the depths, gather signs of the winds beneath the waves and, foreseeing a storm at sea, head for the shore with a cry. Whence men say a very heavy storm is already at sea when diver-birds take refuge on the shores.
Pliny, book 10: diver-birds mostly lay three eggs in trees and begin to nest in spring.
Pliny, book 11: insatiable creatures are those whose food passes at once through a straight intestine from the belly, as with diver-birds.
Pliny, book 18: diver-birds, like other water birds, cleaning their feathers with their beak, or fleeing the seas and lagoons, foretell wind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the diver-bird swims through rivers and lakes and pursues fish, so named because it submerges itself in the water; it cannot, however, stay long under water, since it must recover its breath in the air; when it must be struck, it submerges in the water. Sulpicius Severus reports that there is a certain kind of these which men call the 'horned' one from the fact, since it has red feathers on its head like horns. Contrary to every other kind of bird, they have their feet set toward the tail, so that when they stand on land they are held upright by the posture of the chest, like a man. Saint Martin, by divine power, compelled these birds to leave the water against their nature and seek dry, deserted places. As soon as their chicks come out of the eggs, they are so vigorous that, should it happen that they lose their mother, they live by their own strength.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the merlin is a bird not much bigger than a blackbird, and close to it in color too, but unlike it in beak, feet, and claws; it is greedy for prey. But since it is small and of little strength, it preys on small birds: these, like hawks and 'herodii,' fly together socially, and four of them working together can capture a swan in this way - the first of them attacks the swan's head, the second and third the two wings on either side, the fourth the neck and breast, and so the swan, weighed down, hemmed in by these attacks, unable to move, is overtaken by the fowler and caught and killed. The bee-eater is a bird having a sky-blue color on the back, reddish on the breast, pale on the belly; abounding in natural heat, it digs caves seven feet deep in the ground and there nests and raises its young, feeding and nourishing them there hidden until they reach the proper strength.
Isidore: we call them 'meropes' or 'gauli,' which are said to shelter and feed their parents.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the same place: bee-eaters are attentive to their chicks, and when they in turn grow old and are unable to fly, the chicks care for and feed them as long as they live.

Isidore: the blackbird was anciently called 'medula,' because it sings in modulated tones. Others say it was called 'merula' because it flies alone, as if 'mere volans' [purely flying]. Though it is black everywhere, in Achaia it is white.
Pliny, book 8: blackbird, with laurel leaf, purges its yearly distaste for food.

Pliny, book 10: blackbirds too withdraw to nearby regions, but do not shed their plumage, nor do they hide themselves except for the hope of food, seeking their winter fare. The blackbird turns from black to reddish. It sings in summer, stammers in winter, changes its beak around the solstice, which at that season of the year turns to ivory color, only in the males. Blackbirds are born white only around Cyllene in Arcadia, and nowhere else. Likewise some blackbirds hop as they walk.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the blackbird was formerly called 'medula,' because it produces wonderful modulations of voice, especially when it foresees that spring is approaching. For in winter it is silent or only stammers. Once, a blackbird was a spectacle to behold in a monastery, which, taught by human skill, sang nine notes in order according to music, so perfectly that no musician could imitate it at all with equal harmony. This bird has a somewhat saffron color on its breast, but the rest of its body is occupied by blackness. The tame blackbird eats meat, against its nature, and sings more sweetly for this; it gladly bathes itself and cleans its feathers with its beak. And though it is black and unsightly, it moves itself to delight because of the charm of its voice; the blackbird does not molt its feathers as other birds do, but changes its beak to whiteness every year, and in winter it can scarcely fly because of its fatness. There is a certain kind of blackbird much larger than the rest, called 'agochile,' that is 'goat-milker,' as said above.

Pliny: the 'goat-milkers' are called larger blackbirds in appearance, night thieves, without sight by day; they enter shepherds' folds and fly to the udders of goats for the sake of sucking milk, by which injury the udder dies off and the goats they have so milked go blind.
Haly Abbas: [birds] eat the rice of blackbirds, and if it is crushed and mixed with vinegar and applied to black leprosy, it removes it; it likewise clears away freckles.
Isidore: the kite is called as if a 'soft' bird, that is, in strength and flight, yet it is most rapacious and always lies in wait for domestic birds.

Pliny: the kite is a most rapacious and ever-famished bird. It never snatches anything edible from funeral offerings, nor from the altar at Olympia. Nor even from the hands of those carrying it, except as a mournful omen for towns performing sacrifice. It seems, moreover, to have taught steering by the turns of its tail, nature showing in the sky what was needed in the deep. Kites are of the hawk kind, but differ in size. Kites too hide in the winter months, yet without departing skillfully like the swallow. They are said to be afflicted by gout from the solstices.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the kite has claws on its feet and a hooked beak like the hawk, but curved and not straight wings, in which it differs from it; it is bold against small creatures, but timid against large ones. It is put to flight by the sparrowhawk, though it is three times larger than that bird. It keeps watch around slaughterhouses and around carcasses. Pliny praises its liver as medicinal.

Gloss, on Jeremiah 8: birds know their own seasons, namely when, hastening to warm places, they ought to avoid the harshness of winter, and from the beginning of spring return to their accustomed regions. Whence it is written: the kite in the sky knew its season, and so on. The kite does not appear except in summer, just as neither does the turtledove nor the swallow. For in winter they stay in the nest or hide in hollows of trees or move themselves to warmer places.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: the young kite, when it leaves the nest with its wings fully grown, hunts large birds. And since it is stronger, it catches weaker ones. But at the peak of its strength it hunts flies and gnats and earthworms, and then dies of hunger.

From the Aviarium of Hugh of Fouilloy: the kite lies in wait for domestic birds, especially chicks, and whichever it sees off guard, it seizes at once. It also flies about kitchens and slaughterhouses, so that if any raw meat is thrown outside, it may snatch it up more quickly.
Pliny: kite's liver is praised for anointing eye ailments.
Pliny, book 30: a shoot of vine from a kite's nest, bound with sinews to the neck, is also said to help against epilepsy and 'epistotanus.' Kite's liver, eaten, also cures epileptics.

Isidore: the jackdaw is called 'monetula' as if from 'moneta' [coin], since when it finds gold it carries it off and hides it. Whence Cicero, in defense of Valerius Flaccus, says: no more should gold be entrusted to you than to a jackdaw.
Aristotle: the jackdaw fights with the horned owl, because the owl has weak sight by day; for this reason the crow seizes the owl's eggs and eats them, as said above.

Pliny: in the wooded countryside there are no jackdaws, nor do they live within eight miles of the stone [i.e., a certain marker], but perish. Transpadane Italy, near the Alps by Lake Larius, calls a certain tree the 'anienus,' to which storks do not cross over, just as they do not come within eight miles of it either. But otherwise there are immense swarms of jackdaws in the neighboring territory of the Insubres. This bird alone has a remarkable thieving nature, especially for silver and gold.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the jackdaw is said to be named as if 'taking' or 'loving coin' [moneta]; it is a black bird, but handsome and pleasing, and when taught as a chick it imitates human voices. In the morning, at sunrise, it is said to hold what it has learned more carefully, distinctly, and tenaciously. Its flesh excites itching of the head. For it too likes to have its own head scratched. The flycatcher is a bird larger than a dove, having feathers like the woolly falcon, feet and beak like the swallow; though it has a very wide gape of the mouth because of the flies and gnats on which alone it feeds, yet its beak is, compared to its body, among the smallest of birds, and likewise its feet.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'nicedula' is a kind of crow, which fights with the horned owl. For the crow seizes the owl's eggs, since it sees little at midday, and eats them, but the owl likewise eats the crow's eggs at night.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: [that is,] the jackdaw.

Isidore: the night-raven is itself the owl, because it loves the night. For it is a light-fleeing bird, that is, fleeing the light, and cannot bear to see the sun. It is called 'noctua' because it flies about at night: the island of Crete does not have this bird, and if it comes from elsewhere, it dies at once.

Ambrose: the owl, also called the night-raven, with its large and grey-blue pupils, does not feel the horror of the nocturnal darkness, and the darker the night is, the more frequently it exercises unhindered flight. But by day it cannot see, because its sight is dulled once the daylight has risen. The owl also has its own grey hairs.

Gloss: the night-raven is a wakeful, foul bird, the raven of night, dwelling in ruined walls, which are commonly called ruins, where walls stand without a foundation; whence it is written: I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling-place.
Gloss: the owl is a bird of prey by night.

Pliny: the owl has hooked claws, like other nocturnal birds, such as the horned owl and the screech owl. Illaphus reports that the owl, like the woodpecker and the horned owl, hollows out trees. The owls' fight against [other] birds is a skillful one. Surrounded by a greater multitude, lying on their backs they fight back with their feet, and, gathered into a circle, are entirely covered by beak and claws; the sparrowhawk assists this alliance by a certain natural bond and shares in the war. Nigidius reports that owls sit for sixty days in winter and have nine different calls.
Pliny: the owl, too, if it hoots in the rain or in fair weather, signals a storm.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the night-raven is so called as 'raven of the night,' for it is light-fleeing and seeks its food by night. For if it flew by day, it would be attacked by other birds. By night, as common opinion holds, it seems to foretell the deaths of men with ominous cries; it has a huge head, not shaped like other birds', a hooked beak like the sparrowhawk, and rough, buried claws. It gladly dwells in dwellings and walls, especially ruined ones without a roof, and there tends its chicks; it delights in human voices, is pursued by males and every kind of bird; its flesh cures paralytics.
Pliny: the owl is hostile to bees and wasps, hornets, and leeches. Its brain, cooked in wine or taken with food, is a remedy for headaches.
Pliny, book 30: owl's eggs, given in wine for three days, bring on distaste for it in drunkards.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the sparrowhawk is a bird of noble form and strength, smaller than the 'herodius,' but both share one color of plumage, and yet they refuse to fly together socially. For it is said that, out of envy and pride, when it attacks a bird, it wishes alone to gain the honor of victory - this indeed can be supposed, and perhaps rightly, but in truth it is more credible that it alone craves the prey, lest, having had a companion in flight, it should also have to share a companion in feeding. It is not even a doubtful matter of trust that the sparrowhawk singles out its own equal kind and pursues it as if it were a bird of another kind, and this contrary to the nature of all other birds. For, as Aristotle says: every bird, in seizing prey during flight, spares birds of its own kind. The sparrowhawk alone, then, is without this nobility, and in this it agrees with man himself, who among land animals does not cease to lie in wait for an animal of his own kind.

Alexander Neckam: the sparrowhawk and the merlin, or the tercel, choose a place where they pluck the feathers of birds they have caught each day and clean them with great care, as long as their mates are brooding eggs, to which they also bring these.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the tercel is the smallest of the birds used in falconry, but, given its sex and nature, the most ready for hunting. It is joined to the kinds of falcons.
Thomas Cantimpratensis: the pelican is a bird that at once stores many foods in its belly and afterward draws them out again and eats them.

Pliny: the pelican has the likeness of a swan, and one would not think them different at all, except that in its throat there is a kind of second stomach; into this the insatiable creature gathers everything, so that its capacity is astonishing, and then, once the plunder is complete, it gradually returns it from there through its mouth into its true belly, after the manner of a ruminant. Northern Gaul, nearest the ocean, sends this bird.
Isidore: they call birds with a long beak 'onocrotali,' of which there are two kinds.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the pelican, as is read, is a bird with a long beak, like a swan, but larger. Further, according to Jerome, unless I am mistaken, it is that bird which, with its beak fixed in a marsh, cries horribly, which is also called in Isaiah the 'ulula,' as if from its howling. And it is called in the vernacular 'bittern,' of which mention was made above, which is also thought to draw its food from the depths of the earth or water. Others think it is the golden oriole. Andrew, however, says that the Jews say it is the owl.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the pelican is a bird of the eastern regions, which, when it wishes to produce its call, puts its head in the water and there makes a cry like a roar. It has certain pouches in its throat, in which it first receives food and after an hour sends it into its belly and digests it there. There are two kinds of this bird: one that is aquatic, and another of the wilderness. This bird alone, as Aristotle says, lacks a spleen. And, as Isidore says, it stores up many foods at once.
From the book On the Nature of Things, of an uncertain author: the 'ophimachus' is opposed to serpents and fights with them. For 'ophis' means serpent, 'machus' means fighting.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'ophimachus,' as is read in Leviticus, is among the unclean winged creatures according to the law, namely among those that walk on four feet, but have longer hind legs by which they leap over the ground. I judge, however, that this should be numbered among the small flying creatures, like the locust-grub and the locust, which are of the same kind, as is read in the same place. Of the 'attacus,' however, which is reckoned there in the same kind, I do not recall having read anything at all elsewhere.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the oriole is a bird commonly so called from the sound of its voice, of golden color all over, except that it has dark feathers marked with a certain blue-grey variegation on the cheeks. It hangs its nest on the very smallest branches of trees with wonderful delicacy, so that to those looking up from the ground it seems to hang in the air alone. It also roofs the nest itself against the rain and protects it with dense foliage.
Isidore: the 'ortygometra' [quail-mother] is so called because it leads the flock of quails. Mention of this was made above in the chapter on the quail.

Pliny: quails fly chiefly with the north wind, led by the 'ortygometra'; the hawk seizes the first of them as it nears land, and often for this reason the following flock grows anxious and turns back.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'osina' is a bird as large as a swan, dwelling in rivers and fish-ponds, having a large beak and, from the throat to the breast, a long and ample pouch like a little sack, in which it stores at once a great quantity of fish, so that, with nature spread out over so great a bulk, it need not go hungry, and, its food gradually digested in its belly, it finds ready what it may offer. Birds of this kind never dwell except in more open water and where fish abound, since they would very quickly empty even a small quantity of water, however abundant in fish, into their gullet.
Isidore: the 'ossifrage' [bone-breaker] is a bird commonly so called, which drops bones from a height and breaks them, whence it also received this name.

Pliny: sea-eagles indeed do not have their own separate kind, but are born from the mixed mating of eagles. But that which is born from sea-eagles has the nature of the 'ossifrage' kind. From these, in turn, the smaller vultures are born; and chicks cast down by the eagle are taken up by the 'ossifrage' kind and raised along with their own.

Pliny: the 'ossifrage''s belly, dried and drunk, benefits those who do not digest their food, or, if only held in the hand while taking food, it helps when bound on, but not continuously. There is, moreover, one intestine in the 'ossifrage' that digests everything swallowed, whose furthest part, bound on, benefits against colic.

Pliny: the 'otus' is a bird smaller than the horned owl, larger than the screech owl, with prominent feathered ear-tufts, whence also its name; some call it in Latin the 'asio,' an imitator of other birds, and a parasite, and something of a dancer in its kind. It is caught without much difficulty, like the screech owl, by being lured while one circles about it and another approaches; but if the wind should begin to hinder its flock with an opposing gust, they fly steadily by seizing little weights of stone or filling their throat with sand.
Pliny, book 11: and so both the horned owl and the 'otus' have feathers that serve as ears.
Aristotle: finally, some call the 'otus' the horned owl. It is caught, moreover, when the hunter begins to move to the opposite side.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the 'otus' is a bird commonly called 'huans' from the sound of its voice. For at night it cries out horribly, 'huhu,' imitating, though imperfectly, the human voice, so that you would believe a man contracted with cold was crying out. But it has special regions in which it produces such calls; in others, for the most part, it is silent. This bird is smaller than the horned owl, larger than the screech owl, has a hooked beak and feet, and seems to have ears from its prominent feathers. It lives by prey, feeds on flesh, pursues mice, and is held in hatred by other birds.

Aristotle: wood-pigeons are birds that naturally love one another, yet they fight with one another over nests and steal them from each other. These, like turtledoves, lay eggs twice a year and hatch two chicks. They also keep this fidelity, that if either loses its mate, it does not mate further; they cast their dung outside the nest, and when their chicks have grown, they train them to this same thing, namely to cast it out themselves too. The wood-pigeon is smaller than the dove and is not domesticated like the dove. Its color inclines toward black. Its feet are red and rough. They live on fruit, like the turtledove. And the wood-pigeon is always to be seen, but the turtledove is not. The females of this kind do not love mating.

Pliny: the cuckoo, of the hawk kind, lays in others' nests, especially those of wood-pigeons. Aristotle is the authority that wood-pigeons live to thirty years, other birds even to forty, though with one drawback of the claws, and by the same token a sign of old age, which are trimmed short of harm. Their song is similar in all, and is completed in a threefold verse, except for a moan at the close; they are silent in winter, vocal in spring. They lay around the solstice, mostly three eggs, and scarcely more than twice, and although they have laid three, they never raise more than two - the third is void, called the 'urinum.' Among wood-pigeons, the female broods from afternoon into the morning, the male the rest of the time.

Isidore: the wood-pigeon is a woodland dove, that is, a chaste bird by its habits, named accordingly, for it is a companion of chastity, since, once it has lost its bodily partner, it goes about solitary, nor does it seek carnal union any further.
Avicenna: wood-pigeon has tough flesh.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the female wood-pigeon begins to brood the eggs from midday until morning, the male for the rest of the time. The male wood-pigeon sucks up salty, moist earth and puts it into the chick's mouth so it may grow accustomed to food. The wood-pigeon, once it has lost its bodily partner, seeks no green resting place, nor does it seek carnal union any further.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the wood-pigeon is that very kind of dove commonly called 'ramaria' [of the branches], because it is accustomed to perch on the branches of trees and nest there.
Pliny: wood-pigeon's blood is exceptionally beneficial for eyes suffused with blood.

Pliny: wood-pigeon flesh, boiled in vinegar, heals dysentery and celiac disease. A wood-pigeon chick, boiled in vinegar-water, stops the bowels. Wood-pigeon dung, taken in a bean, is used against stones and other troubles of the bladder. Likewise the ash of wood wood-pigeon feathers with vinegar-mead.

Dioscorides: wood-pigeon dung, being hot and caustic, ground with vinegar and applied, cures scrofula and bursts carbuncles. But mixed with honey and flaxseed and oil and applied as a poultice, it heals burns; and it is a very great remedy for those who have eaten poisonous mushrooms - this works better if drunk with wine and vinegar.

Isidore: sparrows are tiny winged creatures, named for their smallness. The cuckoo eats sparrow eggs found in the nest and lays its own in their place, and afterward the sparrows, having accepted these, warm and rear them.

Pliny: the sparrow has the shortest life span, matched by its lustfulness. Males are said not to last beyond a year, evidenced by the fact that no blackness appears at the start of spring on the beak - a blackness that begins in summer; for females, however, the span is somewhat longer.

Pliny, book 18: know that flocks of starlings or sparrows are driven from millet and panic-grass by a certain herb whose name is unknown, buried at the four corners of the field - marvelous to say, so that no bird at all enters.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sparrow dwells on roofs, flies in flocks to feed, is hotter than all other birds, and quickly digests whatever it swallows. Whence its body is by no means fattened by the food it takes, but only sustained. Its dung, too, is extremely hot when it is expelled. It is also lustful beyond measure and quickly roused to fury, but with no lasting discord. Aristotle says that the male lives only one year, but the female longer - which we believe true of the sparrows of the East, for that blackness which he says is on the neck of the male is not found in those that are among us, that is, in Europe, but instead a certain white patch marked with black on the cheeks, and these persist through winter and summer, both in life, as do their females. The sparrow's age shows in its beak, since a young one has it tender and saffron-colored around the throat, but an old one has it hard and black. In certain parts of the world this bird suffers the falling sickness. And this, as Aristotle believes, is because it eats henbane seed. When its chicks are ready to fly, neighboring sparrows, along with their parents, accompany the attempts of those learning to fly, so that the weak ones, if necessary, may be strengthened by the crowding of the many.

Aristotle: the sparrow has a voice proper to itself, as does the turtledove. It also feeds on worms, like many other similar small birds. It happens to sparrows, as to crows and swallows, that they change from black, tending somewhat toward whiteness. A white sparrow has sometimes been seen, and likewise a white crow. Sparrows rub themselves with ash and wash themselves, as doves do. Moreover certain sparrows, like swallows, produce incomplete chicks, and produce many chicks.
Gloss: the sparrow flies off if something makes a great noise, lest it be caught in the hunters' snare. Whence it says: our soul, like a sparrow, and so on.

Physiologus: the sparrow is a lustful bird, and so it also gets its name from 'suffering,' fickle, wandering, and cunning, harmful to the fruits of human labor, skilled at detecting snares; it is said, moreover, to change its nest easily and to steal the dove's nest.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the sparrow is a very watchful little bird; it dwells on roofs and nests in high places in holes of rock. The male has blackness around the mouth, the female whiteness. This bird is said to hunt flies and to suffer the falling sickness.

div.head: DE CIBO ET MEDICINA EX PASSERE

cit.quote: Avicenna: all sparrows have poor flesh, and indeed all eggs, but especially sparrow eggs, increase lust when mating.
Rhazes: sparrow flesh is very hot and stirs up lust.
Pliny: ash of sparrows burned with vine-shoots, two spoonfuls in honeyed water, resists jaundice.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the sparrow, as said, is hotter than all other birds. Whence its flesh is astringent and stimulates the blood. Its dung, as said, is extremely hot when expelled, but cools very quickly.
Haly Abbas: sparrow eggs increase venery. Its dung clears the face of freckles, and if mixed with human spittle and applied as a poultice to varicose veins, it removes them.
Isidore: the peacock, like the crane and certain other winged creatures, has its name from the sound of its voice.

Aristotle: likewise the peacock lives 25 years, breeds after its third year, only once a year, twelve eggs or fewer; after its third year too its feathers take on color, and it grows them when the first tree sheds its leaves. Then its plumage is born when the trees first begin to bud.

Pliny: the peacock, when praised, spreads its colors, especially facing the sun, since they shine more brightly this way, and gathers all its feathers into a mass, which it delights to have looked at by eyes. Likewise its tail, lost each year with the leaves of the trees, until another grows, it seeks a hiding place, shamefaced and mournful, along with the blossom. Authorities report that this animal is not only vainglorious but also spiteful. It lives 25 years. It begins to shed its colors in its third year.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the peacock has a serpent-like head, weak and crested, a terrible voice, tough flesh, a sapphire-colored breast, a long, eyed tail, reddish wings, misshapen feet, a simple gait; when praised it raises its tail, but lowers it once its feet are seen, since when it raises its tail its hindquarters are also bared.
Physiologus: the peacock walks with a hesitant step and, as if furtively, sheds its feathers with the first tree, and afterward its plumage is reborn to it when the trees begin to bear fruit.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the peacock is a most beautiful bird and a lover of beauty; it has a long, outstretched neck, sapphire-colored, and its breast likewise. On its head it has feathers arranged above like a crown, or rather a crest, and also a long, eyed tail, which, when praised, it spreads out, but if it should see the ugliness of its feet, it lowers it at once. But if it is watched by someone silent, it hides all the feathers it delights to have looked at, drawing its eyes closed; from its third year it begins to shed gem-like colors, and then it breeds. Likewise at night, when it wakes and cannot see itself, set in the darkness, it cries out fearfully, believing it has lost its beauty. It also frightens away serpents with its cry and drives off all venomous creatures, nor do these easily dare to dwell near where its voice is often heard. When the peacock ascends high, it is a sign of rain. If its eggs are placed under hens, chicks emerge. Some peacocks are white all over, and yet the gem-like eyes, which in other peacocks shine with gold or sapphire in varied colors, are in these distinguished by, and gleam with, a white splendor instead. Peacocks also have wild kin in the woods, but by no means similar to the domestic ones in the brightness of their color or tail. Nor is it any wonder, if nature had made the weight of their tails, that it would seem rather to have burdened them for flight than to have honored inexperienced birds with glory.

Isidore: the peacock, as already said, breeds after three years, laying and brooding only twelve eggs, or fewer, once a year. The male mates with his female even while she is brooding the eggs, and they are usually broken. And so they are sometimes placed under a hen to brood. Two eggs are placed there, however, since no more can be drawn from her. The female peacock, the first time she breeds, makes eight eggs, and sometimes makes twenty eggs, and after she has laid one egg, she waits two or three days, and then lays another.

Palladius, in the same place: peacocks begin to be in heat from the ides of February; lightly roasted beans provoke them to lust, if warm ones are given every fifth day. The male also shows his desire for mating whenever he curves the mantle of his jeweled tail around himself and, running about with a rustling noise, displays the tips of each individual feather, hidden in their places.

Pliny: the peacock, from its third year, lays one or two eggs the first year, four or five the following year, and thereafter twelve, no more, resting two or three days between; and it lays three times a year if the eggs are placed under hens to brood, since the males break them from desire for the brooding females. For this reason they lay by night and in hiding places, or brooding aloft; and unless caught on a soft bedding, they are broken. Single males suffice for five mates each. When there is only one female, or two, fecundity is spoiled by lustfulness; the young are hatched in twenty-seven days, or later, in thirty.

Physiologus: the peacock destroys and consumes its mate's eggs, if it can get to them. For it is envious, on the testimony of Aristotle, and does not deign to acknowledge its own offspring, until it has seen the crest grow to resemble its own.

Palladius, book 1: it is very easy to raise peacocks, unless you fear thieves or hostile animals for them, for most of them wander through the fields and feed themselves and rear their chicks of their own accord, and seek out the tallest trees in the evening. One care alone is owed them: that the females brooding through the fields, which they commonly do, be guarded from the fox. And so on small islands they are raised with better fortune. The males pursue their own eggs and chicks as if strangers, before the mark of the crest is born to them. But if peacock eggs are placed under hens, the mother-birds, excused from brooding, produce broods three times a year - the first laying usually of five eggs, the second of four, the third of three or two. But the hens chosen as foster-mothers ought to be, and larger hens ought to be selected, for the reason said above. The peacock eggs placed under a hen also need to be turned often by hand, since she herself will scarcely be able to do this. As for the hatched chicks, if you wish to transfer several to one foster-mother, Columella says twenty-five suffice for one nurse; to me, however, fifteen seem enough. In the first days, spelt sprinkled to the chicks is given, afterward fresh cheese is added, but pressed dry, for whey harms the chicks; locusts too, their legs removed, should be offered; they must be fed thus up to the sixth month. Then barley may be given, and yet by the thirty-fifth day after they are hatched, they can also be safely let out into the field, accompanied by the foster-mother for feeding, whose clucking calls them back to the farm. Catarrh and indigestion should be treated in them with the same remedies used for the hen; their greatest danger is when the crest begins to be produced. For they suffer languors like those of infants, when their little teeth strain to break open the swollen gums.

Augustine: who but God, the creator of all things, gave to peacock flesh that it should not putrefy, even when dead? Though this, when heard, seemed unbelievable, it happened that at Carthage this bird, cooked, was set before us. From its breast we ordered as much of the flesh as seemed fit to be kept, and this, after such a span of days as would putrefy any other flesh whatsoever, being brought out and offered, offended none of our sense of smell. Likewise, put away again after more than thirty days, it was found to be the same as it was. And again after a year, except that it was somewhat drier and more shrunken in substance.

Augustine: when, therefore, we say that the bodies of the damned in hell are to be punished in such a way that they both burn without being consumed and suffer without perishing, let unbelieving men who demand of us a rational account of such things themselves give an account of many wonderful things which are readily at hand for us - such as the non-putrefying flesh of the peacock, when it does putrefy, and of Plato's [lamp, that burned without oil consumed].

Isidore: the peacock's flesh is so tough that it scarcely feels decay, nor is it easily cooked, of which a certain man thus said: You marvel how often it spreads its jeweled wings - if you can, hand this over to a stern cook to boil.
The Physicus: the peacock's flesh long resists putrefaction and is most disobedient to digestion.

Dioscorides: the peacock's gall, moreover, is of great power, of the same kind indeed as that of the partridge, or the white capon, and the sea-scorpion; it is effective against effusions of the eyes and against dimness and roughness of the eyelids.
Jerome, against Jovinian: peacock dung is also said to ease gout.
Pliny: and so peacocks, grudging their dung to the usefulness of men, [hide it].
Pliny, book 8: they call 'pegasi' winged horses armed with horns, which Ethiopia produces among many other monstrous creatures.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the pegasus is a large and terrifying animal in Ethiopia, having the shape of a horse and wings like an eagle's, but much larger, its head armed with horns. It is so monstrous that it terrifies nearly all living creatures by itself. And though it is heavy of body, aided by the help of its wings, it runs rather than flies in a wondrous flight, and, beating the air with the force of its feathers, drives the winds like a whirlwind. It devours great quantities of food and moves restlessly. It is hostile to animals, and especially to man.

Papias: the pegasus is a bird that has the ears of a horse; the pegasus is also said to be the horse of Bellerophon, by whose speed the chimera is said to have been slain. From this comes the Pegasean spring, sacred to the Muses, which Pegasus made with his hoof. The pagans also fashion the pegasus as having been a horse that flew from Bellerophon on wings; this one is said to have been born from the blood of the Gorgon.
Pliny: I consider that horse-headed winged creatures and eared griffins with hooked beaks are fabulous - the former in Scythia, the latter in Ethiopia.
Ambrose: 'pelargos' is the Greek word for the stork, whose name is given from the account of the thanks it renders to its parent.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: for indeed storks, as said above, are in turn fed by their own chicks for as much time as they themselves spent rearing their young.

Isidore: the pelican is an Egyptian bird, dwelling in the wilderness of the river Nile, whence it also took its name. For Egypt is called 'canopos.' It is said to kill its young and mourn them for three days, then to wound itself and, by the sprinkling of its blood, revive its children.

Physiologus: the pelican is an excessive lover of its young, who, when they begin to grow, strike their parents in the face. But the parents, angered, strike them back and kill them, and mourn for three days. On the third day their mother, striking her own side and opening her flank, lies down over her chicks, and, pouring out her blood over their bodies, raises them from death. There are two kinds of this bird. One lives in water and its food is fish. The other lives in the wilderness and its food is venomous creatures, that is, lizards, serpents, crocodiles. And they are called 'onocrotali,' that is, having long beaks.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: mention has already been made above of the pelican, on which, however, opinion varies.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the pelican is so named as if 'having grey [cana] skin,' that is, white feathers. It dwells in Egypt around the Nile and lives on crocodile's milk, which the beast, because of its very great abundance of teats, expels in great quantity in some marshy place. Whence the pelican also gladly follows the crocodile: this bird is always afflicted with thinness, and quickly digests whatever it swallows, since its belly has no pouch in which to hold food, for it has only a single passage of the innards, reaching from the mouth's entrance to the secret parts of nature. It revives its chicks with the blood of its own side, when it has killed them for their unruliness, or has found them slain by a serpent lying in wait for them. But after the shedding of its blood it is so weakened that it cannot leave the nest, but its chicks are compelled to leave for its feeding as well as their own. Some of them, however, sluggish, refuse to leave and perish. Others, indeed, feed themselves, but wholly neglect their mother. And when she sees this, after her recovery, she nourishes the dutiful children, but casts off and despises the undutiful ones.

Aristotle: the pelican is a bird so called because its skin, when handled, seems to sing; while it applauds its chicks, they try to gouge out its eyes, and so it kills them. But she, affected by no small grief, afterward strips herself of her garment of feathers and opens her side with her beak, and, lavish with her own blood, bloodies herself, by which her drenched chicks come back to life. This bird is scrawny, since, as is said, with the intestine stretched taut through its innards, whatever food it takes it passes through without any digestion. And so it happens that it is scarcely stuffed with fat nearby, being restored by the smallest amount of nourishment; it does not fly in a flock, but alone.

Isidore: the partridge has its name from its call, a deceitful and unclean bird. For the male rises up against the male, and headlong lust forgets its sex. Solinus: partridges, though free everywhere like all birds, are not found in Boeotia. For when they fly, they are not their own masters, but have set boundaries even in the air itself, which they do not dare to cross, nor do they fly across into Attic soil.
Pliny: partridges, like wood-pigeons and jackdaws and blackbirds, purge their yearly distaste for food with laurel leaf.
Pliny, book 11: in Paphlagonia partridges have two hearts each; partridges do not grow fat, nor do hares; they have a voice before battle.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the partridge flies close to the ground, and though it is cunning in many things, in this it is said to be foolish, that wherever it can hide its head, it believes its whole self is hidden, and since it itself sees no one, it thinks too that no one sees it; also in this, that it warms and rears others' chicks, though it will soon lose them. Whence the prophet Jeremiah says of it in a parable: the partridge has warmed what she did not lay, has made riches, and not with justice. In the midst of her days she will abandon them, and in the end will be a fool.
Physiologus: the partridge loses her eggs, but her custom is to make up the loss of the lost eggs by stealing another mother's eggs.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the partridge is a deceitful and lustful bird; males fight over females, and the defeated are trodden by the victors in mating. At night partridges sit with their hindquarters turned toward one another, and at the time of lust, with tongues stretched out toward each other, they burn with desire for mating. But when they are caught in a fowler's net-trap, one follows another, and the poor follower does not discern or draw back from the danger of the one already caught, deceived by the company of her companions.

Solinus: partridges continually fortify their nests with skillful defense, for they clothe their shelters with thorny growths, so that harmful creatures may be kept off by the rough spikes of the twigs; dust serves as bedding for the eggs, and they return secretly, lest frequent visits betray the location. For the most part the females move their broods, to deceive the males, who very often harm them, courting too impatiently. There is fighting over mating, and the defeated are believed to endure the role of the females in mating. Lust drives them so much that, if a wind blows from the males, they become pregnant from the scent alone. Then, if any man approaches where they are brooding, the mothers come out and offer themselves willingly to those approaching, and, feigning a weakness of feet or wings, as if they could be caught at once, they feign slower steps; with this deception they lure on those they meet and elude them, until, having gone farther, they are recalled from the nests; nor is their chicks' zeal for caution any less. For when they sense they have been seen, lying on their backs they lift clods with their feet, under whose cover they are so cunningly hidden that they escape detection even when found.

Pliny: partridges fortify their shelter with a thicket of thorn so that it suffices against wild beasts; partridges heap up soft dust as bedding for their eggs, and do not brood in the place where they laid, but move them elsewhere. Nor do they let a place be suspected by too frequent visits. Indeed they even deceive their own mates, since through intemperance of lust they break their eggs, lest they be kept from mating by the brooding; then the males fight among themselves out of desire for the females, and the defeated, they say, submit to being mated. Trogus says: they are also caught through the pugnacity of this same lust, when the leader of the whole flock comes out to fight against the fowler's decoy, and, once he is caught, another comes forward, and then each one in turn. Again, around the time of conception the females are caught, when a female comes out against the fowler, so as to drive him off by quarreling; nor is there then any equal urge for mating with another animal. If the females stand facing the males, they become pregnant from a breeze blowing from these, and, gaping with tongue extended, they burn during this time and conceive from the breath of those flying overhead, often the male's voice alone being heard. And lust conquers even a mother's love for her brood so much, that she, though a female secretly and covertly brooding, when the fowler approaches the male, calls him back and offers herself freely to lust. The partridge, they say, is carried by such a frenzy in mating that they often sit blindly, from fear, on the fowlers' heads. If the fowler begins to approach the nest, the brooding mother runs to his feet, feigning herself heavy with young or lame, and suddenly, in her running or a brief flight, falls as if her wing or feet were broken, and runs on again, eluding his grasp just as he is about to seize her, disappointing his hope, until she has led him far away from the nests; then, freed at last from fear and from maternal care, she covers herself lying on her back in a furrow, clutching a clod of earth with her feet. The life of partridges is thought to last to sixteen years. Partridges do not fly across the borders of Boeotia into Attica.

Ambrose: the partridge is a cunning bird, which steals another partridge's eggs and warms them with her own body, but she cannot enjoy the fruit of her deceit, since, once she has raised her chicks, she loses them; for wherever they hear the voice of the one that laid the eggs, they leave her and go by a certain natural gift and love to that one, whom they recognize as their true mother.

Aristotle: the partridge, if it is near the sea and the wind blows, becomes pregnant. In mating it produces a foul smell. It broods over its eggs and chicks in the manner of a hen, and gathers them under its wings.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the mother partridge flies about the hunters until her chicks flee, and after their flight she herself flees, and then calls them back safely.

div.head: DE CIBO AC MEDICINA EX PERDICE

cit.quote: Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham: partridge flesh is the healthiest of all wild birds. This bird's breast, along with the upper parts, is very tasty, but the lower parts are not so. The partridge, on Pliny's testimony, does not grow fat. Its gall, with honey in equal weight, benefits clarity of vision.
Dioscorides: the partridge's gall is of the same power as the peacock's, whence it is effective against effusion of the eyes and against dimness and roughness of the eyelids.
Haly Abbas: partridge liver too, carefully dried and ground and drunk, benefits epilepsy.

Pliny: partridge gall with an equal weight of honey - the Persians too value this for clarity of vision, and they order it kept in a silver box. Partridge eggs too, boiled in a bronze vessel with honey, heal ulcers and cataracts of the eyes. Partridge blood is exceptionally beneficial for eyes suffused with blood.
Pliny: [partridge broth] restores the stomach. Jaundice too is resisted by partridge brain in three cups of wine.

Isidore: the magpie is called as if 'poetica,' since, like a man, it forms words distinctly in its voice, for hanging from the branches of trees it sounds with troublesome chatter and imitates the sound of the human voice. Of which a certain man fittingly said: chattering magpie, I greet you by your master's name - if you did not see me, you would deny I was a bird.

Physiologus: the chattering magpie makes up for the shortness of its wings with a longer tail; it builds its nest with two openings, through one of which it enters, through the other it puts out its tail. It is commendable in this, that it watches over the safety of the courtyard or garden where it nests, and betrays with much clamor the ambushes of those lying in wait, so that they are called back from their intent, to their misfortune.

Pliny, book 10: the kinds of magpies distinguished by a long tail are various; it is proper to all of these to grow bald every year, when turnips are sown; but a certain kind of magpie has a more pronounced talkativeness. They dote on the words they speak. Nor do they merely learn them, but love them, and, practicing within themselves with care and thought, do not conceal their intent. It is agreed that they die, overcome by the difficulty of a word; and unless they hear the same word repeatedly, their memory fails them, and, seeking it, they are marvelously cheered if in the meantime they hear that word. Nor is their form common, though not much to look at; they have enough beauty in the appearance of human speech. But it is said they cannot learn other than those of their kind that feed on acorns, and among these, more easily those that have five toes on their feet; these have wider tongues than all others that imitate human speech in their kind, although this happens in almost all talking birds: the magpie lays nine eggs. And when it senses that its nest has been carefully seen by a man, it carries its eggs elsewhere.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the magpie is a very hot bird, marked with white and black variegation, having a rather wide tongue, with which it imitates human speech. It builds its nest among thorny places and most carefully hedges and fortifies it with earth on the inside and thorns on the outside, all around, below and above. It leaves only a very narrow opening through which to enter, on the side, and this in the spot where the nest is least accessible; and when it senses that the nest has been seen by a man, it moves the eggs elsewhere, aided by the dexterity of its toes. And when it knows it has been caught in a snare, it stays still with its whole body, struggling only with the effort of its beak to open the snare, nor does it move the rest of its body until the very last despair. The flesh of its chicks is said to be eaten for the sharpening of eyesight, though it does not easily submit to cooking unless first skinned.

Isidore: the woodpecker takes its name from Picus, son of Saturn, who used it in auspices: for they say this bird has something divine about it in this sign, that in whatever tree it has nested, a nail or whatever else is fixed cannot stay stuck there long, since it falls out at once, wherever the bird has perched.

Pliny: the woodpecker of Mars is a small bird with hooked claws, of great importance in auspices; it alone raises its chicks in the hollows of trees. When wedges are driven into these hollows by a shepherd, it is commonly believed that, by a certain herb applied by them, the wedges slip out; many birds of this kind feed on acorns and fruits. This bird is said not to exist in the territory of Tarentum; one of the woodpeckers is hung on a twig on the topmost branches, cup-fashion, so that no four-footed creature can approach.
Pliny, book 11: nature also gave the woodpecker a foldable crest running down the middle of the head from the beak.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the woodpecker of Mars is a small bird, having hooked claws and piercing trees with its beak. And when, lying on its back, it strikes the bark of a tree, it understands there is food beneath. It raises its chicks in hollow trees. If someone shoots an arrow or something similar into these, the woodpecker, by applying a certain herb, at once expels whatever has been driven in, however deep. Of their kind, many are black, like the blackbird, saffron-colored like orioles. But those are more handsome and larger which are reddish on the crown, saffron on the breast, green around the neck, blue on the wings, and shimmering on the tail. The woodpecker is said not to live in the territory of Tarentum. It is proper to it to go bald once a year, namely at that time when turnips are sown. Of this bird a certain man seems to have said this verse: small chattering bird, I greet you by your master's name - if you did not see me, you would deny I was a bird. The 'pygargus' is a second kind of eagle according to Pliny, of which mention was made above.

Pliny: [a bird that] flies down on birds diving in the sea for prey and seizes their heads with a bite, until it wrests away the catch; the same bird, once it has filled itself with swallowed shellfish, disgorges them cooked by the heat of its stomach, and thus, excreting edible matter from these, gathers up the shells.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the plover is a bird close in size to a partridge, adorned with varied feathers marked with saffron and white and black, and is said to live on air alone; the proof of this is that, although it grows fat, nothing at all can ever be found in its innards. Fowlers have leaded sticks, which, throwing them higher into the air, frighten off the birds and force them to fly low, and they stretch nets over the ground and catch them as they flee.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the purple gallinule, contrary to the way of other birds, has one foot broad for swimming, the other cloven for walking. In this it is noted that it delights in both elements, swimming in the water like ducks and walking on land like partridges. This bird alone, besides the parrot, taking up water with its foot like a hand, brings it to its beak and drinks, and feeds itself in a human manner, since it must drink with every food, and not by mouthful alone. For it has a naturally weak power of appetite in drawing in food and incorporating it into itself: the most praised of this kind are those that have a large beak and very long legs.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the purple gallinule, as is reported, is the same as the pelican. Whence in Deuteronomy, where, according to Jerome's translation, the purple gallinule is forbidden to be eaten among the unclean birds, according to the Septuagint translators the pelican is put there instead.

Pliny: other birds drink by sucking, but of these, those with long necks put in their heads, tilted back, as if pouring the water into themselves; the purple gallinule alone drinks by biting. The same bird, of its own peculiar kind, dips all its food in water repeatedly, then carries it to its beak with its foot as if with a hand: the most praised are found in Commagene. Their beaks and very long legs are red. The Balearic Islands also send a nobler purple gallinule than the one described above.

Isidore: the parrot is born on the shores of India, green in color, with a pumice-red collar, and a large tongue, wider than that of other birds, whence it also forms articulate words, so that, if you did not see it, you would think a man had spoken. By nature it greets, saying 'ave' or 'khaire'; it learns other words by training. Hence the verse: Parrot, I shall learn other men's names from you - this I have learned to say on my own: Hail, Caesar.

Solinus: India alone sends the parrot bird, whose beak is of such hardness that, when it is dropped from a height onto rock, it breaks its fall with the effort of its mouth. Its head, however, is so strong that, if ever it must be prompted to learn with blows - for the parrot strives to speak like men - it must be struck with an iron rod at the least. Among the noble and common ones, the number of toes makes the distinction, for the superior ones have five toes on their feet, the rest three. This bird, while a chick and in its first year of age, learns what is shown to it more quickly and retains it more tenaciously; a little older, it becomes forgetful and untrainable.

Pliny, book 10: above all birds, parrots reproduce human voices, and indeed converse. India sends this bird. The parrot is green over its whole body, but marked at the neck with a scarlet collar. It greets emperors and pronounces the words it hears, wanton especially when in wine. The hardness of its head is the same as that of its beak; when it is taught to speak, it is struck with an iron rod, otherwise it does not feel the blow. When it flies down, it catches itself with its beak, leans on it, and thus lightens itself against the weakness of its feet.
Pliny, book 11: the bones of the parrot's head are extremely hard.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: the parrot tolerates other waters in any manner, but dies from rain. For this reason it is said to nest on the mountains of Gilboa, since it rarely or never rains there. It guards its tail with the utmost care and wipes its feathers very often with its beak; it is an excessively wanton bird and drinks wine, feeds itself with its foot and carries food to its mouth with it, as a man does.

Physiologus: the parrot, commonly called 'papagayo,' that is 'chief or noble gambio,' inhabits the eastern or Indian shores. It also gladly inhabits Mount Gilboa because of its dryness, since it dies from too much moisture in its skin. It is somewhat similar to the 'obelus' and to the falcon. It has green feathers, a round breast, a hooked beak of such strength that it can only be broken by a cage of iron bars; it imitates the human voice. It is also of a wonderfully clever nature in provoking laughter. It is accustomed to kiss the people of the household too; shown a mirror, it is deceived by its own reflection and becomes now like one rejoicing, now like one grieving. It also greatly delights in the sight of a maiden, and grows drunk with wine.

Pseudo-John of Foulsham: the wren, also called 'parra,' is said to be, as it were, a small bird, but great in offspring and chatter. Birds once agreed among themselves, as the fable relates, that whichever surpassed all the others in the highest flight should be held as king. And when the wren, hiding under the eagle's wing, was carried by the eagle above all the other birds, the wren, leaping out, perched on the eagle's head and from there claimed itself the victor. It is said, moreover, that its body, fixed on a spit, turns itself on the spit even after death, as if not forgetful of its royal nobility.

div.head: DE SELEUTIDE AC STRYGE ET STROPHYLO

cit.quote: Pliny, book 10: birds called 'seleutides' are those whose arrival the inhabitants of Mount Cassinus obtain through prayers, when locusts are laying waste to their crops; nor is it known whence they come or whither they go, they never being seen except when their aid is needed.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the same is said further below about the 'seleutis' according to the book On the Nature of Things, from which it seems there is a scribal error on one side or the other.

Isidore: the screech-owl is a nocturnal bird, having its name from the sound of its voice, for when it cries out, it screeches. Of which: what does the timid horned owl, what does the nocturnal screech-owl complain of? This bird is commonly called 'ama' or 'amatrix' [lover], from loving little ones, whence it is also said to offer milk to newborns.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: note that 'strix' is a word applying equally to that bird spoken of, and to a beast similar to the hedgehog, of which mention will be made below in its own place.

Solinus: the 'strophilus' is a very small bird, which, while seeking food, gradually scratches the mouth of the crocodile, and, the crocodile's sense being soothed by the flattering scratching, makes for itself an entrance right into its jaws. When the ichneumon observes this, it penetrates the beast, and, its innards having been ravaged, gnawed, exits from its belly.

Isidore: the ostrich is so called by a Greek name, since the creature seems to have feathers in the likeness of a bird. Yet it is not lifted any higher off the ground. It neglects to warm its eggs, but, merely left buried, they are brought to life by the warmth of the dust. Whence the Lord says to Job: will you perhaps warm them in the dust? This bird is called by some the 'asida.'

Physiologus: the ostrich, or 'asida,' has feathers, but does not fly like other birds; it has feet like a camel, and so is called 'chameleon' in Greek. It does not lay eggs until the star called Vergilia rises, which rises around the month of June, when it is summer; then, raising its eyes to the sky and seeing that it has risen, it digs in the ground and lays its eggs and covers them with sand, and, rising at once, forgets them. For it is a forgetful creature and does not return to them further; but what would have been the warming for them, sitting on them with the heat of its body, this the mildness of the air seems to provide for them instead. For in summer the heated sand bakes the eggs, so that it hatches the chicks.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the ostrich sometimes raises its wings, but cannot fly, for it is huge in body, sparse in feathers. It has wings similar to the 'herodius' and the sparrowhawk's, but it eats iron.

Aristotle: there is an opinion about the ostrich, that it is not of the kind of birds because of the peculiarity of its formation, for it is partly similar to four-footed animals, partly to birds. It does not have wings, but shapes of wings, which are not suited to flight, since they are not fine like feathers, but as in four-footed animals: it has upper eyelids, and hairs on them; it also has much down on the lower part of its body, and two feet like a bird, but a cloven hoof like a four-footed creature. For it is of great body, whereas birds' bodies must necessarily be small, otherwise they cannot fly. It has three toes on each foot, because of the wings and because of the weight. And since it is of heavy body and poor flight, it has much surplus and mates much, like the hen and partridge.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the ostrich is a bird of an almost bestial kind. For it has feathers, but never uses them for flight; it has slight wings and feathers like hairs. In walking it raises its wings and runs so fast on the ground that it outstrips horses in speed. It has cloven hooves for grasping stones, which it hurls in flight against its pursuers: it eats and digests iron, since it is of a very hot nature, and it naturally hates the horse and pursues it in a wondrous manner. The horse too hates and fears it so much that it does not dare to look at it. It has a small bone under its wings, with which it pricks and stirs itself in the side when it is provoked to anger. On its breast, moreover, it has a large, wide bone, created for the protection of its great body. Its stupidity, moreover, is so great that when it has hidden its neck in a bush, it believes the breadth of the rest of its body is hidden as well. It naturally goes bald and so sheds its feathers that it is left almost bare. But it has a very strong hide, by which, featherless, it is protected against the harshness of the cold. It has a body about the size of a donkey, of moderate stature. Its eggs, too, are so large that, cut crosswise, they become vessels for drinking, in proportion to their size.

Physiologus: the ostrich warms its eggs, buried in the sand, by sight alone, so that chicks emerge from them into the light. This bird alone, among other birds, has only two toes, like the hooves of a ram, so that from the hollow of its foot below, as if pouring, it throws stones at a man. They say too that it looks at the sky with one eye and the earth with the other.
Rhazes: [on the ostrich - the citation breaks off in the source after this heading word].

Pliny: the African or Ethiopian ostriches are very large birds and almost of the kind of beasts; they exceed the height of a rider mounted on a horse, and surpass in speed, to which end feathers are given them only to aid their running, otherwise they are not fliers, nor are they raised off the ground. Their hooves are similar to a stag's, cloven, with which they fight and which are useful for grasping stones; these they hurl with their feet against pursuers in flight. It is a marvel of nature that they digest whatever they swallow indiscriminately. But no less remarkable is their stupidity, in that, for all the height of the rest of their body, once they have hidden their necks in a bush, they believe themselves hidden. Their eggs are prized as vessels of a sort for their capacity, and their feathers adorn military helmets and crests.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'struthiocamelus' is a kind of ostrich, or even the same kind itself, so called because, as said above, it has feet similar to the feet of a camel. Ostriches go bald, moreover, as Pliny says in book 10.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: starlings are small birds, outstretched for flight, gleaming with a dusky color. They fly in flocks and wheel about in a kind of circle, all tending toward the middle, and this because of the hawks that lie in wait for them. In the evening, indeed, they gather together, and even in immense crowds murmur among themselves; at night they are silent; at the reddening dawn they stir up their murmuring. Finally, however, divided into groups, they fly off to feed.
Pliny: the starling too is among the talking birds, whence Caesar's young men had a talking starling.
Rhazes: starling flesh is thicker than that of chick or quail. It binds the belly and nourishes greatly.

Isidore: it is called 'tarda' [the slow one] among us, since, held back by its slow and heavy flight, it is by no means raised up with the speed of feathers as other winged creatures are. It is also called 'grandipes' [big-foot].
Avicenna: the eggs of the bustard, according to what is said, are a good dye. This is tested at the hour when they are prepared for it, with a thread of wool passed through them.
Avicenna: bustard dung benefits impetigo.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'tragopa' is a bird in Ethiopia of a rust-colored hue, larger than the eagle. It has a head like the phoenix, except that it has horns on it like a ram. Whence it displays this armed head against all birds that oppose it.
Solinus: the 'tragopa' is a bird larger than eagles, presenting a head armed with ram-like horns.

Isidore: the 'turdela' is called as if 'the smaller thrush,' from whose dung mistletoe is thought to be generated. Thrushes, moreover, are named from slowness [tarditas], for they return around the boundary of winter.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: thrushes are birds small in body indeed, but great in foresight. On the tops of trees they build nests of mud, and breed almost continuously, that is, one brood right after another following mating, and remarkably, in ten days the eggs ripen in the womb, and after this they lay.

Pliny: thrushes too depart for nearby regions. But these do not shed their plumage, nor do they hide themselves except for the hope of food, seeking their winter fare. And so in Germany thrushes are seen especially in winter. And they are birds of three months' span, like turtledoves; their color in summer is varied around the neck, in winter uniform. Nesting with mud on the tops of trees, they breed almost continuously in a hidden spot. Agrippina, wife of Caesar Claudius, had a thrush that imitated human speech, unheard of before.

Palladius: thrushes should be raised in a chamber, so that they may be shut in unharmed and, if freshly caught, mixed with some already tamed, by whose company they may be consoled from the fearful sadness of their new captivity, so as to take food. Let the place, moreover, be clean and bright and smoothed on every side, in which perches should be fixed crosswise, on which they can sit once flight is prevented by confinement. Green branches too should be changed often. Crushed carob, mixed with meal, should be offered, and also, if means allow, myrtle, mastic, and wild-olive seeds given at times to relieve their distaste for food, and above all clean water should be provided. For thrushes, if fattened by feeding, offer both the pleasure of food and the greatest return, luxury supplying the benefit that frugality provides.
Avicenna: the dung of thrushes that eat rice benefits ringworm and vitiligo and also impetigo.

Isidore: the turtledove is named from its voice, a modest bird, always dwelling on mountain ridges and in deserted places, for it flees the roofs and company of men and dwells in the woods. It is also said to live, molted of feathers, in the hollow trunks of trees in winter; the dove, by contrast, loves human lodgings, always a friendly inhabitant of houses.

Ambrose: the turtledove is a modest bird, which, once widowed by the loss of its own mate, refuses to renew union, lest it dissolve the rights of modesty or the compacts pleasing to its mate; and its first love, betraying it, produces more grief from death than sweetness from the affection of the beloved. Learn, then, women, how great is the grace of widowhood, which is praised even in birds. For the turtledove does not know how to make its first faith void, since, having lost the lot of its first union, it knows how to preserve chastity. This bird throws leaves of squill over its nest, lest a wolf attack its chicks. For it knows that wolves are accustomed to flee leaves of this kind.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the turtledove loves its mate, and when it is dead or captured, goes about solitary, perching on dry branches of trees, moaning and sad; it is hostile to no bird, but most patient of the attacks of all. It dwells in the safest and most pleasant places; through the whole winter it lies featherless in hollow trees, but in spring it is renewed: many of them indeed seek warm lands in winter, and many stay behind, if they have a place facing the sun suitable for resting. Sometimes they are naturally so weak that they can be caught by hand. They often lay three eggs, but never raise more than two, likewise wood-pigeons. The turtledove lays eggs twice in spring, and often three times, but this when one pair of eggs has been spoiled or has perished by chance. Alone among birds it feeds its chicks at night; the blood from its right wing, applied, is medicinal for the eyes.

Physiologus: the turtledove grows fat only in summer; when the south wind blows, it cannot fly well because of the heaviness of its body, since that wind is moist and heavy. And so, tired out in flight by that wind, they do not cry out because of their weariness, and are then easily caught by hunters. And when they move from the south to the north, they have no leader, whereas they do when going the other way. The turtledove and the dove, according to Aristotle and Pliny, have this peculiarity, that they do not raise their heads while drinking until they have had enough.

Aristotle: the turtledove lives on fruit, like the wood-pigeon, but the wood-pigeon is always to be seen, while the turtledove is not. Male birds in general live longer than females. Yet male turtledoves, it is said, die before the females, which is known from those raised in houses. Birds' testicles enlarge at mating time, and this appears especially in partridges and turtledoves. The turtledove has a voice proper to itself, and does not appear except in summer, for in winter it stays in its nest or hides in hollows of trees or moves itself to warm places, but in summer to cool places. Often, too, they stay in their own places in winter, when they have places facing the sun. It is paired with a single mate for its whole life, and once that mate is dead, it in no way accepts a second. The turtledove, like the wood-pigeon and the swallow, breeds twice a year, and the male and female each brood two eggs. The turtledove mates after three months; it is pregnant for fourteen days and broods for as many. It lives and broods, like the dove, for fifteen years.

Palladius: to be raised, turtledoves should be kept enclosed in a small and rather dark chamber; they are very easy to raise, since they require nothing except that in summer, when alone they grow especially fat, they always be given wheat or millet soaked in honeyed water; and clean water should of course be offered them often.
Avicenna: the turtledove's blood, warm, is dripped over an aching, bruised ear.
Pliny, book 19: turtledove's blood is exceptionally beneficial for eyes suffused with blood; their dung reduces white spots of the eyes.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: lapwings are birds that Pliny calls 'symphalides,' fairly handsome, of dove-like size, with a crested head like the peacock, a neck indeed of green and gleaming color, but the rest of the body marked with variegation. This bird, when it senses a man approaching its nest even from far off, at once goes out to meet him with a cry. And thus foolishly, while it believes it is drawing the man away from its nest, by the very signal of its cry it betrays the nest, which the man, having advanced, then strives to plunder.

Aristotle: bats have feet like birds and lack a tail, since they are wild creatures. And their wings are membranous, that is, undivided like a hide, and if they had a tail, this would obstruct the form of the wings, since these are not divided. Like mice they have teeth in each jaw, and they procure their sustenance by night, like horned owls.

Ambrose: the bat is a creature both flying and four-footed at once, using teeth too, which are not usually found in other birds. It gives birth, as four-footed creatures do, not to eggs but to living young, is accustomed to fly at twilight, and flies in the air supported not by any oarage of feathers but by that of its membrane.
Isidore: the bat is so called because, fleeing the light, it flies about at evening twilight, driven by a headlong motion, resembling a mouse, resounding not so much with a voice as with a squeak.

Pliny: the bat alone among winged creatures gives birth to living young, and it has a membrane instead of feathers. The same is the only winged creature that nurses with milk, putting its teats to its young; it flies while embracing its twins and carries them with it. To it alone a single hip-bone is attributed; for it, gnats are the most welcome food.
Pliny, book 11: no winged creature has teeth except the bat, and likewise milk and teats. Its wings have joints.

Pliny, book 29: bat's blood with thistle is praised among the chief remedies against the strikes of serpents. Its gall with vinegar is a remedy against the bite of the shrew-mouse. Its heart is effective against 'salpingae,' which is a kind of venomous ant.
Pliny: bat's head, dried and bound on, wards off sleep. Its blood too, smeared on, prevents hair from growing. Finally, colic pains in beasts of burden are ended by binding on a bat.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the bat surpasses other four-footed creatures in flight. In parts of India there are bats larger than doves, having, as it were, human teeth; these strike men in the face, cutting off their nostrils and ears and other members. This bird is said to seek out noise, and its blood removes hair.
Gloss: the bat flies close to the ground and walks with its wings; it is unclean according to the law.

Avicenna: the bat's milk, as is said, is its urine. In it there is a cleansing and vehement heating power. Ointment of bat prevents girls' breasts from enlarging. Its brain with honey helps at the onset of dropsy descending into the eye. Its ash sharpens sight. [Certain compounds] help nail-disease and white spots of the eye.

Isidore: the screech-owl [ulula] is a bird named from wailing and mourning, for when it cries out it either imitates weeping or a groan. Whence among augurs, if it wails it is said to show sadness, but if silent, prosperity.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: 'ululae,' as the gloss on Isaiah says, are birds of the size of a crow, sprinkled with spots, which screech horribly with their beak fixed in a marsh, having a voice similar to the howling of wolves, whence they also received their name, and are called in French 'buhort' or 'butor.' Mention has already been made of this above, where the bittern and the pelican were discussed, which are names for the same bird.

Isidore: the hoopoe is a most filthy bird, helmeted with standing crests, always dwelling among tombs and human dung. It is called 'upupa' in Greek, since it examines human excrement and feeds on the dung it finds. Whoever anoints himself with its blood and goes to sleep will see demons suffocating him.

Pliny: the hoopoe, as the poet Aeschylus relates, changes both form and color; otherwise a foul bird in its feeding, with a remarkable foldable crest, which it draws in and raises along the length of its head.
Gloss: the hoopoe is mournful and loves grief. Whence it is also forbidden to be eaten in the Law, since worldly sadness works death.

Physiologus: when the chicks of the hoopoe see that their parents have grown old, so that they can neither fly nor see, they pluck out the very old feathers of their parents and anoint their eyes and warm them under their wings, until their feathers grow again and their eyes are relit, and thus they render the same service back to their parents in turn.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba, in the book On Animals: the chicks of the hoopoe, warming their parents, breathe upon their eyes, so that they may recover their sight.

Pythagoras, in the book of the Romans: hoopoe's blood, smeared on a sleeping man, produces demonic phantasms. Hoopoe feathers placed on a man's head calm 'soda,' that is, headache. Its tongue, too, hung on one who suffers greatly from forgetfulness, benefits him.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the hoopoe is a rather beautiful bird, but unclean, troublesome with one call, like the cuckoo; in winter it hides and is bare, in spring it is renewed; its parents, growing old among their now-grown chicks in the nest, shed their feathers and meanwhile are fed by the chicks, until they recover their strength and feathers. Another kind of devotion also seems present in them toward their parents. For when, through old age, they have lost their sight, the chicks gather an herb known to them by nature, and anoint their blinded eyes with it, so that they recover their sight. This bird's heart is said to be effective for evildoers and enchanters.
Pliny: hoopoe's heart benefits pains of the side.

Isidore: the vulture is thought to be named from its slow flight, for, given the size of its body, it does not have a swift flight; it is said to live almost up to a hundred years. Vultures, like eagles, sense carcasses even across the seas. For, flying higher, they see from on high things hidden by the great darkness of the mountains.

Pliny: among vultures, the black ones prevail; no one finds their nests, and so there were even those who wrongly thought they flew in from another world. The vulture, and almost all heavier birds, do not fly except launched from a run or a higher hillock. Eagles indeed see more clearly, but vultures smell more keenly.

Ambrose: vultures are said to breed and conceive without mating. They are also accustomed to announce a man's death by certain signs. For when battle-lines draw up for a lamentable war between themselves, vultures follow in a great host, and by this signify that a great multitude of men is going to fall in the war, destined to be prey for the vultures.

Aristotle: the 'sycatus' fights with the vulture and breaks its bones. But the bird called 'obrix,' which does not appear by day since it is not of sharp sight, hunts by night like the vulture and fights fiercely with it, so that shepherds very often catch them at it.
Gloss: [the Law] forbids eating the vulture, which delights in wars and deaths.
