Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the vulture is a heavy bird, but quite skilled at flying, although, before it lifts into the air, it makes three hops. Whence it is sometimes overtaken by a dog's agility before it can raise itself into the high air by its usual hops for flight. And so if it sees a man, it gladly walks on the ground because of the weight of its body, whence it is also called 'walker' [gradipes]; in flight it notices a smelling carcass and lands to eat it, seeking out the eye first in it. And since it inclines indiscriminately toward every carcass, it does not avoid the dangers and snares of hunters, and so is more easily caught. It follows armies, moreover, so as to be sated on the corpses of the dead. The vulture fights with the 'herodius' and rushes upon it. But since the 'herodius' is agile, it yields to the rushing attack, and the heavy bird, unable to hold itself back, kills itself.

Physiologus: the vulture sits, moreover, in a very high place, since it is slow in rising from the ground, and ascends to so great a height that it sees remote places, and so it is said that the vulture alone is the bird of God; this bird also pursues even larger birds of prey, like the sparrowhawk, as owed to its own predation, sparing smaller birds.

Aristotle: the vulture is heavy and of bad temper, ravenous and noisy; it hunts in places very far from its nest, and in order to see very remote places, it rises to the highest place and sits there, since rising from the ground is difficult for it. And so it is said that the vulture alone is the bird of God. It catches hares and small deer and captured foxes and other animals it can hold. What it hunts or fights with, it strikes and stuns with its wings and wounds with its claws. There is a certain bird which, when it sees the vulture, fears it, descends into water and, submerging itself, waits for the vulture to pass by from that place. But the vulture, since it has sharp sight, seeing it in the depths, does not leave that place, but flies over it until, exhausted or suffocated, it returns to the surface of the water, and then it takes it, alive or dead. Nevertheless, when it hunts something and catches it, it does not carry it to the nest at once, until it has tested its weight. The vulture hunts from midday to night, and rests from sunrise until that time. It is, moreover, of great hunger. And when it grows hungry, it catches much.

Aristotle: there are several kinds of vultures, of which one is called 'hargor,' by some called 'abiachon,' and lives in places of many trees, and sometimes even near cities. It also flies around mountainous regions and places of much food, out of confidence in its own strength. There is another kind, called 'planoior' in Greek, and it is smaller than the first kind. Its dwelling is in mountains and deserts. Further, according to Homer, there is another kind called 'ianachor' in Greek, of black color, smaller in size than the others, but of greater vigor. And this is the black vulture, which properly kills hares. This one alone feeds its chicks with good nourishment, and then draws them out, and it too hunts quickly. There is likewise another kind of vulture, of poor wings, which is called by some the 'pygargus'; it has a white tail and a white head. Its size is about half that of the other vultures. It has very small wings, and the middle of its body is long, and it dwells in places of many trees; this one is said to be caught easily. Out of its malice, like other birds, it seizes dead carcasses, but gains nothing by it, since black crows and other similar birds catch it and drive it off. It is, moreover, heavy and of bad temper, and always hungry and noisy. There is also another kind, called 'asbaton,' which has a thick neck, a broad breast, and twisted wings. And it dwells on the shores of the sea, and when it seizes something, it carries it off to the sea with it. There is, again, another kind of vulture, called in Greek 'crassion,' that is, 'true,' for this kind alone is the true kind of vultures. The other kinds, however, are mixed, or born from the mating of vultures and hawks and birds of larger body, and this vulture is very large, one and a quarter times larger than all other vultures. It has a strong voice and a citron-yellow color, but is seen only rarely.

Pliny: vultures, as said above, nest on the highest crags; their brood is often seen to be about two. Umbricius Melior, however, most skilled in our age, reports that they lay thirteen eggs, and survey the rest of the eggs and the nest with one of these, then discard it. From the 'ossifrage' kind smaller vultures are bred, and from these in turn the large ones, which do not breed at all.

Physiologus: some say that vultures do not mix in mating, and conceive and breed without coupling, and that their offspring extend their life almost up to a hundred years. Ambrose, however, seems to extend this to all vultures.

Aristotle: the vulture, as said, nests in the highest places, and often above trees. It begrudges its chicks when they grow fat, and does not feed them except from the remains of its own food, and casts them out before they can fly. There is, however, another bird, which feeds those cast-out chicks along with its own. One pair of vultures occupies one large territory, and so does not allow others to nest with it; it is, moreover, long-lived, which is known from the fact that its nest always remains the same. But when it grows old, its beak lengthens above and becomes curved, and in the end it dies of hunger.

bibl.author: Iorath sive Iuba II rex Mauritanie

cit.quote: Juba: while the vulture's chicks are being fattened, their father removes fat from them by striking with his wings and by pricking, and thus they are made lean, lest they fail in flight.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the vulture feeds its chicks until they can fly, and exposes itself to danger for them; it wounds with its claws and strikes with its wings even one stronger than itself that wishes to seize them. After this, casting them from the nest, it forbids them to come near the places where they were born, out of rivalry for food, since one pair of vultures occupies a large territory. Nor does it hunt in places near the nest, but in the most remote ones, nature teaching it, a friend of peace, lest it stir up the hatred of neighboring peoples against itself. What is surplus to it of food, it stores in the nest, so as to feed itself and its chicks from it, since it does not easily acquire food. But if it sees its chicks growing fat too quickly, it grieves. And so it wounds them in the feet with its beak, to make them lean. When the vulture has grown up and sees its mother old and weak for flight, it kills her.

Aesculapius: burnt vulture feathers drive serpents from a house. Its liver, ground, drunk with blood for ten days, frees epileptics. Its blood with the juice of horehound heals dimness of the eyes. Its fat heals pain of the eyes and eliminates pains of the sinews.
Dioscorides: vulture's dung is medicinal, for its fumigation expels the afterbirth.

Pliny: if the vulture's teeth are scraped, they produce a foul breath. Its blood, ground with the root of the white chameleon-herb and mixed with cabbage-herb, heals leprosy: vulture's lung, too, burned, benefits those coughing up blood. Vulture's liver, ground with its own blood, drunk three times over seven days, cures epileptics. Likewise a vulture chick's heart, bound on. Vulture's fat too, dried with the belly and ground with aged pig fat, eases pains of the sinews.
Pliny: vulture's gall too, diluted with water, heals white spots of the eyes.

div.head: DE IBOZ ET YDRIO ET ISIDA ET IXIONE ET SELEUTIDE

cit.quote: Pseudo-John of Foulsham, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'iboz' is a bird of weak sight, which imitates the horse's voice and, sometimes flying above it, stuns it and forces it to flee.

Aristotle: the 'iboz' fights with the horse for this reason, that the horse drives it from pastures and eats the grasses. And so, stunning it, it forces it to flee, and perhaps kills it. This bird, moreover, is of beautiful color and has a good life, and dwells by rivers and their banks. The 'hydrus' is a flying creature in the river Nile, quite hostile to the crocodile. For, by nature and habit, when it sees the crocodile sleeping on the riverbank with mouth open, it wraps itself in mud so as more easily to slip into its jaws. And thus, creeping into its jaws, once the crocodile's innards have been eaten away, it finally leaps out alive.

Thomas Cantimpratensis, from the book On the Nature of Things: the 'isida' is so named from the sound of its voice. It is indeed a small bird, but most brilliant in the beauty of its feathers; on its back it has a color between green and sky-blue. On its breast, moreover, it shows the image of burning coals. It has only two toes on its foot, hooked claws, but a small and straight beak. It stays constantly near water, lives on little fish, hollows out the earth with its beak, and there gathers a nest and raises its young. Common folk believe of this bird that, if you strip the skin with feathers from the dead bird and fix it to a wall, it will change its feathers every year as if it were alive in its body.

Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: the 'ixion' is an unclean bird according to the Law, whose nature is not well enough known to us. It is, however, as is read, of the kind of vultures, but smaller than the vulture.

Thomas Cantimpratensis: birds, as Pliny says, whose help the inhabitants of Mount Cassinus seek from the god Jupiter, when their crops are laid waste by locusts. And so, sent by the god, they destroy the locusts, and it is not known whence they come or whither they go.

From sacred history: once the winged creatures were created from water, God said to them: increase and multiply upon the earth. Which was to say nothing other than that he implanted a generative power for the multiplication of their own kind.

Pliny, book 10, on birds: the generation of birds indeed seems simple, though it too has its own marvels. Winged kinds that have hooked claws are infertile. None of these lays more than four eggs. Nature has granted to the kind of birds that the timid ones among them are more fertile than the strong. Ostriches, geese, hens, and partridges alone lay the most. Some mate at every season, like hens, and lay, except in the two wintry months of winter. Among these, young birds lay more than old ones, but smaller eggs. There is such fecundity, moreover, that some lay sixty, some daily, some twice a day, some so much that they die exhausted. Of winged creatures, the bat alone gives birth to living young and nurses with milk, applying its teats. Doves lay two eggs, the wood-pigeon and turtledove mostly three. The peacock, from its third year, lays one or two eggs the first year, four or five the next, twelve thereafter. The hawk lays generally one, never more than three. The one called the 'egolios' [owlet] lays four. The raven sometimes lays five too. The blackcap lays more than twenty, always an unequal, odd number, nor is such fecundity found elsewhere among many birds, yet it is greater in small ones.

Aristotle: the mating of birds happens in two ways, either with the female crouching on the ground, as with hens, or standing, as with cranes. The kinds of birds mate at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, and then lay eggs and hatch chicks. But the kingfisher lays hers at the beginning of winter and broods for fourteen days before they are complete, as said above. There are, moreover, certain chaste birds, like the one that mates only once in its lifetime. Songbirds, except for those noted, produce their broods before the spring equinox or after the autumn one. Before the solstice, indeed, the broods are uncertain, afterward viable. Fertility is not great in birds of good flight nor of curved claws, since birds of many eggs are of much surplus. But in birds of hooked claws the surplus passes into wings and feathers and claws, and their body is small, dry, sharp; but heavy birds of poor flight, like the hen and the 'cubeth,' that is the partridge, and other similar kinds, have much surplus, and for this reason the males mate much and the females have much matter. Doves, however, are as it were midway between the two kinds. For they are of good flight, like those of hooked claws, and have bodies that are, as it were, heavy. Since, then, they are of good flight, their surplus of necessity passes into feathers and wings. And their eggs are few, that is, two; but because of their stoutness and the heat of their bellies, they lay often, that is, ten times a year, especially since their food is easily found. But birds of hooked claws acquire food only with difficulty.

Aristotle: again, small birds - the more fearful they are, the more eggs they have, since their bodies are of greater moisture and their growth passes into semen. Other kinds are drier, and so more irascible, since strong anger occurs only in bodies of much dryness. The slenderness of legs in small birds, too, and their weakness, suits this kind of mating and multitude of eggs, as happens with men, since food passing to the legs turns in them into surplus of semen. But birds of hooked claws have strong feet and thick legs for the governance of their life, and do not drink. And so, since natural and incidental moisture is fitting for the generation of semen, birds of this kind do not lay more than four eggs at most. Finally, just as it happens with trees, that those that bear much fruit quickly dry out, since the nourishment passes into seed, so too certain hens that lay much, perhaps two a day, die quickly, since the nourishment passes into semen. Likewise female birds do not desire mating as males do, since their wombs are beneath the wall near the kidneys, while the males' are drawn in more within and need much mating because of the abundance of semen. Likewise small birds, which produce many chicks, produce them incomplete, for they do not generate food sufficient for their development. Hence if the eye of a chick swallow is removed while it is still small, it grows again. The hen and the dove mate and breed all year, except in the tropical months. The turtledove mates after three months, is pregnant fourteen days, and broods for as many. The peacock breeds after three years. The swallow alone among flesh-eating winged creatures breeds twice a year. And so the turtledove and the wood-pigeon and the swallow breed twice a year, and two chicks each time. The dove often, the peacock only once, the hen and the goose and the duck and the partridge and the pheasant many at once. But the eagle and the other birds of prey lay only two, once a year, or if more, they cast them out. Birds' calling, moreover, is greater at mating time. The partridge produces a foul smell in mating. The hen has shivering fits after mating.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: much was also said above about the lustfulness and mating of the dove and the 'cubeth,' that is, the partridge.

Aristotle: when the swallow wants to prepare its nest, it mixes mud with straw. But if it does not find mud, it goes into water and afterward into ash, and builds the walls of its house as man does. It places the hard parts in the foundation and builds a house large enough to suffice for itself. But heavy birds do not have a nest like other birds, but go to flat places and there make their dwelling of thorns and other material, this because of the sparrowhawk and the vulture, and because of the heat. Certain birds nest in caverns and among stones, and the 'kiche' bird nests above trees, of wool and hair. The 'cinnomulgus' makes its nest of cinnamon, spherical, above tall trees which no one can climb. The 'hacha kox,' that is the hoopoe, makes its nest of human dung.

Pliny: the shape of the kingfisher's nest also alerts us to the skill of the rest. For no talent of birds is more to be admired in any respect. Swallows, as said above, build with mud, strengthen with straw. If ever there is a shortage of mud, they sprinkle, soaked in much water, dust on their feathers; the nest itself, too, they line with soft feathers and down, to warm the eggs, and likewise so it is not hard for the tender chicks. The kingfishers' nests too are marvelous: the shape of a ball, with an opening projecting slightly and very narrow, resembling large sponges. Belonging to the riverine class of life, this bird's nest is made of dry moss, so put together into a ball that no entrance can be found. The woodpecker's craft hangs a twig on the topmost branches, cup-fashion, so that no four-footed creature can approach. Orioles, they affirm, sleep hanging by their feet, since they hope they are safer this way. Now it is common to all, indeed, to choose a platform of branches to support the nest, and to roof and protect it from rain with dense foliage. In Arabia, the 'cinnamon-bird' nests with twigs of cinnamon. And so the natives knock them down with weighted darts and arrows for the sake of the merchandise. In Scythia there is a certain bird the size of a bustard, that lays two eggs in a hare's skin, always hung on the tops of branches. Magpies, when they sense their nest has been seen by a man, move their eggs elsewhere. And in birds whose toes are not suited for grasping and carrying eggs, this marvelous skill is reported: placing a twig fastened over their two eggs with the glue of their belly, they carry them, their neck bent beneath, balanced evenly on both sides, elsewhere. No less is the skill of those which build their cradles on the ground, since the heaviness of their body prevents them from seeking high places. The bee-eater nests in a cave dug six feet deep. Partridges fortify their shelter with thorn and bramble so as to be well defended against wild beasts. They also heap up soft dust as bedding for their eggs, and do not brood in the place where they laid, but move them elsewhere.
Isidore: the kinds of winged creatures are born twice. For first eggs are produced, then they are formed and given life by the warmth of the maternal body.
[Pliny:] on the bat. [The citation breaks off in the source after this heading word.]

Aristotle: certain animals generate animals not yet distinct or formed, and what among these has blood makes eggs. And when the animal is generated from one part of the egg, the remainder will be food for the newborn. Eggs having two colors are not entirely round, but sharp on one side, because of the difference that is always in them, from the white in which the beginning is. And the sharp part of the egg is harder on the lower side, since it must guard the beginning that is in the egg, and the sharp part exits last, since it is continuous with the womb. Of egg-laying animals, the kinds of birds make complete eggs, of hard shell, unless it happens otherwise through some weakness. And eggs indeed are made from semen and have two colors, white and yellow-orange. And in animals whose nature is hotter, these two are distinct, and the yellow is greater than the white and more earthy. But in more moist animals of lesser heat, the white is greater and more moist, as happens to those dwelling in watery places and abounding in trees. Such too is the kind of fishes, whence in these the white is not separated, because of the smallness of the heat and the abundance of the cold earthy part, but it is, as it were, a mixture of white and yellow-orange, and so it has one color. Wind-eggs, too, have two colors. The cause of the difference of colors is not male and female, as if the white were from the male, the yellow-orange from the female. Rather both are from the surplus of the female, and there is a hot part and a cold part. And when there is much heat in them, the two colors will be separated there. But when it is slight, it cannot divide them there. The male's semen, however, only sustains. And so at first small white eggs appear, afterward they become yellow-orange because of the abundance of the mixture of blood.

Aristotle: at completion, however, the color emerges and the white becomes formed around the yellow-orange, like bubbling liquid all around, since the white is naturally hot and the heat of the soul is in it. The yellow-orange, however, is within, because it is earthy. Finally, if one mixes many eggs and, putting them in a bladder, cooks them, one will find the yellow-orange in the middle and the white containing it. The egg grows, however, as an embryo grows, by the reception of food that goes into the womb through the umbilicus. But the shell, which is around the egg, is soft at first and afterward hardens, yet not too much, since it would cause pain to the one laying it. But when it emerges, it curdles and becomes hard at once, since it is chilled. The sharp part emerges last, since it is continuous with the womb. And according to this same manner it happens also with the seeds of trees and grains that are eaten: for where there is a gathering of two parts, as in the bean and similar things, there is the beginning at completion, and there is the beginning of the seed. Therefore the exit of eggs is contrary to the exit of the animal, since the exit of the animal is head-first, over the beginning, but the egg comes out as if feet-first. And the cause of this is its continuity with the beginning, that is, the womb. Hens and doves and other birds of much mating produce more eggs than all others, in which there are two yolks because of the gathering of two seeds from a double mating, and in such eggs twins are found. The eggs of four-footed creatures, too, are of hard shell and have two colors and are warm, and are completed by the heat of the earth and of the season.

Isidore: eggs [ova] are said to be named from 'uva' [grape], since they are called so because they are filled inside with moisture. For 'humidum' [moist] is what has moisture outside, 'uvidum' [juicy] what has it inside. Some eggs, moreover, are conceived from empty wind, but these are not capable of generation, except those conceived by mating with a male and penetrated by seminal spirit. They say the power of eggs is so great that wood soaked with it does not burn, nor does even cloth touched by it get scorched. Mixed with lime, too, it is said to glue together fragments of glass.

Pliny: eggs, soaked in vinegar, are so softened that they pass through rings. It is most useful to keep them in bean-meal, or in winter in chaff, in summer in bran. They are believed to be emptied out by salt, however.

Pliny, book 29: the firmness of the shell is such that it does not break straight from force or weight, nor except when its whole roundness is somewhat bent. And lest anything be lacking to the merit of eggs, the white from them, mixed with quicklime, glues fragments of glass, and its power is so great that wood soaked with an egg does not burn, nor does even cloth get scorched.
Aristotle, in the book On Plants: an egg sinks in fresh water, but floats in salt water.

Aristotle, in the book On Animals: the arrangement of the yellow-orange in the egg is like the arrangement of the womb; from the watery part the food of the embryo goes forth, which is in the womb. The outer membrane is bloody. The hard shell, however, is only the egg's protection, because of the accidents that could happen to it once it emerges outside. The yellow-orange congeals in cold weather, and once warmed becomes moist again. The white, however, is not congealed by cold, but becomes more moist instead, and when roasted becomes hard. Further, at the generation of the chick it thickens, since the sustenance of the chick comes from it. The yellow-orange, however, is the chick's food. And so the yellow-orange and the white are distinguished by membranes because of the difference of their nature. The chicks in eggs come out from the sharp end, by which the eggs are continuous with the womb. As has been said, moreover, the eggs of birds are complete, of hard shell, and all have two colors, namely white and yellow-orange. But the eggs of fish are of one color and are not complete, since they receive their growth outside.

Aristotle: some eggs of winged creatures are hard, some soft, like those of hens. Eggs are also diversified in color according to the diversity of birds, since some are of white color, like those of doves and partridges. Some are yellow-orange, like those of birds dwelling near marshes. Some are, as it were, spotted, and some are red. Also, the eggs of birds living near rivers differ from the eggs of those living in dry places, since the yellow-orange is more than double in the former compared to the yellow-orange of birds dwelling near marshy pools. Likewise eggs differ in shape, since some are sharp, some wide, and the wide part comes out first, the sharp part after. They also differ according to the kinds of animals, since some make complete eggs, like birds and four-footed creatures and most kinds of serpents, but some incomplete ones, like fish and soft-shelled creatures and mollusks. For all the eggs of these kinds grow after being laid. Indeed some four-footed creatures too lay eggs, like the small lizard and the 'cenchris,' that is the crocodile, and the tortoise.

Pliny, in the same place: and so not only birds produce eggs, but also four-footed creatures, like the chameleon and the lizard; the viper alone among land creatures gives birth to eggs within herself, as fish do, of one color and soft. Of eggs, some are white, as with doves and partridges. Others are pale, as with water birds, others marked with spots, as with guinea fowl, others of red color, as with pheasants and partridges [cenchrides]. Inside, every egg of a winged creature is two-colored. That of fish, however, is of one color, in which there is no white at all. Birds' eggs are fragile from heat. Those of serpents are smooth from cold, those of fish soft from the liquid. Those that are oblong you may think of more pleasing taste.
Horace: those that are laid rounder produce a female, but the rest a male.

Avicenna: fresh hen's eggs are better than other eggs, and what is better in them is the yolk. And their best preparation is that they should not be curdled with anything. After hen's eggs come the eggs of other birds, which follow in their order. Duck eggs and the like, however, are of bad humor.

Rhazes, in the same place: hard-boiled eggs nourish more. But they are harder to digest and descend more slowly from the stomach. Soft ones descend more quickly, and are beneficial for those from whom much blood has flowed and whose strength has diminished.

Isaac Judaeus, on diets: eggs are to winged animals what blood and semen are to walking animals: for just as blood and semen are the matter and nourishment of all walking creatures, so eggs are the matter and nourishment of winged ones. For the eggs of winged creatures submitting to males are said to hold these two things within themselves, namely semen and nourishment. And so they nourish and strengthen quickly and abundantly; they nourish quickly because of the fineness of their substance and the temperateness of their liquid. They are strengthening to the body, because the more natural heat operates in them, the more they harden, as we see happen in outward things. For the more the heat of fire works on them, the more they begin to harden. They give much nourishment, since their whole substance nourishes, and is assimilated to the members according to its nature, akin to human nature. And especially their yolks, since they are temperate in heat and moisture, seem more like the human constitution. But yet if roasted by fire they take on heat and dryness, whence they become drying and less cooling. But if boiled with water, they take on moisture. And so they become less drying and more soothing of heat. Their white, however, is somewhat cold and thick, whence it is hard to digest. Moreover, eggs differ among themselves in four ways. The first is according to the natures of the animals and their ages. The second because of the length of time the eggs remain in the open air. The third is the manner of their cooking. The fourth is if they are cooked more or less than they should be.

Avicenna: eggs indeed tend toward the mean, but their white tends toward cold and the yolk toward heat, and both are moist, especially the white. Of these, goose and ostrich eggs are stronger. In them there is astringency, especially in their roasted yolk. The white, however, calms biting pains, because of its gluey quality. Curdled ones are of slower digestion and more nourishing. Of these the better ones are those sipped, cooked in water, and they are of quicker penetration. A poultice made of egg white prevents and removes discoloration from the sun; roasted and ground yolk is a useful poultice for ringworm and blackness. The eggs of the bustard, according to what is said, are good for black dye, and this is tested at the hour they are prepared for it, with a thread of wool piercing them, and it is left until one sees whether it blackens. Likewise eggs are put in plasters for abscesses and in enemas, for ulcers and abscesses. They are also smeared with oil on erysipelas. They also help burns from fire and water. They soothe the sinews and help all pains of the joints and catarrh, and also roughness of the chest and throat. Sipped eggs help cough and pleurisy and hectic fever, hoarseness of voice from heat and tightness of breath and spitting of blood, especially when the warm yolk is sipped. Eggs cooked in vinegar prevent flux of the bowels and dysentery. Also roughness of the wine-passage and stomach and the overflow of matter to the stomach and intestines. And their yolk benefits ulcers of the kidneys and bladder, especially if sipped raw. Eggs roasted over ashes without smoke help loosening of the bowels and dysentery, if eaten with some astringents and unripe grape juice. They also help roughness of the intestines and bladder. Egg white calms pain of the eye. The yolk, however, with saffron and rose oil, greatly benefits a blow to it. And with frankincense it is smeared on the forehead for fluxes of the eye. The white again, if sipped raw, helps flux of blood and blood in the urine. All eggs, especially those of sparrows, increase mating.

Haly Abbas: egg white, cold and moist, benefits hot ophthalmia if dripped into the eye, and also cough that comes from sharpness of humors, and roughness of the throat if the whole egg is sipped, and burns from fire, if broken over the spot. Eggshells, if carefully washed and ground, and the eye rubbed with them, where there are pustules or ulcers, clear the whiteness from it.

Pliny, book 29: eggs mixed with wool are placed on the forehead against watering eyes. Nor is anything else needed than white of egg poured in with powder of frankincense. Eggs too, by themselves, with the white poured in, check watering eyes and cool burning ones. For infants against eye discharge, with fresh butter mixed in, there is scarcely another remedy. The same, ground with oil, ease shingles, bound on with beet leaves. In the eyes, too, ingrown eyelashes are made to lie flat with ground and mixed gum-ammoniac in egg white. And pimples on the face, with pine kernels and a little honey mixed in. The face itself, smeared with these, does not need [further remedy]. Scalds from water, if covered at once with egg, do not develop blisters. Some also mix in barley flour and a little salt. For ulcers from burns, roasted barley with egg white and pig fat is wonderfully beneficial. The same treatment is used for ailments of the rear. For infants, too, if anything prolapses there. For cracks of the feet, egg white boiled with white lead to the weight of two denarii, an equal amount of litharge, then a little wine; for shingles, egg white ground with starch. They say too that wounds are glued shut with the white. And that stones are expelled by egg yolk cooked until it hardens, with a little saffron mixed in. Likewise, mixed with honey from woman's milk, applied, they ease pains of the eyes. Or with rose oil and honeyed wine, wool soaked and placed on the eyes; or with ground celery seed and barley meal applied in honeyed wine, the liquid yolk of an egg, swallowed so it does not touch the teeth, helps those coughing. It benefits fluxions of the chest and roughness of the throat, and is smeared on privately against the bite of hemorrhoids; the raw yolk too is sipped and benefits the kidneys, bladder, gnawing pains, ulcerations, and those coughing up blood. Five egg yolks are sipped in a measure of wine. For dysentery sufferers they are given with the broth of their own shell and poppy juice, or with wine. For celiac sufferers, with an equal weight of raisins and pomegranate rind, in equal portions over three days. And in another way, egg yolks ground with old lard and honey in quarter portions. Ground with three cups of old wine to the thickness of honey, and, when needed, drunk from water in the size of a hazelnut. Likewise fried with oil, three whole eggs soaked the day before in vinegar. Thus applied they also help those with a diseased spleen. For those coughing blood, three cups of mixture are used, and for bruises, if these are more longstanding, with bulbs and honey. Boiled eggs drunk with wine also stop women's menses; likewise raw ones, with oil, applied, [ease] swellings of the womb. They are also useful for pains of the neck, with goose fat and rose oil. Also for ailments of the rear, hardened by fire so as to be beneficial also by their heat, and for condylomas, with rose oil. Likewise for scalds, hardened in water then quickly in embers, the shells burnt and applied with yolk in rose oil. Whole yolks too are made, which they call 'sitista,' when after three days' incubation they are taken. Chicks in the egg strengthen a weakened stomach, with half a gall-nut, so that no other food is taken for two hours before. They are also given to dysentery sufferers, chicks boiled in the egg itself, mixed with a measure of dry wine and equally of oil and barley meal. The membrane pulled from the shell, whether raw or cooked, heals cracks of the lips. Shell ash too, drunk in wine, for hemorrhages of blood. It must be burnt without the membrane; thus a tooth-powder is also made. The same ash also stops women's menses, applied with myrrh. Whole eggs also aid childbirth, drunk in wine with rue and dill and cumin. They remove skin scabies and itching, mixed with oil and cedar resin. Also moist sores of the head, with cyclamen mixed in. For coughing up pus and blood, a raw egg with the juice of cut leek and an equal measure of Greek honey, warmed, is drunk. They are also given boiled and ground with honey to those coughing, and raw with raisin wine and oil in equal measure. Also poured in for defects of virility, singly with three parts raisin wine and half an ounce of starch, after baths. Against the bites of serpents, boiled and ground with cress added, they are applied. They soothe the swelling of the throat with heat as they pass through, and alone in food nourish without burdening, and together take the place of both wine and food. We have said that eggs soaked in vinegar have their shell softened; kneaded with flour into bread this way, celiac sufferers are restored. Some think it more useful to roast them thus dissolved in pans, by which method not only the bowels but also women's menses are checked. Or, if the flux is greater, raw eggs are drunk with flour in water, and by themselves their yolks, boiled from these, again in vinegar until they harden, and roasted again with ground pepper, to check the bowels. A special remedy is also made for dysentery sufferers, an egg poured into a new earthenware vessel, with an equal measure of the same egg's shell, so that all are equal, mixed with honey, then vinegar. Likewise mixed with oil and stirred frequently, whichever of these was finer, that will make the more effective remedy. Others, in the same measure instead of oil and vinegar, add red resin and wine, and temper it in another way, with an equal measure only of oil and two sixtieths of a denarius of pine bark, together with the grape they call 'rhus,' boiled together with five obols of honey, so that other food is taken only after four hours. Colic pains, too, are much helped by two eggs ground together with four fish fins and warmed in a measure of wine and so drunk.

Aristotle, in the same place: conception sometimes occurs in birds by itself, and they make wind-eggs. But this happens only in birds of much breeding, like hens and partridges. It does not happen in birds of good flight nor in birds of curved claws. Birds that lay from wind receive the wind in spring. Nor are there wind-eggs except because of the seminal matter that is in the females, and these are imperfect, since they lack the male's seed. Wind-eggs too, like other eggs, have two colors, and are more numerous than eggs suited for breeding, but smaller, since they are not complete. They are also of less pleasure when eaten because of their abundance, since what is digested in all things is sweeter and more pleasant; so too fish eggs are not completed without males. They say, moreover, that birds do not lay before mating once. But if they have mated once, they will always have eggs in them, but very small ones. For this reason some have said that wind-eggs come from the remainder of mating. But this is false. For we have seen young hens and geese, small ones, which had eggs without mating. Female 'cubeth,' that is partridges, too, whether or not they mate, are filled with eggs by smelling or hearing the voices of males. The female dove too mounts on the female, and if there is no male, they kiss one another in turn and from that mating make eggs, but do not breed chicks. For without the male's seed, eggs are not suited for conception. Wind-eggs, then, occur in hens, doves, partridges, peacocks, and even geese. Nor are they changed under them, but remain such as they are.

Pliny, book 10: doves alone, but also hens, partridges, peacocks, geese, fox-geese: sterile eggs, which we have called 'hypenemia,' that certain females conceive by mutual imagining of desire between themselves, or from dust. These are barren and smaller and of less pleasant taste and more moist. Some think they are even generated by the wind, whence they are also called 'zephyria.' These, however, occur only in spring. They are produced when left in the nest during brooding, which others called 'cynosura.'

Pliny, in the same: it is most useful for eggs to be brooded within ten days of being laid. Old or fresher ones are infertile. They should be placed in an odd number. On the fourth day after brooding begins, if, held up to the light with the tip of the egg grasped, that is, by hand, a pure and uniform color shines through, they are thought to be sterile and others should be substituted for them. But there is a test in water. For an empty one floats. And so they want full ones, that is 'silent' ones, to be set. But they forbid shaking them as a test, since if the vital veins are disturbed they will not breed. Brooding is given its start after the new moon, since those begun earlier do not succeed. In wood-pigeons, the female broods from afternoon into morning, but the male the rest of the time. Geese mate in water, and the females brood for only thirty days, twenty-five if it is warmer. They do not hatch others' eggs. The raven sometimes broods for five days and lays as many. Serpents too, except the viper, brood eggs woven together in the earth, and in the following year hatch their young. Crocodiles brood in turns, male and female. The male feeds the crow while she broods.

Aristotle: some female birds brood alone, and the male provides food for them. Others share the time of brooding, others even the eggs themselves, and some indeed the male broods, others the female. Turtledoves, however, the male and female both brood the eggs. Doves too brood them, the male by day, the female by night. The peacock mates with the female even while she is brooding the eggs. But the 'cubeth,' a lustful bird, if it finds the female's eggs, breaks them, so that the female will not be occupied with them. Yet the 'cubeth' itself, that is the partridge, sometimes makes two clutches of eggs, and the female broods one, the male the other. And when the shells are cracked, each of them will be attentive to their own chicks. If the hen does not brood over her eggs, they weaken and spoil. Sometimes, however, in a dung heap or in warm earth or even under a pillow or in a lap, they are brought to completion for hatching, as if a hen were brooding. There is a bird that does not brood her eggs, but wraps them in the hide of a fox or hare until they break open. Eggs that a hen broods in summer crack open in eighteen days, but in winter in twenty-five. The eagle and the goose and other large birds brood for thirty days. Medium ones for twenty, like the kite and the hawk. The eggs of four-footed creatures are warm and are completed by the heat of the earth, since they lay on the ground, and by the heat of the season, because of their sturdiness. And so, sitting on them, she does this not for brooding, as birds do, but for guarding. But the eggs of birds, because of their weakness, need warming.

Aristotle: birds of hooked claws, as said, have few eggs, and often one is found spoiled, because this is the manner of birds of hot nature. Finally, the first eggs of certain twice-laying birds are spoiled because of winter, and the later eggs are completed and produce chicks, as with the swallow. The hen too, as already said, if she does not brood over her eggs, they weaken and spoil. Thunder, moreover, occurring at the hour of brooding, spoils the eggs; in hot weather too they spoil, just as wine also becomes cloudy. This happens in both because of their earthy parts - in eggs because of the yolk, in wine because of the lees, which mix with it. And this rightly happens to birds that lay many eggs, since it is not easy for there to be sufficient heat in all of them. But it happens to birds of hooked claws, since they lay one or two eggs, and often one is spoiled. For the nature of the yolk is very hot in these, and, as it were, contrary to the nature of the white, and it moves toward the moisture that is in the white itself as if boiling.

Pliny: [eggs] are spoiled by the hearing of a hawk's voice. The remedy against thunder, however, is an iron nail placed beneath the straw of the eggs, or earth from a plough. Moreover they forbid shaking them as a test, since they will not breed, the vital veins being disturbed within.

Augustine: as already said above, when eggs are brooded by the winged creatures sitting over them, that warmth of the maternal body assists too in forming the chicks, through a certain affection of love proper to its kind.

Aristotle: eggs, when placed in the earth, warm and are completed by themselves, as in Egypt, since there they open the earth and place them in dung. Often, too, eggs are placed in warm vessels and chicks are hatched from them this way. The generation of chicks from eggs varies, moreover, according to time and the kinds of birds; in hens, after they have brooded, signs of the chick appear after three days, and in larger birds this happens after many days, in smaller ones after fewer. At this time the yolk rises toward the sharp end, to the place from which the crack begins, and there appears in the white something like a drop of blood, which is the heart and moves with the motion of a living thing. But when ten days of the chick's development have passed, the chick will be complete and all its parts will be evident. It has a head larger than its whole body, though its eyes do not yet see at that time. On the twentieth day the chick, as it were, pipes, and if the egg were moved, it would move. And when the egg is broken before the tenth day, its head is found above the right leg; before this time it is, as it were, sleeping, and its eyes tremble and it does not cry out, and in its eyes and heart is found a bubble, as if it were panting. And many eggs of hens and doves and other birds do not produce chicks even after mating.

Pliny: [as] they think of birds. They suppose this is first generated in every body. But inside the egg the head is larger than the whole body, the pressed-together eyes larger than the head; as the chick grows, the white is turned to the center, the yolk spreads around it, on the twentieth day if the egg is moved. And by then the voice of the living creature is heard within the shell. From that same time it grows feathers, positioned so that it has its head above its right foot. Its right wing is over its head; the yolk gradually diminishes. All birds are born feet-first, contrary to other animals.

Aristotle: thus, then, the generation of birds happens from eggs, when Aristotle sat over them and warmed them, since the animal comes out from one part of the egg and the rest receives growth: since indeed the creation of birds cannot be completed internally, nature placed the chick's food in the egg, namely the yolk, just as in an animal there is milk in the teat. For the beginning of the chick's generation is from the white of the egg, since the beginning of the soul is from heat, but its food is from the yellow-orange, that is the yolk. For the white is naturally moist, and in it is the heat of the soul. And the yellow-orange indeed congeals, but the white does not. And the first thing that is generated of the members is the heart and the great vein, from which a branching occurs into two umbilical cords, of which one proceeds to the membrane containing the yolk, the other to the membrane containing the wings, and is beneath the membrane of the shell. Through the one, then, the chick receives its food, from the yolk namely; the other extends and reaches to the membrane containing the chick and is likened to the afterbirth. The outer membrane, indeed, is bloody, since its arrangement is like the arrangement of the womb, and around the yolk is the afterbirth, the shell of the egg, and it is likened to the membrane containing the womb, as a covering, since it covers the embryo and the womb.

Aristotle: when, however, the chick has grown, the umbilicus diminishes, since the animal must exit from there. But the remainder of the yolk and of the umbilicus that reaches to the yolk comes out last, since the newborn must have food at once. And the yolk will still be inside with the umbilicus, because it cannot yet have food from the mother nor can it acquire food immediately. Chicks are completed quickly in warm days, since then the warm season aids the digestion of formation. But when, as said, the egg is broken before ten days, its head is found above the right leg. Long eggs of sharp head produce males, round and blunt ones produce females; and from eggs of two yolks, which come from two matings, if there is a membrane dividing between the seed of the first mating and the seed of the second, twin chicks are produced. But if it is continuous, the chick will be monstrous.
Isidore: 'pulli' [chicks] is the name given to all the newly born young of birds, since they are 'polluted' [defiled, from lying in the nest], whence also black clothing is called 'pullus.'

Pliny: but all birds are born feet-first, contrary to the other animals. It is reported, however, that the screech-owl, the horned owl, the woodpecker (which hollows out trees), the trogon, and the crow emerge from the egg tail-first, since, the eggs being tipped by the weight of the heads, they turn the hindquarters of their bodies toward the mother for warming.

Pliny: chicks are hatched more quickly on warm days. And so in summer the brood is brought forth on the nineteenth day, but in winter on the twenty-fifth; swallow chicks are blind at first, as are almost all those of a more numerous brood.

cit.quote: Pliny: whatever among animals is more intelligent has greater care for its offspring. And so, after completion, a bond remains between parents and children, as happens with men and with four-footed creatures. It is not usual for males to be attentive to their offspring, but females more so. Yet the dove, once she has bred, the male at once governs the chicks. And if the female is slow to return to them, the male strikes her and forces her to return to the nest. The eagle, however, casts out an egg or a chick, if more than two occur, and likewise the raven, but there is a bird that raises the eagle's cast-out chick, and one that raises the crow's chick. Likewise the eagle and all birds of hooked claws, as soon as they see their chicks able to fly, strike them with their wings and cast them from the nest, except the 'haum,' that is the crow, which is concerned for its chicks even after they fly. Birds of heavy flight, too, cast out their chicks, since it is heavy work for them to bring food. There is a bird that forces its chicks to look at the sun, and whichever one's eye waters first, it kills, and feeds the others with it. The vulture, being a ravenous bird, begrudges its chicks when they grow fat and does not feed them except from the remains of its own food, and casts them out even before they can fly. But there is a bird that raises those cast-out ones along with its own chicks.

Isaac Judaeus, on diets, book 1: chicks are of lighter digestion than other domestic winged creatures and generate praiseworthy blood, and are strengthening to the appetite and suited to all constitutions.
Vincentius Belvacensis, the compiler: what the nature of dove chicks is has been said above, where the dove was discussed. Let this suffice concerning birds.
